Turning the Altar into a Platform for Sustained Revival
Memory Verse: “The fire shall ever be burning upon the altar; it shall never go out.” Leviticus 6:13
Key Texts: Leviticus 6:12–13; 1 Timothy 4:12–16; 2 Timothy 4:1–5; Acts 20:28; Romans 12:1–2

Seminar Objectives:
 • Understand that the first responsibility of a minister is to keep the personal altar alive before attempting to revive
 a congregation.
 • Recognise the pressures faced by ministers who pursue genuine revival and preach the authentic gospel in
 difficult church environments.
 • Establish practical spiritual disciplines, accountability structures and support systems that preserve ministerial
 fire and integrity.
 • Maintain financial integrity, sexual purity, family stability and freedom from unhealthy dependence on
 individuals.
 • Use every posting, parish or ministry platform to lead people toward salvation, discipleship, holiness and
 sustained revival.

Introduction: Building a revival altar that never goes out even amid difficulties and challenges
The altar is more than the physical place from which a minister preaches. It represents the minister’s private walk with
God, personal consecration, prayer life, knowledge of Scripture and spiritual authority. A minister cannot consistently
produce publicly what does not exist in the secret place. This is especially important in The African church. A minister who
genuinely desires revival may discover that resistance can arise even from within the church, including from those who
prefer tradition to truth, and activity to genuine spiritual transformation. Some ministers also face inadequate or irregular
salary and poor welfare support for their families. Others experience fierce church politics, ungodly expectations,
discouragement, loneliness or opposition when they preach truths that confront sin.

Paul’s charge remains true for all seasons: “Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season…” (2 Timothy 4:2–3). The
deeper question for every minister on the altar is how to remain spiritually alive, emotionally stable, financially responsible,
morally pure and doctrinally sound enough for God to continually use the minister as a true altar and platform through
which people are brought to salvation and revival.

Key principles
(1) Keep your own altar burning: God’s instruction in Leviticus 6 is that the fire must not go out. Ministry activity must
never replace intimacy with God. Jesus Himself maintained a disciplined prayer life (Mark 1:35).

Practical guideline for sustained spiritual life
 • Daily prayer altar: Maintain consistent personal time with God that is not merely preparation for a sermon.
 • Daily Bible study: Follow an annual Bible-reading cycle with deliberate meditation and Scripture memorisation.
 Ministers can participate in the TACEF Read-the-Bible-in-One-Year cycle.
 • Weekly and monthly waiting: Maintain a weekly prayer and fasting discipline, with a regular extended period of
 waiting on God for renewal, direction and self-examination.
 • Continuous spiritual learning: Read sound Christian books, revival biographies, missionary literatures and
 ministry-development materials regularly.
 • Personal retreats: Create regular periods of intentional fasting retreats.
 • Pre-Sunday prayer discipline: Create good prayer time before Sunday service, with a recommended minimum
 target of about one to two hours of personal prayer and spiritual preparation. Always prepare for every message
 you preach. Never preach until there is a clear burden from the Lord. The congregation should encounter a
 minister who has first encountered God.

(2) Preach the Word even when it is not popular: “Take heed unto thyself, and unto the doctrine; continue in them” (1
Timothy 4:16). Every minister who wants to sustain an altar of revival must resist building ministry around what attracts
the largest crowd, what influential members want to hear, what produces the greatest financial response, or endless

 ~ 40 ~

ceremonies without spiritual substance. The altar must consistently call people toward Christ, repentance, salvation,
holiness, Christian character, and readiness for eternity.

Practical guideline for preaching the Word
 • Preach from prayer and a clear burden: Seek the Lord concerning what the congregation genuinely needs and
 minister as the Lord has burdened your heart at His feet.
 • Let Scripture govern the message: Build preaching on careful Bible study and the whole counsel of God, balancing
 salvation, grace, holiness, discipleship, Christian living and eternity.
 • Resist manipulation and personality-centred ministry: Do not flatter influential members, twist Scripture for
 financial response, exaggerate testimonies or use fear and sensational claims.
 • Preach truth with courage and love: Confront sin without bitterness or needless combativeness. Let biblical truth
 be spoken with compassion and love of Christ.

(3) Build a support system: One of the greatest dangers in any challenging ministry is isolation and loneliness. Every
minister pursuing a revival mandate needs relationships with other ministers who share the same burden. “Iron sharpeneth
iron” (Proverbs 27:17).

Practical guideline for building a strong support system
 • Be actively involved in MOTA: Every minister on the altar should intentionally participate in the TACEF Missionary
 on the Altar (MOTA) fellowship and its activities, like peer prayer sessions. MOTA should be a spiritual support
 community where ministers pray together, share ministry experiences, learn from more experienced ministers,
 receive encouragement, discuss difficult situations, correct one another in love and carry one another’s burdens.
 • Remain active in TACEF fellowship: Ministerial posting must never become an excuse for disconnecting from the
 fellowship that helped nurture one’s spiritual life. No matter how demanding church responsibilities become,
 remain deliberately connected to the local TACEF fellowship.
 • Build a local intercessory network: Prayerfully identify spiritually inclined and trustworthy believers within the
 church who you can meet to regularly meet to intercede together on salvation of souls, restoration of backsliders,
 the spiritual atmosphere of the church and genuine revival.

(4) Protect the integrity of the altar: A minister of God in The African Church must walk in discipline and caution with total
integrity to be a true platform of revival. Paul therefore warned, “Take heed unto thyself…” (1 Tim. 4:16). Clear boundaries
are essential to serve on the altar.

Practical guideline for ministerial integrity
 • Sexual purity: Avoid secret or emotionally dependent relationships, sexually suggestive communication and
 compromising one-on-one meetings. Maintain appropriate counselling boundaries and seek accountability
 immediately when inappropriate emotional attachment begins.
 • Financial integrity and unhealthy dependence: Keep all church funds, gifts and expenses transparent and
 properly accounted for. Avoid manipulative fundraising and preferential treatment based on gifts or support.
 Beware of becoming dependent on one wealthy or influential individual whose support may later become a bait
 for control, silence or compromise.
 • Personal accountability and relational boundaries: Have mature and trusted brethren who you submit to for
 accountability. Never allow ministry admiration to become emotional attachment or personal control.

(5) Protect your family and build sustainable support: Many sincere ministers in The African churches serve under
significant financial pressure. Some churches provide inadequate or irregular salary. Where church income is inadequate,
ministers should prayerfully and responsibly consider legitimate additional means of family support without breaking
church rules or compromising ministry. Paul sometimes worked with his own hands while fulfilling ministry (Acts 18:3; Acts
20:33–35). The aim is not materialism but sustainability and freedom from avoidable financial desperation.

Practical guideline for sustainable family support
 • Develop legitimate supplementary income where appropriate: Consider suitable business activity, agriculture,
 skilled services that is done at convenient time, or responsible investments that do not compromise ministry
 duties, church rules or integrity.
 • Plan finances with your spouse: Budget realistically, avoid a lifestyle you cannot afford, build emergency savings,
 and plan for children’s education and other family responsibilities.

 ~ 41 ~

• Strengthen the household income base: Where appropriate and mutually agreed, support your spouse in
 maintaining suitable employment, small business or another legitimate source of income that contributes to
 family wellbeing.
 • Avoid irresponsible borrowing: Do not allow debt, unpaid obligations or financial recklessness to discredit your
 testimony or place the family under avoidable pressure.

(6) Manage opposition and challenges: A revival-minded minister must expect moments of misunderstanding, criticism
and resistance. The goal is not to become combative, bitter or isolated, but to remain spiritually alert and emotionally
stable in challenging seasons.

Practical guideline for managing challenging times
 • Choose your battles prayerfully: Do not answer every accusation or fight every battle. Commit yourself to God
 in prayer and allow Him to defend you where necessary.
 • Reject entitlement and bitterness: Do not assume that the church owes you everything or that unmet
 expectations justify resentment. The God who called you remains your ultimate source.
 • Receive genuine correction: Distinguish persecution for truth from correction that should honestly be received.
 Humility is part of revival spirituality.
 • Keep integrity visible and real: Live in such a way that no one can accuse you on issues of integrity.
 • Seek mature counsel: Consult experienced and trusted ministers before making major confrontational decisions
 or taking steps that may have long-term consequences.
 • Respect church structures without diminishing the truth: Do not allow frustration with church committees or
 church councils to become disrespect, rebellion or a justification for excesses.
 • Let hardship deepen your altar: Allow pressure to sharpen discernment, strengthen prayer life and increase
 dependence on God rather than reduce spiritual discipline.
 • Measure ministry by spiritual fruit: Do not measure fulfilment in ministry by congregation size or popularity.
 Focus on seeing more people genuinely saved, young people being raised for Christ, homes becoming stronger,
 members becoming witnesses of Christ, etc.

Conclusion:
The great need of The African church is for God-sent ministers who will become platform for sustained revival as burning
altars. These are men and women who will refuse to become victims of church politics, financial recklessness, moral
compromise or sexual scandal. They remain connected to the Lord through a consistent personal walk with God in
consistent prayer life and fasting routine, connected to MOTA, active in TACEF fellowship, and intentional about protecting
their marriage and family.

They also guard their finances, maintain sexual purity, reject unhealthy dependency to certain “rich” people in the church,
study the Bible deeply, read continuously, and prepare spiritually before entering the pulpit. They remain faithful at their
duty post and preach the authentic gospel regardless of pressure from the church or their superiors. They are also prepared
for the difficult side of ministry. They have learned how to manage misunderstanding, financial hardship, resistance, and
opposition from within the church in such a way that these challenges drive them deeper into God rather than away from
Him because they know their calling and remain connected to the Lord who has called them to the ministry.

Knowing the Will of God for Life, Career and Marriage
Memory Verse: “Shew me thy ways, O Lord; teach me thy paths. Lead me in thy truth, and teach me: for thou art the God
of my salvation; on thee do I wait all the day.” Psalm 25:4–5

Key Texts: Romans 12:1–2; Ephesians 2:10; Psalm 16:5–6; John 10:27; Proverbs 3:5–6; Luke 22:42

Seminar Objectives:
 • Understand the will of God as an expression of His love, wisdom and purposeful leading for every believer.
 • Distinguish God’s sovereign, revealed, perfect and permissive will, and understand the believer’s responsibility to
 choose obedience.
 • Recognise modern pressures, personal desires and human influences that can distort major decisions in life, career
 and marriage.
 • Apply biblical principles and safe discernment practices when seeking God’s direction through Scripture, prayer,
 counsel, providence and other channels.
 • Respond to God’s leading with surrender, faith, patience and obedience even when His path is costly or contrary
 to popular opinion.

Introduction: Christian ife is not a game of trial and error
The life of a believer is never designed to be a game of trial and error. God knows the end from the beginning and desires
to lead His people as a shepherd leads sheep into the pasture prepared for them. Scripture presents our lives as purposeful
rather than accidental. For we are God’s workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works which God prepared
beforehand that we should walk in them (Ephesians 2:10). The Psalmist could therefore say, “The LORD is the portion of
mine inheritance and of my cup: thou maintainest my lot” (Psalm 16:5). God does not promise that every step will be easy,
but He does promise His presence, wisdom and ability to work even difficult circumstances for the good of those who love
Him (Romans 8:28).

This truth is especially important in today’s world. Social media and digital world constantly present new ambitions,
lifestyles, careers, relationships and definitions of success. Comparison and competition can make people feel late,
inadequate or pressured to follow what is trending. Parents, friends, mentors and motivational voices may also have strong
opinions about what is “best” for us. Yet the believer’s deepest question must remain: “Lord, what wilt thou have me to
do?” (Acts 9:6). The will of God is an expression of His love so that we are not lost in a maze of attractive but distracting
options. Our posture must remain that of Jesus: “Nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done.” (Luke 22:42).
Key principles
(1) Understand what the will of God means: Knowing God’s will begins with understanding that God has both a revealed
purpose for all believers and personal leading for the stewardship of each life. His will is the outworking of His character,
Word, purpose and shepherding in our lives.

A biblical framework for understanding God’s will
 • God’s sovereign will: This refers to what God in His authority purposes and ultimately accomplishes. His counsel
 cannot be frustrated by human power (Daniel 4:35; Isaiah 46:9–10).
 • God’s revealed or moral will: This is what Scripture clearly commands for every believer. E.g. holiness, truth, love,
 purity, justice, thanksgiving and obedience. We do not need a special revelation to obey what God has already
 written (1 Thessalonians 4:3; Micah 6:8).
 • God’s perfect and personal leading: Within biblical boundaries, God guides individuals concerning assignments,
 timing, career, ministry, relationships and other major decisions. Romans 12:2 describes the will of God as “good,
 and acceptable, and perfect,” while Ephesians 2:10 reminds us that there are good works prepared for us to walk
 in.
 • God’s permissive will: This shows that God sometimes allows people to insist on choices that are not His best
 desire for them, with real consequences (1 Samuel 8:4–22). God calls us to choose obedience because He will
 never force His will on us (Joshua 24:15).

 ~ 43 ~

(2) Make surrender the starting point: The greatest obstacle to knowing God’s will is often not that God is silent, but that
our own will is already loud. We may pray for direction after secretly deciding the answer we want. A surrendered heart is
willing to receive “yes,” “no,” “wait,” “leave,” “stay,” or a completely different path from the one it imagined.

Practical guideline for a surrendered heart
 • Build relationship before seeking answers: Jesus said, “My sheep hear my voice” (John 10:27). Learn God’s
 character through consistent fellowship rather than seeking Him only at moments of decision.
 • Present yourself before presenting your request: Romans 12:1–2 places surrender before discernment. Ask God
 not merely to approve your plan but to transform your desires and thinking.
 • Identify the idols in the decision: Be honest about family approval, fear of being left behind, social status, location,
 comfort or personal ambition that may already be controlling your preference
 • Adopt the posture of Christ: Make “not my will, but Yours” a genuine prayer. God’s perfect will may not be the
 most popular, glamorous or immediately comfortable option, but obedience positions us for the life He has
 designed.

(3) Resist the pressures that compete with divine direction: The modern believer makes decisions in a noisy environment.
What is trending can quickly become what we assume is desirable, and what others celebrate can become the standard by
which we judge our own lives. Comparison can therefore create a false urgency to marry, relocate, change career, pursue
money or accept opportunities before we have heard from God.

Practical guideline for managing competing voices
 • Do not let social media define your destiny: Online visibility shows selected contents that are not actually real,
 not the full story of people’s lives. Do not build life decisions around another person’s timeline, title, income,
 marriage, relocation or success story (2 Corinthians 10:12).
 • Respect counsel without surrendering responsibility: Parents, mentors and spiritual leaders can provide wisdom,
 but no human adviser should replace your personal responsibility to seek God. Motivation is not divine direction.
 • Do not confuse majority opinion with God’s voice: The fact that everyone believes an option is sensible does not
 make it God’s specific path for you. Israel once demanded a king because surrounding nations had one (1 Samuel
 8:5).
 • Count the cost of obedience: God’s will may require waiting, turning down an attractive offer, entering an
 unfashionable field, remaining faithful in an unnoticed season or refusing a relationship that others approve.

(4) Know the biblical process of discerning God’s will: God can guide through several means. Major decisions require
spiritual alertness, Scripture, prayer, time and testing. God is not the author of confusion, and genuine leading will never
require us to violate His revealed Word.

Practical channels of guidance and the cautions required
 • The Word of God: Scripture is the first and final test. No dream, prophecy, desire, relationship or opportunity that
 contradicts God’s Word can be called His will (Psalm 119:105). For example, God will not lead a believer to break
 a valid marriage covenant to marry a person who is already lawfully married to someone else.
 • Prayer, fasting and waiting: Seek God deliberately and give major decisions enough time. The caution is to avoid
 turning prayer into repeated requests for God to endorse a decision already made.
 • Inner witness and peace: The Spirit can give settled conviction and peace (Colossians 3:15), but peace alone may
 be wrong. Familiarity, excitement or avoidance can also feel peaceful; therefore test inner impressions by the Holy
 Spirit, time and counsel from many witnesses.
 • Godly counsel: There is safety in mature counsel (Proverbs 15:22). Choose people who know God, understand you
 and are free from selfish interest. Counsel should confirm and sharpen discernment, not manipulate you or make
 the decision for you. TACEF Professional Fellowship may be a channel for counsel for professional leadings and
 TACEF MOTA can provide structured counsel for those who feel lead into or out of ministry/College of Theology
 • Gifts, burdens and abilities: Natural capacities and recurring spiritual burdens may reveal areas God has been
 preparing. A naturally caring person may discover a path in healthcare or service; a strong analytical gift may point
 toward engineering These are clues to prayer over, not automatic commands.
 • Providence, opportunities and interruptions: God can use transfers, closed doors, unexpected meetings, retreats,
 delays and unplanned opportunities to redirect or prepare us. However, not every open door is God’s will and not
 every obstacle means “no.” Test all circumstances.

 ~ 44 ~

• Dreams, visions, prophecy and inner witness: God can speak in diverse ways, but these must be tested by
 Scripture, spiritual fruit, mature counsel and time (1 Thessalonians 5:20–21). Never use “God told me” to pressure
 another person, especially in marriage, or to bypass wisdom and consent.

(5) Apply divine direction to life, career and marriage: The same God who leads us spiritually is interested in how we
steward our whole lives. In every area, the believer must seek God sincerely, test every impression by Scripture, and
patiently discern the path that best aligns with His will and purpose.

Practical guideline for major life decisions
 • For life and purpose: Begin with what is already clear, that is, you were created for God’s glory and for good works
 prepared in Christ (Isaiah 43:7; Ephesians 2:10). Ask what God is forming in you, whom He has burdened you to
 serve, and what gifts He has entrusted to you.
 • For career: Consider biblical integrity, God-given abilities, competence, opportunities, burdens, service and long-
 term stewardship, not just salary, status or what is currently fashionable. A career can change across seasons while
 the deeper divine purpose remains. Prepare diligently for the path God is opening because spiritual leading does
 not excuse poor training or lack of excellence.
 • For marriage: Start with clear biblical boundaries: salvation, godly character and freedom from unequal yoking (2
 Corinthians 6:14). Pray, seek wise counsel and allow divine conviction. Follow the TACEF marital process for step-
 by-step guide. Attraction, family pressure, age anxiety, or one person’s claim that “God said” must never replace
 discernment and the other person’s free consent.

(6) After knowing God’s will, obey and trust His pathway: Knowing is not the end of guidance. God reveals His will so that
we can walk in it. Every believer must therefore move from discernment to obedience, while accepting that the path may
contain waiting, preparation, opposition and unexpected turns.

Practical guideline for walking in God’s will
 • Obey what is clear: Delayed obedience can become disobedience. When God’s direction is settled and
 convincingly confirmed, respond faithfully (John 14:21).
 • Trust without demanding the full map: Abraham obeyed without knowing every detail of the journey (Hebrews
 11:8). Proverbs 3:5–6 calls us to trust the LORD with all our heart rather than leaning only on our own
 understanding.
 • Respect God’s timing: A correct direction pursued at the wrong time can still create difficulty. Wait when God says
 wait, prepare while waiting, and do not manufacture fulfilment through anxiety or manipulation (Habakkuk 2:3).
 • Do not abandon the path because it becomes difficult: Opposition, delay or sacrifice is not automatic proof that
 you missed God. At the same time, remain humble enough to review your assumptions when Holy Spirit prompting
 and mature counsel reveal that you were wrong.
 • Trust God with interruptions and recovery: Even when our choices or circumstances depart from what God
 desired, He remains able to redeem surrendered lives and work through repentance, correction and renewed
 obedience. His shepherding is greater than our mistakes.

Conclusion: “Not my will, but Yours be done”
The safest place for a believer is not the place with the highest salary, loudest applause, easiest path or strongest human
approval but it is the place of obedience to God. The Lord who made us knows our frame, our future, the people we will
meet, the work prepared for us and the path by which our lives can fully glorify Him. He gives us intelligence to reason,
make choices but He does not ask us to make our understanding the final authority. We plan responsibly while remaining
interruptible by God.

Therefore, refuse the pressure to live by comparison or trial and error. Renew your mind in Scripture, maintain a consistent
relationship with Christ, pray until your will is surrendered, seek godly counsel, test every leading carefully, allow time to
expose false leadings, and obey what God makes clear. Whether the issue is life purpose, career, ministry, location or
marriage, let the governing prayer remain: “Not my will, but Yours be done.” The Shepherd who knows the end from the
beginning is able to lead His sheep into the path He has prepared and to make their lives count for His glory.

Pursuing Academic Excellence as a Christian Student
Memory Verse: “Seest thou a man diligent in his business? he shall stand before kings; he shall not stand before mean
men.” Proverbs 22:29

Key Texts: Daniel 1:17–20; Proverbs 18:15; Proverbs 22:29; Luke 14:28; Colossians 3:23–24; 2 Timothy 2:15; Matthew
5:14–16

Seminar Objectives:
 • Understand education as a stewardship, a present revival duty post and an opportunity to represent Christ through
 both excellence and character.
 • Set clear academic performance targets and translate them into realistic semester, weekly and daily study plans.
 • Identify the study methods, learning conditions and support systems that help each student understand, retain
 and apply knowledge most effectively.
 • Build disciplined academic habits, use technology and AI with integrity, and recover intelligently when
 performance falls below target.
 • Choose relationships that provoke excellence without compromising faith, while balancing academics, TACEF
 fellowship, health, campus witness and preparation for life after school.

Introduction: Education is a stewardship, not merely a certificate
Academic life is one of the important duty posts where a Christian student is expected to glorify God through diligence,
competence, integrity and godly character. Daniel and his friends did not choose between spiritual conviction and
intellectual excellence. They remained faithful to God and were found ten times better in matters of wisdom and
understanding (Daniel 1:17–20). A Christian student should therefore reject the false choice between being spiritually
serious and academically excellent.

For a TACEFite, school is more than a place to obtain grades or certificates. It is a Place of Primary Assignment where the
student should learn seriously, prepare for future usefulness, witness for Christ and demonstrate the disciplined life of a
revival soldier. Fellowship activities must also not become an excuse for poor academic performance, just as academic
pressure must not become an excuse for abandoning spiritual life, fellowship or Christian character.

Academic excellence is also more than “reading hard.” It requires clear performance expectations, intelligent planning,
knowledge of how one learns most effectively, disciplined execution, honest review and willingness to adjust. Jesus said
that anyone intending to build a tower should first sit down and count the cost (Luke 14:28). In the same way, a student
who desires a particular score, grade or GPA should understand what that target will require and build a daily system
capable of producing it.

Key principles

(1) See education as stewardship and your present duty post: God has entrusted every student with time, ability, access
to books, technology and opportunities for development. These resources should be managed faithfully. Academic
excellence should therefore be pursued as service to God, not merely for status, parental approval or competition. The
aim is to become competent enough for God to use while remaining visibly Christian in conduct.

Practical guideline for a student-steward
 • Take your present assignment seriously: Attend classes regularly and punctually, complete assignments, prepare
 before lectures and refuse the habit of doing only what is necessary to pass.
 • Study your Bible and study your books: Build a schedule that protects both your walk with God and serious
 academic work. Prayer cannot replace preparation, and preparation should not eliminate your daily quiet time of
 fellowship with God.
 • Let your result and character agree: Good grades without integrity are not Christian excellence; strong Christian
 living with academic carelessness is also a poor testimony.
 • Use the campus as a mission field: Let classmates know your convictions through your conduct, relationships,
 reliability and willingness to share Christ appropriately.

 ~ 46 ~

• Remain connected to TACEF: Participate responsibly in campus fellowship while learning to plan ahead so that
 spiritual commitments and academic responsibilities are not unnecessarily placed in conflict.

(2) Set clear performance targets and count the cost: Excellence becomes easier to manage when the desired result is
defined. A student should not enter a term or semester with only the vague hope of “doing well.” Set an expected score
or grade for each subject or course and, where applicable, an expected GPA or CGPA for the semester. Then work
backwards from the target to the effort, resources and time required. “Which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not
down first, and counteth the cost?” (Luke 14:28).

A practical performance-planning system
 • Define the target: Write the score or grade you are aiming for in each subject/course and the overall GPA or
 performance level you want for the term or semester. Trust the Lord and do your best.
 • Count the cost: Ask what the target requires in daily study time, assignments, practical work, tutorials, past
 questions, revision and help with difficult topics.
 • Translate targets into a timetable: Break the semester into monthly or weekly learning goals and convert them
 into specific daily reading and practice periods. A target without a schedule is only a wish.
 • Track leading indicators, not only final grades: Monitor class attendance, completed topics, practice-question
 performance, assignment scores and weak areas early enough to make corrections.
 • Recalibrate when you miss a target: Do not allow one poor test, grade or semester to become a verdict on your
 ability. Diagnose what went wrong, adjust the target or method where necessary, strengthen the plan and
 continue. The principle is to keep setting a standard that stretches you without turning the target into a trap that
 destroys confidence when you miss it.

(3) Know how you learn best and build disciplined study systems: Students do not all learn most effectively under the
same conditions. “Know thyself” academically by identifying the study environment and methods that consistently help
you understand, remember and apply what you are learning. Do not copy another student’s method. At the same time,
avoid rigid labels; use evidence from your actual performance to identify what works best for different subjects and tasks.

Practical guideline for effective learning
 • If you learn best alone, protect focused individual study: Do not spend hours in a study group that becomes
 conversation, distraction or social activity simply because others prefer group reading.
 • If discussion helps you, use a serious study group: Work with disciplined students who solve problems, compare
 answers, explain difficult concepts and keep one another accountable.
 • If visual explanation helps, find the right teaching videos: Search by the exact topic or learning objective, use
 credible educational channels, compare explanations and pause to solve examples yourself rather than watching
 passively.
 • Maximise classroom explanation/lecture time: Sit where you can concentrate, take structured notes, ask
 questions and, where school rules and the lecturer permit, use a small recorder or approved device to revisit
 difficult explanations later.
 • Use active methods: Practise active recall, solve past examination questions, explain concepts without looking at
 your notes, use spaced revision and test yourself repeatedly instead of only rereading.
 • Seek help early: Ask lecturers, teachers, tutors or better classmates when a topic remains unclear. Do not allow
 one weak concept to become the foundation for several other weak topics.
 • Manage distraction deliberately: During lectures and study periods, control WhatsApp, social media, short videos,
 gaming and unnecessary notifications. Focus is an academic advantage.

(4) Use technology and AI to increase learning and not destroy integrity: Technology gives today’s student access to
explanations, simulations, past questions, practice tests, online courses, internships and global learning opportunities.
Used wisely, these tools can accelerate understanding but when used dishonestly, they can produce plagiarism, laziness
and false achievement. Christian integrity must therefore govern the use of AI, smart devices and online resources.

Practical guideline for technology with integrity
 • Use AI as a tutor, not a substitute for thinking: Ask for explanations of difficult concepts, alternative examples,
 practice questions, study plans or feedback, then work through the material yourself.
 • Verify what technology gives you: AI and online sources can be wrong. Check important facts, calculations and
 references against textbooks, course materials or reliable sources.

 ~ 47 ~

• Respect academic rules: Do not submit AI-generated work dishonestly as your own, fabricate references, copy
 another person’s work or use prohibited tools during examinations and tests.
 • Use technology to deepen understanding: Educational videos, simulations, digital flashcards, online worksheets
 and practice platforms can help you master difficult concepts when used intentionally.
 • Explore legitimate opportunities: Use the internet to find internships, fellowships, project opportunities,
 competitions, virtual work exposure and learning programmes that strengthen your future preparation and work
 readiness.

(5) Choose environments that provoke excellence without compromising faith: The people around a student influence
punctuality, discipline, ambition, and academic standards. Proverbs teaches that walking with the wise makes one wise.
Intentionally stay close to students whose habits challenge you upward: those who attend class on time, take assignments
seriously, ask intelligent questions, perform well in coursework and pursue excellence. However, academic advantage must
never become a reason to compromise Christian conviction.

Practical guideline for relationships and character
 • Choose peers who raise your standards: Learn from high-performing and disciplined students, not merely from
 people who make you comfortable.
 • Admire excellence without unhealthy comparison: Another student’s result should provoke learning and
 improvement, not envy, inferiority or desperation.
 • Never borrow ungodly methods: Do not join cheating networks, exam malpractice, leaked-question groups,
 online fraud, substance misuse or immoral relationships because the people involved appear successful.
 • Protect your Christian identity: Do not become ashamed of Christ, TACEF or biblical convictions in order to fit into
 academically influential circles.
 • Guard against performance anxiety: Your grade is important, but it is not your identity. Let high standards push
 you toward disciplined effort, not fear, dishonesty or self-condemnation.

(6) Balance academics, spiritual life, health, mission and future preparation: Sustained excellence requires a whole-life
system. Poor sleep, unmanaged stress, unhealthy relationships, excessive fellowship activity (e.g. daily long hour vigils),
social-media addiction or poor time planning can undermine good academic intentions. The Christian student should
therefore learn to plan the whole season of life, not only examinations.

Practical guideline for sustainable excellence
 • Protect sleep and health: Consistent sleep, appropriate nutrition, exercise and rest support concentration and
 memory. Do not make chronic sleep deprivation your normal study strategy.
 • Plan around TACEF activities early: Know fellowship, Convention, outreach, subzonal/zonal events and leadership
 commitments in advance and adjust study schedules to plan for your academic and spiritual lives
 • Stay connected during transitions: Remain connected to the local fellowship during holidays, industrial
 attachment, pre-NYSC, NYSC and the Back-from-NYSC stage rather than disappearing spiritually during transitions.
 • Prepare for life after school: Be actively aligned to TACEF CCMT leadership for guidance, Son of Purpose, NYSC
 Fellowship and the TACEF Professional Fellowship to seek mentors, internships, projects, professional skills, CV
 development and career exploration.
 • Review yourself periodically: At least monthly, ask whether you are growing academically, spiritually, physically
 and relationally. Correct imbalance before it becomes failure.
 • Keep the ultimate purpose clear: Seek academic excellence so that you can become a competent, trustworthy
 and useful agent of revival in your generation, while shining as a light for Christ wherever He places you.

Conclusion:
Christian academic excellence is not simply the pursuit of high grades but a disciplined stewardship of opportunity under
the lordship of Christ. The excellent Christian student sets clear targets, counts the cost, knows the study methods that
work, plans time carefully, practises consistently, uses technology responsibly, seeks help early and refuses dishonest
shortcuts.

Do not be discouraged when a target is missed. Review the result, understand the gap, recalibrate the plan and set another
standard that keeps stretching you. Learn from people who provoke you to excellence, but never borrow success at the
price of your faith or character. Let your spiritual life, academic result, integrity, relationships and future preparation
increasingly tell the same story: that Christ has raised a disciplined student who can be trusted with greater responsibility.

 ~ 48 ~

Managing Personal Finance and Family Finances with Godly Wisdom
Memory Verse: “Through wisdom is an house builded; and by understanding it is established.” Proverbs 24:3

Key Texts: 1 Chronicles 29:11-14; Psalm 24:1; Proverbs 3:9-10; Proverbs 6:6-8; Proverbs 24:3-4; Luke 12:13-21; Luke 16:10-
11; 1 Corinthians 4:2; 2 Corinthians 9:6-8; 1 Timothy 6:6-10

Seminar Objectives:
 • Understand personal and family finances as stewardship of resources that ultimately belong to God.
 • Understand biblical principles of diligence, productive capacity, contentment and responsible prosperity.
 • Build practical systems for budgeting, spending, saving and planning for irregular or future obligations.
 • Manage debt, emergencies, family pressures and contemporary financial risks with wisdom.
 • Develop financial literacy and invest responsibly without greed, speculation or fraudulent shortcuts.
 • Build a biblical culture of generosity, transparent family financial planning and accountable Kingdom giving.

Introduction: Stewarding rightly, managing wisely
Financial wisdom begins with the conviction that what we possess is ultimately entrusted to us by God. “The earth is the
Lord’s, and the fulness thereof” (Psalm 24:1). Income, opportunities, skills, property and other resources should therefore
be managed as a stewardship, not merely consumed as personal possessions. This perspective affects how we earn,
budget, spend, save, invest, give and account for what has been placed in our care.

Many personal and family financial crises are not caused only by low income. They may also be worsened by poor planning,
impulsive spending, debt, pressure to maintain certain public perception, irregular salaries, inflation, extended-family
responsibilities, emergencies, or fraudulent investment schemes. A person can receive more money and still remain
financially unstable if waste and poor decisions continue.

Biblical financial wisdom therefore combines faith in God with diligence, contentment, planning, generosity and
accountability. Godly stewardship is not a promise that every faithful Christian will become materially wealthy but a call to
manage faithfully whatever God entrusts to us, grow our productive capacity, provide responsibly, avoid greed and use
resources for His purposes and the good of people.

Key principles

(1) Steward divine resources: I do not own them; I manage them: Faithful financial management begins when we
recognise God as the ultimate owner and ourselves as stewards. “Moreover it is required in stewards, that a man be found
faithful” (1 Corinthians 4:2). This mindset produces accountability, contentment and restraint. It helps a believer resist
waste, impulse spending and pressure to impress others because every resource must be used with purpose.

Practical guideline for faithful stewardship
 • Put God first: Let your relationship with God shape how you earn, spend, save, invest and give.
 • Be faithful with little: Manage small resources responsibly rather than waiting for a larger income before
 becoming disciplined.
 • Track what comes in and what goes out: Review personal and family income and expenses regularly so that
 financial decisions are based on facts, not assumptions.
 • Keep fellowship and church funds completely separate: Never treat TACEF or church money in your care as an
 informal personal loan. Follow the required financial accountability and reporting processes.
 • Practise contentment without complacency: Be grateful for what God has provided while continuing to build
 capacity and pursue legitimate opportunities for growth.
 • Avoid waste and impulse spending: A purchase may be affordable and still be unnecessary. Let purpose and
 budget guide spending. Do not be deceived by promotion and discounted sales offers.
 • Keep a generous heart: Stewardship is not selfish accumulation. Remain sensitive to genuinely needy brethren,
 vulnerable families and legitimate ministry needs.

 ~ 49 ~

(2) Pursue productive capacity, diligence and contentment: Scripture consistently honours diligence and warns against
laziness. The ability to earn more usually requires increased capacity to create value. Prayer and faith do not replace
learning, work, building skills, going the extra mile with legitimate additional income generating streams, competence or
responsible effort. At the same time, financial ambition must remain under godliness and contentment. The desire for
wealth must not become the measure of spiritual success or personal worth.

Practical guideline for productive and godly prosperity
 • Acknowledge God as the source: Deuteronomy 8:18 reminds us that God gives power to get wealth. Work
 diligently without becoming self-sufficient or proud.
 • Build capacity for the next level: Identify skills, qualifications, business knowledge or professional competence
 required to create greater value and improve earning capacity.
 • Do not wait idly for a “perfect” opportunity: Where appropriate, learn a trade, reach out to do any work available
 if the best has not come, volunteer for experience or begin small while preparing for greater responsibility.
 • Let grace produce labour, not laziness: Paul could say, “I laboured more abundantly… yet not I, but the grace of
 God” (1 Corinthians 15:10).
 • Guard against comparison and lifestyle pressure: Do not borrow or overspend merely to look successful before
 friends, relatives, colleagues or brethren.
 • Remain content: Pursue growth without allowing money to become an idol, a source of anxiety or the basis of
 your identity.

(3) Budget, spend and save with foresight: Planning turns good intentions into financial discipline. Proverbs points us to
the ant, which prepares ahead. A budget simply gives every expected income a purpose before it is spent. It also helps a
family distinguish necessities from wants, prepare for future obligations and identify wasteful leakages before they become
crises.

Practical guideline for budgeting and saving
 • Prepare a monthly budget before spending: List expected income, giving (putting God first in your tithe, offering
 and other kingdom seed, then your immediate family, your parents, savings as a gift to your future needs, the
 household of faith (brethren/ministers/missions) and general charity), essential expenses, savings and planned
 discretionary spending.
 • Plan for irregular income: If income is seasonal, delayed or unpredictable, build the budget around conservative
 expectations and prioritise essentials.
 • Convert annual obligations into monthly plans: Rent, school fees, hospital bills for a new baby and other
 predictable payments should not become emergencies simply because they are not monthly.
 • Build an emergency fund gradually: Create a financial buffer for genuine emergencies, especially where salary
 delays, health costs or family responsibilities are common.
 • Spend according to your resources: Do not buy every “aso ebi,” latest gadgets/device, trip or social obligation
 when you do not have it. Do not live to impress people and destroy yourself
 • Save consistently: Develop the habit of setting aside part of income rather than spending everything that comes
 in.
 • Plan transparently as a couple: Spouses should have honest conversations about income, debt, obligations,
 savings, giving and major spending. Avoid secret financial lives within marriage.

(4) Manage debt, emergencies, family pressure and contemporary financial risks: Godly wisdom requires a realistic
understanding of obligations and risk. Repeated spending above income, expensive digital app loans, unplanned extended-
family demands, medical emergencies, betting and get-rich-quick schemes can rapidly destabilise personal and family
finances. Debt should never become the normal solution to a lifestyle that has not been adjusted to reality.

Practical guideline for managing financial pressure
 • Keep recurring expenses below sustainable income: If expenditure consistently exceeds income, reduce costs,
 increase legitimate income or do both.
 • Use debt cautiously: Avoid borrowing for appearances, consumption or speculative investments. Understand the
 interest, fees and repayment obligations before taking any loan. If you borrow, use it for asset and not liability
 with a clear plan to pay back.

 ~ 50 ~

• Be cautious with digital loan apps: Easy access to short-term credit can become a cycle of high-cost borrowing if
 repayment depends on another loan.
 • Plan for health costs: Use employer health coverage, an HMO or another suitable health-insurance arrangement
 where available, while we continue to trust the Lord for perfect health
 • Set healthy boundaries around extended-family responsibilities: Be generous within your capacity, but do not
 destroy your own household finances trying to meet every request.
 • Reject betting, Ponzi schemes and fraudulent “investment” opportunities: High promised returns, pressure to
 recruit others or unclear sources of profit are major warning signs.
 • Seek help early: Where debt has become unmanageable, speak with a competent and trustworthy adviser rather
 than hiding the problem.

(5) Build financial literacy and invest without greed or speculation: Knowledge helps a steward make better decisions.
Basic understanding of income, expenditure, assets, liabilities, cash flow, interest, inflation, risk and return makes it easier
to evaluate financial choices. Investment can be part of wise stewardship, but no Christian should invest merely because a
friend, church member or respected believer recommends an opportunity.

Practical guideline for financial literacy and responsible investing
 • Learn the basics: Take a credible course, read reliable financial materials and understand the language of personal,
 family and business finance.
 • Understand before you invest: Know what the investment does, how returns are generated, what risks exist, how
 liquid it is and who regulates or manages it.
 • Use qualified advice where necessary: For stocks, bonds, treasury instruments, real estate or other investments,
 seek appropriate professional guidance rather than acting on rumours.
 • Diversify and match risk to your circumstances: Do not put essential household money, school fees or emergency
 savings into highly speculative opportunities.
 • Never fabricate certainty: Every investment carries some form of risk. Be suspicious of “guaranteed” extraordinary
 returns.
 • Teach children age-appropriate financial wisdom: Introduce saving, budgeting, generosity and the difference
 between needs and wants early.

(6) Build a Kingdom culture of giving and family financial harmony: Generosity is part of Christian stewardship, but biblical
giving is cheerful, voluntary and free from manipulation. TACEF has a culture of responding to genuine ministry needs,
supporting brethren through accountable welfare scheme and sowing as led by the Lord, while maintaining transparency.
Giving should flow from love and obedience, not competition, public recognition or pressure.

Practical guideline for Kingdom generosity
 • Make giving part of your financial plan: Give intentionally rather than only from what remains after every other
 desire has been satisfied.
 • Give from love, gratitude and conviction: Do not give because you have been frightened, manipulated or
 promised a guaranteed financial return.
 • Give as led by the Lord, not by comparison: Another person’s amount should not determine yours.
 • Support genuine needs responsibly: Be generous to people in real need while respecting TACEF welfare and
 accountability processes designed to prevent abuse.
 • Keep giving and family responsibility in healthy balance: A married believer should not create avoidable hardship
 at home through secret or reckless financial commitments.
 • Let generosity remain discreet where possible: Resist the desire for public recognition as proof of spirituality.

Conclusion: There is nothing we have that we have not received
Everything entrusted to us ultimately comes from God. Faithful stewardship therefore begins with recognising Him as
owner and ourselves as managers. It continues through diligent work, growing productive capacity, contentment,
budgeting, saving, responsible investing, generosity and honest family financial planning.

 ~ 51 ~

The goal of kingdom financial discipline is not to accumulate more money but to become trustworthy with whatever God
places in our hands. A financially wise TACEFite should be increasingly free from waste, manipulation, fraudulent shortcuts
and avoidable debt, while becoming more capable of providing responsibly, supporting legitimate Kingdom work and
helping people in genuine need.

Growing in Personal, Professional, Business, and Career Effectiveness
Memory Verse: “And beside this, giving all diligence, add to your faith virtue; and to virtue knowledge; and to knowledge
temperance; and to temperance patience; and to patience godliness; and to godliness brotherly kindness; and to brotherly
kindness charity” (2 Peter 1:5–8)

Key Texts: 2 Peter 1:5–8; 2 Timothy 2:15; 2 Timothy 3:17; Genesis 1:28; Ezekiel 37:1–14

Seminar Objectives:
 • Understand whole-person growth as a fundamental aspect of Christian stewardship and covenant responsibility.
 • Recognise the specific demands and expectations of your present career or professional stage.
 • Learn to conduct an annual skills-gap assessment to identify personal strengths, weaknesses and targeted growth
 areas.
 • Know how to build competence, digital/AI literacy, exposure, mentorship and professional standards.
 • Develop critical soft skills, including communication, elocution, emotional intelligence, workplace etiquette and
 leadership.
 • Understand Christian walk, work and life balance in the pursuit of marketplace excellence and career progression
 without compromising Christian character, family commitments or spiritual vitality.

Introduction: A Thoroughly Furnished TACEF Professional
Our God is an excellent God and expects His children to exhibit the same character of excellence in their personal,
professional, career and business lives. Spirituality is not an excuse for mediocrity. Daniel was very spiritual and yet had a
phenomenal career. As New Testament believers, we cannot do less. As workplace demands become more challenging
and dynamic, with organisations looking for solution providers, the expectation of heaven is that the inspiration of the
Almighty deep within us will find expression through our skills to deliver exceptional results. However, this cannot happen
when our current skill sets are obsolete and at variance with the challenges of our world. It takes a thoroughly furnished
professional to interpret complex puzzles. This means that there is a need to grow in every area of our lives - personal,
professional, career and business - as we navigate the marketplace with wisdom, diligence and excellence.

Our anchor text in 2 Peter 1:5–8 reminds us that faith is only the beginning and that we have to intentionally add virtue,
knowledge, self-discipline, etc. to it. This is the whole idea behind the TACEF Professional Fellowship, a development
platform where professionals in the Great House converge to deepen their growth using the 4Cs of a TACEF Professional:
Calling, Character, Competence and Capacity. This seminar is therefore designed to ignite our hunger for effective growth
in our personal, career and business lives as we transform our daily work into an instrument of revival by moving from
passive survival to dominant excellence in our profession, career and business.

1. Understanding Whole-Person Growth as Christian Stewardship: Growth is not an option for the believer; it is a core
requirement of Christian stewardship. Everything God entrusts to us - our intellect, spiritual gifts, education, career,
business, relationships and time - demands faithful management and compounding yield. In 2 Timothy 3:17, Scripture
emphasises that the person of God should be “thoroughly equipped for every good work.” When we see our profession,
career or business as a calling, we will understand the need to steward it effectively to the glory of Him who has called us
out of darkness into His marvellous light. True spiritual maturity manifests in practical readiness, so that a Christian
professional becomes a sharper strategist, a more punctual employee, a more disciplined entrepreneur and a reliable
professional.

Practical guidelines for understanding whole-person growth as Christian stewardship
 • See your career or business as a calling: Why are you in that profession? Do you understand your calling? This is
 the first growth dimension.
 • Grow in character: The character of Jesus is expressed in the fruit of the Spirit. Embrace these virtues and grow in
 them until you attain the measure of the stature of Christ.
 • Sharpen your competencies: Do not encourage complacency; keep your skills on the cutting edge.
 • Continuously increase your capacity: A commitment to continuous improvement - learning, unlearning and
 relearning - is key to achieving whole-person growth.

 ~ 53 ~

2. Know Your Present Career and Professional Stage and What to Do: The TACEF family spans multiple life and career
stages. Growth requires understanding the specific demands, transition requirements and priorities of your current career
and professional stage.

Practical guidelines for knowing your present career and professional stage and what to do
 • Secondary School Leavers: Focus on building strong foundational academic excellence, career-path exploration,
 personal discipline and early digital literacy. Personal discipline to study and excel in JAMB and WAEC
 examinations, or any other examination required for university admission, is critical at this stage. Also develop
 strong communion with God as the foundation on which to build everything else.
 • Undergraduates: Focus on high academic performance, practical skills acquisition, active involvement in
 leadership and building early networks. Avoid distractions and maintain a laser focus on achieving excellent results.
 Continue to develop strong communion with God as the foundation on which to build everything else.
 • Fresh Graduates & NYSC Members: Acquire relevant skill sets for your desired job. Focus on employability,
 marketplace readiness, securing relevant internships and mastering workplace ethics.
 • Entry-Level Professionals: Focus more on learning than earning; pursue jobs that will support your training and
 prepare you for your future career. Practise execution excellence, master industry tools, learn workplace culture
 and build strong work ethics. Continue to develop strong communion with God for guidance.
 • Middle-Level Professionals: Focus on team-management and leadership skills, strategic problem-solving, project
 management, cross-functional mastery and specialised certifications. Continue to develop strong communion with
 God for guidance.
 • Senior Professionals: Focus on organisational leadership, executive decision-making, industry influence,
 mentorship and building generational legacies. Continue to develop strong communion with God for guidance.
 • Business Owners: Focus on building top-quality products/services and a solid company with strong financial health
 - more assets and fewer liabilities - and strong regulatory compliance. Focus on strategies for client retention,
 market expansion, talent development and succession planning. Deepen your walk with God.
 • Public Servants: Focus on policy execution, institutional integrity, professional upgrades, service delivery and
 ethical leadership under pressure. Deepen your walk with God.
 • Clergy & Ministry Workers: Focus on ministerial impact, spiritual development, administrative efficiency,
 organisational governance, continuous intellectual development and people-management systems. Ensure that
 the fire is continually burning on the altar.

3. Conduct an Annual Skills and Development Audit: Intentional growth requires accurate diagnostic data. Without a
regular audit, good intentions rarely translate into measurable capability. Every TACEFite should establish a formal Annual
Career Development Plan driven by a systematic skills-gap assessment that can be tracked through quarterly reviews.

Practical guidelines for conducting an annual skills and development audit
 • Check your technical competence: Ask yourself the right questions. Is your current skill set current or outdated?
 Are you conversant with new ways of doing things in your field? When did you last read books relevant to your
 domain or for general development? What developmental training have you received in the last two years? Rate
 your teamwork, communication and project-management skills. Check your mastery of essential tools, software,
 methodologies and knowledge frameworks in your domain.
 • Assess your digital & AI literacy level: Check your proficiency in leveraging AI tools and other productivity tools.
 Do you struggle with such tools, or do you enjoy using them?
 • Check where you are with respect to acquiring relevant professional certifications: Identify and pursue high-
 value and credible certifications relevant to your field.
 • Check how strong your soft skills and emotional-intelligence skills are: Evaluate how well you communicate,
 resolve conflicts, manage stress and work across teams.
 • Make the assessment and audit actionable: Get an accountability partner to help track specific actions arising
 from your development audit. Measure progress, identify lingering weaknesses and adjust your development plan
 periodically.

 ~ 54 ~

4. Building Competence, Exposure, Mentorship and Professional Standards: Preparation must precede opportunity.
When God opens doors, He expects to find structured competence, not just spiritual enthusiasm. There is also a platform
in the Great House for development and mentorship. TACEF Professional Fellowship serves as a platform where
experienced professionals mentor younger members, review CVs, provide career exposure, recommend verified
opportunities, explain professional qualifications and connect members to legitimate internships and projects.

Practical guidelines for building competence, exposure, mentorship and professional standards
 • Acquire relevant skills: Take relevant online or onsite courses. Go back to school if you have to.
 • Network with industry colleagues: Attend industry conferences, workshops and exhibitions to connect with
 others and see what is new in your field.
 • Tap into the experience of senior colleagues: Identify a mentor in your field and commit to a robust mentorship
 process.
 • Join professional associations: Do not grow in isolation; take advantage of professional associations as you build
 relevant competencies.
 • Be visible: Do not wink in the dark. Build a credible CV and evidence-based portfolio via LinkedIn, GitHub, etc.

5. Developing Communication, Leadership and Personal Effectiveness: Technical skills can open doors, but you need
excellent communication, strong leadership and outstanding personal effectiveness to keep those doors open. Whole-
person effectiveness requires combining technical depth with strong interpersonal capability.

Practical guidelines for developing communication, leadership and personal effectiveness
 • Communication & Elocution: Master effective writing, articulate speech and public speaking, professional
 presentations and confident elocution.
 • Emotional Intelligence & Conflict Management: Practise self-awareness, be a good listener, receive feedback,
 manage your feelings and recognise the feelings of others. Learn to manage workplace disagreements
 constructively.
 • Workplace Etiquette & Grooming: Maintain high personal hygiene, a professional appearance, neat dressing,
 punctuality and office decorum aligned with industry standards.
 • Leadership Before Title: Take ownership of small assignments and deliver them with excellence before seeking
 bigger positions.
6. Growing Without Sacrificing Christian Character: The ultimate objective of whole-person growth in personal,
professional, career and business life is to produce professionals who are highly successful in career/business and, at the
same time, rich in character towards God. We should never sacrifice our character and consecration as Christians in the
name of growing and building a successful career.

Practical guidelines for growing without sacrificing Christian character
 • Remember that you are a Christian first and foremost before being a professional: Never lose your identity as a
 Christian - a “little Christ” - no matter the level of growth you experience in your career or business.
 • Surrender your career and business pursuits to the Lordship of the Lord Jesus: Remind yourself that Jesus is the
 Lord of your life - not your boss, money, fame or position.
 • Maintain your integrity at all times: No matter the pressure, never compromise your integrity.

Spirituality is not an excuse for workplace mediocrity, nor is professional success an excuse for spiritual decay or domestic
neglect. Refuse to compromise your biblical values for promotion, money or recognition. Protect your devotional life and
family, and use your career advancement to serve others and advance the Kingdom of God.

Conclusion: Your Career - a Calling, Reflecting the Character of Christ, Competence at All Times, and Continuous Capacity
Building
God does not expect us to remain at the same level year after year; He expects compounding fruitfulness and increasing
measure. As TACEFites, we must not allow the realities around us to become an excuse for mediocrity.

Like the dry bones in Ezekiel’s vision, we must allow God to assemble us through rigorous preparation, skill sharpening,
strategic networking, character development and continuous improvement as we grow effectively in our personal,
professional, career and business lives. Know who you are, understand what you need to develop, deliberately build
yourself and remain faithful to Christ while you grow. More importantly, see your career/business as a calling and not only
as an income generator.
