Standing as a Revival Intercessor in the Local Church
Memory Verse: “I have set watchmen upon thy walls, O Jerusalem, which shall never hold their peace day nor night... and
give him no rest, till he establish, and till he make Jerusalem a praise in the earth.” Isaiah 62:6–7

Key Texts: Ezekiel 22:30; Isaiah 62:6–7; Nehemiah 1:1–11; 1 Timothy 2:1–4; Hebrews 7:25; Daniel 9:3–19; Ephesians 6:10–
18

Seminar Objectives:
 • Understand the watchman’s calling and the burden of standing before God for the spiritual condition of the local
 church.
 • Build the disciplined life of an intercessor through prayer, the Word of God, holiness, fasting, spiritual sensitivity
 and perseverance.
 • Learn the high-priestly pattern of identification, compassion and responsible intercession rather than criticism and
 superiority.
 • Practise revival intercession with biblical discernment, including identificational repentance, spiritual warfare and
 mature handling of divinely inspired prophetic burdens.
 • Use spiritual gifts responsibly in intercession while submitting revelations and major directions to appropriate
 leadership review.
 • Build sustainable prayer networks aligned with the TACEF Upper Room team, central prayer leadership and the
 local fellowship.

Introduction: Standing in the gap as a priest before the Lord to activate God-glorifying interventions
Throughout Scripture, God looks for men and women who will carry His burden in prayer until His will is fully established
on earth. Nehemiah heard about the broken walls of Jerusalem; he sat down, wept, fasted, prayed, confessed sin and
became an instrument for rebuilding the broken walls, a picture of a God-led intercessor. Daniel identified himself with
the failures of his people in prayer and became a prophetic intercessor for Israel in Babylon. These examples provide
guidance on how a revival intercessor carries the condition of the church, nation, families and individuals into God’s
presence with tears, faith, repentance, persistence and a readiness to become part of the answer.

This calling is particularly important in many of our local churches where there may be spiritual coldness, compromised
leadership, church politics, unhealthy traditions, doctrinal confusion, counterfeit revival activities or practices that mix
biblical faith with unbiblical prayer objects. Historical concerns about syncretism or occult influence associated with some
past church leadership and traditional practices can also create an ungodly spiritual atmosphere that requires sustained
intercession. The response of a revival intercessor must always be Spirit-governed prayer, biblical discernment, compassion
and confidence in the authority of Christ.

An intercessor is therefore a true watchman who stands before God for the people, carries burdens responsibly, honours
church structures, speaks when God and responsible leadership require it, and labours until Christ is formed in people and
the atmosphere of the church is increasingly shaped by truth, holiness, salvation and genuine revival.

Key principles

(1) Understand the watchman’s calling and burden: A biblical watchman is spiritually alert, sensitive and responsible.
Ezekiel 22:30 describes this role as “standing in the gap”, while Isaiah 62 presents watchmen as those “who refuse to
remain silent until God establishes His purpose”. This calling carries a sustained burden for God’s honour, the salvation and
maturity of people, the holiness of the church, the spiritual health of leaders and the fulfilment of God’s purpose in a life,
family, church or territory. A true watchman does not merely recognise spiritual gaps; the watchman accepts responsibility
to carry those burdens before God persistently until His purpose is established.

Practical responsibilities of a revival watchman
 • Pray for leaders rather than only discussing them: Carry ministers, clergy, fellowship leaders, workers and their
 families before God for genuine salvation, purity, wisdom and spiritual renewal.
 • Pray for genuine salvation and restoration: Labour for churchgoers to encounter Christ personally, for backsliders
 to return, and for homes to become spiritually healthy.

 ~ 56 ~

• Pray about the spiritual atmosphere: Bring before God patterns of prayerlessness, immorality, division, false
 teaching, manipulation, unhealthy tradition, fear and other conditions that weaken genuine revival.
 • Pray for evangelism and mission: Ask God for open doors, bold witnesses, conviction of sin, effective follow-up
 and the multiplication of disciples beyond mere church attendance.
 • Remain at the prayer duty post: A true burden survives beyond one emotional prayer meeting. Intercessors may
 sustain the same burden for a long period; therefore, keep praying until there is direction, measurable spiritual
 fruit or God clearly changes the burden.

(2) Build the disciplined life of an intercessor: Powerful intercession does not grow mainly from occasional prayer
marathons but grows from a life that is continually being brought under the government of God. An intercessor who wants
to carry sensitive burdens must cultivate a personal altar of prayer, the Word of God, fasting, holiness, obedience, humility,
discernment and emotional stability. The secret life must be strong enough to carry the weight of the burden; the altar
must sustain the assignment.
A sustainable intercessory rhythm
 • Daily altar: Maintain personal prayer and Bible study that are not limited to praying for church problems. Know
 God personally before attempting to interpret burdens concerning others.
 • Regular fasting and waiting: Maintain disciplined periods of fasting and extended prayer as led by the Lord.
 • Scripture-shaped prayer: Pray from the Word of God so that intercession remains anchored in God’s revealed
 character, promises and purposes rather than sensationalism, fear, imagination or rumours.
 • Holiness and obedience: Deal quickly with personal sin, bitterness, pride, unforgiveness and moral compromise.
 The heart of a watchman must always remain under God’s searchlight.
 • Spiritual sensitivity with sobriety: Pay attention to burdens, impressions and discernment, but do not treat every
 thought, dream or emotion as a divine message.
 • Perseverance: Learn to continue in prayer even when there is no immediate visible change. Revival intercession
 requires patience, faith and endurance.

(3) Intercede like a high priest: identify, carry and plead: Biblical intercession is not prayer from a position of superiority.
The Old Testament high priest carried the names of the people before God, while Nehemiah and Daniel identified
themselves with the sins and failures of their people. This is an important part of compassionate revival intercession: we
do not stand outside the problem as critics, but we identify with the burden, carry it before God and plead for divine
intervention. Compassion must shape the burden-bearer.

The high-priestly posture of revival prayer
 • Identify with the burden: Pray, “Lord, have mercy on us,” genuinely recognising that you are part of the people
 for whom you are standing in the gap, and carry the burden with humility.
 • Practise identificational repentance: Confess before God the sins and patterns evident among the people for
 whom you are standing in the gap.
 • Carry people with compassion: Let the burden move beyond the act of prayer into genuine compassion for the
 people and situations you are carrying before God.
 • Plead for mercy and transformation: Mercy that triumphs over judgement is a critical instrument in the hands of
 destiny-shaping intercessors.
 • Refuse superiority: If intercession is making you more suspicious, proud, angry or contemptuous of people,
 something has gone wrong. Genuine intercession should deepen compassion, humility and dependence on God.

(4) Practise revival intercession in the local church with biblical discernment: Revival prayer sometimes engages difficult
spiritual realities. Scripture must guide our spiritual warfare and our interpretation of spiritual conditions. Intercessors
must avoid presumption in which every problem in the local church is explained by hidden enemies, territorial spirits or
occult activity. The safest approach combines serious prayer with Scripture, divine leading, and responsible submission to
fellow intercessors and leadership. Discernment must remain biblical, humble and accountable.

Guidelines for difficult spiritual burdens
 • Handle historical spiritual concerns with grace: Where there are memories or reports of past syncretism, occult
 practices or unbiblical spiritual activity within a local church, affirm Christ’s authority and pray for cleansing by the
 blood of Jesus and freedom from associated covenant and curses without creating fear and sensationalism.

 ~ 57 ~

• Discern counterfeit revival: Pray against practices that introduce unbiblical traditions into the church, including
 the use of prayer objects (praying into eggs etc.), manipulation, false prophecy, or financial exploitation.
 • Engage spiritual warfare biblically: Resist the devil through truth, righteousness, faith, the Word of God, prayer
 and obedience. Do not make unverified accusations against named individuals or treat every disagreement as
 demonic opposition.

(5) Use discernment and spiritual gifts without creating fear or private authority: Intercessors may experience unusual
burdens, dreams, visions, impressions, words of knowledge or prophetic insights. Scripture teaches that spiritual
expressions should be tested and judged. The existence of a burden does not automatically establish the correct
interpretation of that burden. Mature intercession therefore combines sensitivity with humility, accountability and
restraint. Spiritual insight must never become a licence for fear, control or private authority.

Prayer ethics and safeguards
 • Do not assume you know every hidden problem: A strong impression is not permission to draw conclusions, label
 people or speak as though God has revealed everything to you alone.
 • Submit revelations for review: Important dreams, perceived prophetic warnings and directions concerning the
 local church should be shared privately with appropriate TACEF leadership for prayerful review and guidance.
 TACEF Upper Room leadership are always available to guide.
 • Never use “God told me” to intimidate: Divine language must not be used to force agreement, silence questions,
 demand access or place yourself above responsible leadership.
 • Do not scare the congregation: Intercession should increase faith in Christ, repentance and responsible prayer,
 not create panic about demons, occultism, enemies or hidden conspiracies.
 • Judge fruit as well as intensity: A healthy prayer burden should increasingly produce humility, love, holiness,
 patience, truthfulness and service, not only louder prayer or stronger claims of revelation.

(6) Build a sustainable prayer network that labours until revival comes: Revival intercession should not depend on one
person or one season. Sustainable prayer is strengthened by coordinated believers who share biblical burdens, pray
faithfully, respect leadership and remain connected to the wider fellowship. TACEF intercessors should therefore align
actively with the Upper Room team, daily morning prayer network at 5am every day and central prayer leadership so that
local burdens can benefit from wider discernment, support and coordination.

Practical guideline for a healthy local prayer network
 • Align with TACEF prayer leadership: Participate in Upper Room and central prayer burdens, and communicate
 significant local needs through responsible channels rather than operating as an isolated group.
 • Build a small, trustworthy prayer team: Include mature believers who are discreet, teachable, spiritually stable
 and committed to the local church. Prayer meetings should not become centres for rumours or the careless sharing
 of confidential information.
 • Define clear prayer burdens: Pray specifically for salvation, revival, leaders, families, young people, holiness,
 evangelism, restoration, church unity and other verified needs rather than vague or fear-driven concerns.
 • Keep prayer confidential and compassionate: Do not turn personal information received for prayer into
 discussion material. Protect the dignity of the people being prayed for.
 • Review fruit periodically: Ask whether the prayer network is producing greater unity, holiness, evangelistic
 burden, restored lives and stronger growth within the local fellowship.

Conclusion:
God is still looking for watchmen who can be trusted with His burden. The revival intercessor must be prayerful without
becoming suspicious, discerning without becoming proud, courageous without becoming rebellious, and spiritually
sensitive without becoming sensational. The intercessor carries the church before God and pleads for mercy that triumphs
over judgement, remaining at the duty post until there is visible divine intervention, even when a burden must be sustained
for a prolonged period.

For every TACEFite with an intercessory burden, keep your personal altar burning, remain aligned with the local fellowship
and TACEF prayer leadership, and pray for The African Church with love and biblical discernment. Revival advances when
Christ is exalted, people are saved and restored, holiness grows and the church responds to God. May God find among us
watchmen who will faithfully “stand in the gap” (Ezekiel 22:30).

 ~ 58 ~

Discovering and Developing Ministry Gifts
Memory Verse: “As every man hath received the gift, even so minister the same one to another, as good stewards of the
manifold grace of God.” 1 Peter 4:10

Key Texts: Romans 12:3–8; 1 Corinthians 12:4–11, 27–31; Ephesians 4:7–13; 1 Peter 4:10–11; 2 Timothy 1:6; Galatians
5:22–23

Seminar Objectives:
 • Understand the difference between spiritual gifts, natural talents, learned skills, calling, ministry office and the
 fruit of the Spirit.
 • Discover how God has equipped each believer without comparison, pressure to copy others or obsession with
 visible platforms.
 • Test and confirm gifts through prayer, service, spiritual fruit, feedback and responsible leadership oversight.
 • Develop gifts through disciplined learning, practice, mentoring, character formation and faithful service in small
 assignments.
 • Deploy gifts through TACEF, The African Church and wider Kingdom service with humility, accountability and a
 clear focus on building people rather than building personal visibility or self-focused platforms.

Introduction: Gift is grace for service, not a title for status or a platform for self-promotion
We are not saved and bought with the precious blood of Christ merely to become spectators in the Body of Christ. The
Bible teaches that grace is given to every believer for service and that the different members of the Body have different
functions. A ministry gift is therefore not first about a microphone, a title, an office or public recognition, but about the
particular grace through which God enables a believer to strengthen other people and contribute to the work of His
Kingdom.

Many sincere believers struggle in this area because they assume that the person who preaches, sings, prophesies or leads
publicly is more useful than the person who quietly follows up converts, teaches children, organises people, encourages
the weak or carries a burden in prayer. In TACEF, every local fellowship must help TACEFites discover that the Body
becomes healthy when every member functions faithfully, supplies what God has given, and occupies his or her place
responsibly.

At the same time, gifts must never be confused with maturity. A person may be genuinely gifted and still be proud, careless,
morally weak, unteachable or immature. Spiritual manifestation does not place anyone above correction. The safest
ministry is therefore a combination of genuine grace, Christlike character, biblical truth, accountable relationships and
faithful service.

Key principles

(1) Understand what God has given you: The Bible presents different forms of grace and service while also showing that
character remains essential in every expression of ministry. A believer should therefore learn to distinguish what God has
naturally placed in a person, what has been developed through training, what the Holy Spirit enables for service, and what
God may be assigning the person to do in a particular season. The central principle is clear: gift is not the same as maturity,
and every gift must remain under Christlike character and correction.

Essential distinctions for every TACEFite
 • Spiritual gift: A grace-enabled capacity given by God for serving and building the Body of Christ. The purpose is
 service, not personal importance. Examples include the nine manifestations of the Spirit listed in 1 Corinthians
 12:8–10.
 • Natural talent: An ability a person may possess naturally and which can be consecrated, trained and used for God’s
 glory. Examples include singing, writing, administration, organisation, generosity and welfare service. Unbelievers
 may also possess natural talents.
 • Skill: A capacity developed through learning, instruction, repeated practice and experience. Skill can strengthen
 the responsible expression of a gift. Examples include video editing, playing a musical instrument, cooking,
 engineering and medical care.

 ~ 59 ~

• Calling or assignment: The direction or responsibility God places on a person for a particular work, people, place
 or season. A calling may use several gifts and skills. An example is Acts 13:2, where the Holy Spirit called for
 Barnabas and Saul to be set apart for a specific assignment.
 • Ministry office or recognised responsibility: A defined function within the Body or church structure. Possessing a
 gift does not automatically appoint a person to an office. Ephesians 4:11 identifies the ministry functions of
 apostle, prophet, evangelist, pastor and teacher. Many people who have gifts wrongly assume that the gift
 automatically confers a ministry office.
 • Fruit of the Spirit: Christlike character produced by the Holy Spirit. Love, humility, self-control and faithfulness are
 not optional because someone is gifted.

(2) Discover how God has equipped you without comparison: Romans 12 describes different graces within one Body;
therefore, discovery is a prayerful process of serving, observing, receiving feedback and recognising where God repeatedly
gives grace and fruit. In this process, we must guard against comparison, which can make a person despise a genuine but
less visible grace or manufacture an expression that God did not give. Faithfulness with what God has actually entrusted
to you matters more than visibility.

A practical discovery pathway
 • Pray for understanding, not a title: Ask the Lord where He wants you to serve and what burdens, capacities and
 opportunities He has placed around you.
 • Start serving where there is a genuine need: Gifts are often discovered in use. Do not wait for a special platform
 before helping in follow-up, Sunday School, evangelism, intercession, administration or other legitimate church
 responsibilities.
 • Observe repeated grace and fruit: Notice areas where people are consistently helped, strengthened, taught,
 organised, encouraged or drawn towards Christ through your service.
 • Receive confirmation from mature believers: Ask trusted leaders, disciplers and brethren what strengths and
 ministry patterns they have consistently observed. Confirmation should be based on service and fruit, not flattery.
 • Separate burden from ambition: A recurring burden for children, souls, prayer, teaching, welfare or another area
 may be significant, but it should be tested over time through obedience and fruit.
 • Refuse comparison: Another person’s gift is not the standard for your usefulness. The question is not whether
 your expression looks impressive, but whether you are faithful with the grace God has actually entrusted to you.

(3) Test and confirm gifts through service, fruit and accountability: A strong feeling, a dream, a prophecy about oneself,
an invitation to minister or one successful experience should not be treated as final proof of a ministry gift or calling. The
New Testament pattern allows grace to become visible through service and to be recognised within the Body. Healthy
testing protects the believer from presumption and protects the church from immature or unaccountable ministry.
Genuine gifts become clearer through biblical alignment, sustained fruit, character and accountability.

Practical guideline for testing a perceived gift
 • Test by Scripture: No gift, revelation or ministry expression should contradict the Word of God or produce
 behaviour that Scripture condemns.
 • Test by edification: Ask whether people are genuinely being strengthened, instructed, comforted, corrected,
 saved, discipled or helped towards Christ rather than merely impressed by the person ministering.
 • Test by character: Watch what happens to humility, purity, truthfulness and teachability as opportunities increase.
 A growing platform with declining character is a warning sign.
 • Test over time: One dramatic moment is not the same as sustained grace. Faithful service across ordinary seasons
 gives clearer evidence than occasional visibility.
 • Test under leadership: Allow local TACEF leadership to observe, guide, correct and gradually release responsibility.
 Healthy oversight is not an enemy of gifting; it helps gifts mature safely.
 • Test motives honestly: Check how you respond when you are not allowed to use the gift or minister, even after
 you have prepared. Does it make you feel slighted, resentful or eager to leave the fellowship? These may be
 warning signs of ungodly motives that need to be surrendered to God.

 ~ 60 ~

(4) Develop the gift through discipline, learning and mentoring: Paul told Timothy to stir up the gift of God. Genuine grace
should therefore not become an excuse for laziness or poor preparation. The more serious the assignment, the more
intentionally the believer should grow in biblical knowledge, spiritual depth, practical competence and character. A gifted
teacher should study; a worshipper should develop both spiritual and musical discipline; an administrator should learn
organisation; an evangelist should grow in Scripture, communication and follow-up. Development should make the gift
more useful while making the vessel more Christlike.

A practical gift-development system
 • Study the Scriptures deeply: Every ministry expression must remain rooted in truth. Learn the whole counsel of
 God, not only verses that appear to support your preferred ministry identity.
 • Learn the craft responsibly: Read sound materials, attend relevant training, observe mature examples and build
 the practical skills that make your service more useful and delivered with excellence.
 • Practise in small assignments: Faithfulness in less visible responsibilities builds competence, humility and
 endurance. Do not despise opportunities that appear small.
 • Seek mentoring: Learn from mature people while allowing God to shape your own expression. Receive guidance
 without merely copying another person’s style or mannerisms.
 • Allow correction: Ask for specific feedback after teaching, leading, organising or ministering. A person who cannot
 be corrected will eventually become unsafe, no matter how gifted.
 • Develop character alongside capacity: Deliberately work on a consistent quiet time, a lifestyle of holiness,
 integrity, emotional maturity, financial discipline and humility. Capacity without character can damage both the
 minister and the people being served.

(5) Protect the gift from pride, power-seeking and platform obsession: Spiritual gifts can become dangerous when we
begin to love the attention attached to the gift more than Christ and the people the gift was meant to serve. Jesus warned
against showmanship and ambition, while Paul repeatedly directed attention back to love, service and the building of the
Body. The goal is usefulness, not celebrity culture in the name of “my own platform”. A gift is safest when Christ remains
greater than the platform.

Major safeguards for growing gifts
 • Do not chase spiritual power: Desire God Himself and usefulness in His hands, not manifestations that make
 people admire you.
 • Do not chase titles or copy another person’s gift: A title does not create grace, and imitation does not create
 calling.
 • Do not manufacture manifestations: Never exaggerate experiences, force prophetic language, imitate unusual
 behaviours or present strong personal feelings as divine revelation merely to appear gifted.
 • Do not use gifts for money, control, attention or self-promotion: Financial gain, emotional dependence, loyalty
 demands and personal branding must not become the hidden purpose of ministry.
 • Do not bypass character development: If leadership asks you to slow down, learn, correct a weakness or serve
 quietly for a season, receive it prayerfully rather than treating every restraint as opposition to your calling.
 • Be careful about seeking online visibility: Building a personal online platform to showcase your gift or ministry
 requires caution and guidance, especially as a member of a shared vision such as TACEF. Do not equate online
 reach, likes, followers or growing popularity with reliable evidence of spiritual fruit or God’s endorsement. If you
 have a singing grace, do not rush to release an album simply because others are doing so. If you are clergy or
 MOTA, be cautious about creating your own prayer/outreach platform on Facebook because it is now popular.
 Avoid anything that places you at the centre rather than Christ, the Kingdom and the shared vision.

(6) Deploy gifts through TACEF, The African Church and wider Kingdom service: TACEF fellowship should function as a
safe training ground where gifts are observed, tested, corrected, mentored and released. The African Church also provides
many opportunities for members to serve as we execute the vision of revival and as led by the Lord. Deployment should
therefore follow divine leading, accountable service and the needs of the Body, not personal ambition.

A simple path to deploy your service
 • Divine leading: Seek the Lord’s direction concerning where, when and how the gift should be expressed. Divine
 leading should govern deployment, not ambition, pressure or the desire to be visible.
 • Discover: Prayerfully identify possible areas of grace, burden and usefulness without forcing a label too early.
 • Serve: Begin with real needs in the local TACEF fellowship and church rather than waiting for a preferred platform.

 ~ 61 ~

• Observe: Look for sustained fruit, recurring grace, personal growth and the effect of the service on others.
 • Confirm: Receive honest feedback from mature believers and responsible leadership.
 • Develop: Build spiritual depth, knowledge, skill, discipline and character appropriate to the gift and assignment.
 • Deploy and review: Accept increasing responsibility as appropriate, remain accountable, and periodically ask
 whether the gift is still producing Christlike fruit and genuinely building people.

Conclusion:
God has not called every believer to the same function, but He has called every believer to faithful service. The great
question is therefore not, “What title do I carry?” but, “What grace has God entrusted to me, who is being helped by it,
and am I becoming trustworthy enough for God to use it more?”

Let TACEF and your local church become places where gifts are discovered without competition, tested without
humiliation, developed without pride and deployed without personality worship. Everyone who has received a gift to serve
the Lord must remain focused on building godly character and staying teachable. In the same way, less visible workers
must know that their service matters, and every growing gift must remain under the government of Scripture and healthy
accountability.

Stir up the gift and pursue excellence in Kingdom service, but guard the life carrying the gift. Serve faithfully where God
has placed you, develop what He has given you, and allow the fruit of your life and service to point people to Christ rather
than to yourself.

Managing Church Dynamics and Administration with Excellence
Memory Verse: “Moreover it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful.” 1 Corinthians 4:2
Key Texts: Acts 6:1–7; Daniel 6:1–5; 1 Corinthians 4:1–2; Mark 10:42–45; Colossians 3:23–24

Seminar Objectives:
 • Understand church administration as a sacred stewardship and spiritual responsibility, not an opportunity for
 status, influence or financial gain.
 • Discern whether God is genuinely leading them into an administrative role or they are accepting it through
 pressure, politics or emotional blackmail.
 • Recognise the spiritual, political, relational and financial pressures that can accompany leadership responsibility
 in The African Church.
 • Apply professional standards of accountability, reporting, punctuality, documentation, financial management and
 resource stewardship.
 • Use administrative influence to strengthen revival, discipleship, welfare, institutional sustainability and the
 spiritual mission of the church.

Introduction: When church administration becomes a spiritual test
The church is the Body of Christ, yet people, money, property, projects, programmes and relationships must be managed.
Acts 6 shows that administration is necessary, but those appointed were required to be people of honest report, full of the
Holy Ghost and wisdom. Administrative competence must therefore never be separated from spiritual character.

This is especially important in The African Church. A believer who becomes a Church Warden, Pastor’s Warden, Secretary,
Financial Secretary, Treasurer, Council Member, Committee Chairman, or other office holder may encounter other office
holders with competing interests. Some see church office as an opportunity for visibility, political influence, preferred
vendor recommendations, access to church funds or even inflated project costs for personal gain. Others may try to use
the credibility of a godly believer to strengthen a faction or pursue an agenda.

The deeper question is therefore not simply whether a believer can occupy an office, but whether the assignment can be
carried in a way that preserves personal walk with God, family life, TACEF fellowship and testimony while making the
church more spiritually focused, accountable and sustainable.

Key principles
(1) Do not take the role without divine leading: Not every position offered to a believer must be accepted. Statements
such as “Why should a TACEF member refuse?” or “Do you want those who are not born again to rule the church?” can
become emotional blackmail. Pressure is not the same as divine direction. Seek God carefully before taking responsibility,
because God will only sustain what He genuinely leads us into.

Practical guideline for accepting administrative responsibility
 • Pray before accepting: Seek clear direction from the Lord before taking significant responsibility; do not accept
 because of title, prestige, pressure or fear of disappointing people.
 • Count the cost: Understand the duties, time demand and possible impact on your life, family, work schedule and
 fellowship. Discuss major implications with your spouse.
 • Seek godly counsel: Speak with mature brethren who can help you discern motives, risks and whether the
 assignment fits God’s present leading for your life.
 • Refuse political recruitment: Do not allow your name, credibility or TACEF identity to be used as a political
 instrument or to legitimise an agenda you do not understand.
 • Learn to say no: A respectful refusal is better than accepting an office that eventually destroys your spiritual life,
 family or testimony.

(2) Protect your spiritual life, family and fellowship: Church administration can become so demanding that meetings,
projects management and committee responsibilities gradually replace prayer, Bible study, family time and fellowship.
Some eventually spend much of the Sunday service in the vestry room while the Word is being preached. Administration
must support spiritual life, not consume it.

 ~ 63 ~

Practical guideline for maintaining spiritual balance
 • Guard your personal altar: Maintain daily prayer, Bible study and regular seasons of fasting irrespective of
 administrative pressure.
 • Remain active in TACEF fellowship: Church office must never become an excuse for disconnecting from the
 fellowship and spiritual relationships that nurture your life.
 • Protect family time: Do not allow endless meetings and avoidable church assignments to make your spouse and
 children permanent casualties of service.
 • Avoid unnecessary vestry occupation: Plan administrative work so you can participate meaningfully during church
 services.
 • Review your spiritual health: Regularly ask whether the position is making you spiritually stronger or gradually
 weakening your walk with God and Christian testimony.
 • Actively grow with the MICA: Actively join the TACEF Missionaries in Church Administration (MICA) to pray, grow,
 learn, share and be supported in your assignment.

(3) Use administrative influence to advance the spiritual mission: Joseph and Daniel used positions of influence with
wisdom, integrity and a sense of divine purpose. In the same way, TACEFites in church administration should use influence
to strengthen the church spiritually and institutionally, not just to sustain activities and traditions.
Practical guideline for using administrative influence
 • Prioritise spiritual purpose: Ask whether programmes genuinely strengthen salvation, discipleship, prayer,
 evangelism and Christian living.
 • Redirect activities wisely: Where activities such as harvest events become dominated by bazaars, fundraising or
 social display, respectfully help restore emphasis on thanksgiving, evangelism, generosity and the true harvest of
 souls.
 • Invest in the next generation: Advocate for serious discipleship and spiritual development among children,
 teenagers and young people.
 • Strengthen welfare and compassion: Promote responsible support for ministers, widows, children who need
 financial help and genuinely vulnerable members rather than publicity-driven assistance.
 • Think beyond the present tenure: Build systems, documentation, leadership development and sustainable
 investments that leave the church stronger after you have left office.

(4) Serve with professional excellence: Spirituality does not excuse incompetence. Daniel distinguished himself because
an excellent spirit was in him (Daniel 6:3). When a revival-minded believer takes responsibility, there should be a visible
difference in preparation, documentation, accuracy, punctuality, follow-through and accountability.

Practical guideline for administrative excellence
 • Secretary and reporting roles: Prepare accurate minutes, circulate reports on time, track agreed actions, maintain
 proper records and archives, and protect confidential information.
 • Financial roles: Apply sound accounting practices, maintain supporting documents, reconcile accounts, prepare
 clear reports, keep all receipts, and insist on proper authorisation and oversight.
 • Projects and procurement: Define requirements clearly, seek fair quotations, document decisions, monitor quality
 and cost, do not inflate cost, and disclose conflicts of interest.
 • Meeting discipline: Be punctual, prepare beforehand, communicate clearly, follow through on assignments and
 avoid meetings that consume time without producing decisions or action.
 • Build relevant skills: Learn the technical, financial, digital, reporting or governance skills required for your specific
 role. Let standards rise because a believer is serving.

(5) Protect integrity, church money and church assets: Access to church assets and information can create temptation.
Administrative office will give privilege to know about the church funds, contracts, and vendor information. Always
maintain firm boundaries and caution.

Practical guideline for financial and resource integrity
 • Reject personal gain from church transactions: Never inflate project costs, receive secret commissions or
 manipulate procurement to favour yourself, friends, relatives or business associates.
 • Declare conflicts of interest: Where you have a relationship or potential benefit connected with a decision,
 disclose it and allow proper independent consideration.

 ~ 64 ~

• Protect privileged information: Do not use confidential budgets, vendor information or internal decisions for
 private advantage.
 • Respect church assets: Do not use church buses, vehicles, tools, facilities, workers or equipment for personal
 assignments without proper approval and subject to the existing church policy.
 • Keep decisions defensible: Handle funds and privileges in a manner that can withstand open examination.
 “Moreover it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful” (1 Corinthians 4:2).

(6) Manage church politics and opposition with wisdom: Church administration brings believers into contact with
influential people, factions and competing interests. Some may behave as though they own the church because of wealth,
age, family history or long-standing influence. Others may try to recruit you into attacks against ministers or leaders. A
believer must never become anybody’s political weapon.

Practical guideline for managing difficult church dynamics
 • Respect without surrendering conviction: Treat everyone honourably, but do not compromise biblical truth or
 your conscience merely because a person is influential.
 • Refuse factional battles: Do not spread damaging rumours, join coordinated attacks on godly ministers or sign
 actions you know are dishonest, vindictive or politically motivated.
 • Speak with wisdom and respect: Be ready to explain your position calmly and clearly.
 • Keep records and seek counsel: Document important decisions and consult mature believers before major
 confrontations or steps with long-term consequences.
 • Receive genuine correction: Do not label every disagreement as persecution. Admit mistakes where necessary
 and remain teachable.
 • Know when participation becomes compromise: If remaining in a role repeatedly requires dishonesty, ungodly
 alliances or violation of conscience, prayerfully seek God concerning whether you should continue.

Conclusion:
The great need of The African Church is for believers who combine spiritual depth with professional excellence in
administration. They do not enter office for title, visibility, politics or financial opportunity. They seek God’s leading, guard
their personal altar, remain active in TACEF fellowship, serve in MICA, protect their families, and refuse to become
instruments of ungodly factions.

They handle church money transparently, reject inflated projects and secret benefits, respect church assets, keep accurate
records, meet deadlines and apply professional standards. They use influence to strengthen evangelism, discipleship,
children and youth ministry, ministerial welfare, care for vulnerable people, sound governance and the long-term spiritual
and institutional sustainability of the church.

Like Joseph and Daniel, their presence should make a visible difference. Their tenure should leave the church more orderly,
more accountable, more sustainable and, above all, more spiritually focused than they met it. “Be thou an example of the
believers” (1 Timothy 4:12).

Running an Effective Local Fellowship with Kingdom Excellence
Memory Verse: “Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might.” Ecclesiastes 9:10
Key Texts: Acts 2:42–47; John 10:11–14; 2 Timothy 2:2; Daniel 6:3; Ephesians 4:11–14; Ezekiel 37:1–10

Seminar Objectives:
 • Understand the TACEF local fellowship as a platform for sustained discipleship, accountable Christian growth,
 evangelism, soulwinning and revival.
 • Run church-based and campus-based fellowships effectively despite competing activities, schedules and
 responsibilities.
 • Plan fellowship activities with prayer, advance scheduling, prepared session leads, back-up arrangements and
 appropriate timing.
 • Shepherd members intentionally through spiritual follow-up, welfare support, children’s engagement and
 integration into the wider TACEF vision.
 • Apply kingdom excellence to finance, reporting, information management, communication, leadership
 development, succession and alignment with TACEF structures.

Introduction: The local fellowship as a place of deepening the vision of revival
A TACEF local fellowship is more than a weekly meeting or another group within the church or campus. It is a deliberate
platform for sustained discipleship where believers are taught, followed up and groomed into the character of Christ. It is
also a revival outpost through which members are strengthened to live as witnesses of Christ, win souls, intercede for the
church and community, and carry the burden of revival into their everyday lives.

Running such a fellowship today requires wisdom and excellence. In a church-based fellowship, members may also belong
to the choir, Brigade, youth groups, and other units that meet at the same time, while frequent church programmes can
further reduce available time. On campuses, lectures, tests, examinations, departmental activities, other Christian
meetings, and holiday calendars create similar pressures. Kingdom Excellence therefore means protecting the essence of
fellowship while prayerfully finding workable structures that help people participate consistently.

The danger is either to abandon the fellowship because the environment is busy or to become so immersed in church or
campus activities that the TACEF mandate is lost. A vibrant fellowship must continually produce disciples, intercessors, and
soulwinners who understand the vision and become salt and light wherever God has placed them.

Key principles
(1) Treasure the TACEF fellowship and understand what it is: TACEF fellowship exists to deepen personal growth in an
accountable community of believers and to raise a revival army through discipleship, prayer, evangelism, welfare and
alignment with the current burden of the ministry. Members should not treat it as an optional meeting that is attended
only when nothing else is happening.

Practical guideline for preserving the fellowship mandate
 • Keep discipleship central: Use the fellowship to teach the Word, apply the TACEF manual and current ministry
 burden, pray together, and deliberately groom members into Christlike character.
 • Make intercession a defining culture: Pray for members, the local church or campus, salvation of souls, and the
 wider revival mandate. The fellowship should carry people and territories before God, not merely run
 programmes.
 • Know what fellowship is not: Using the TACEF manual to teach the church’s Sunday School, taking an English
 Service, or running a youth church can be valuable outreach, but these do not replace the distinct TACEF
 fellowship where members are discipled, followed up, and aligned to the vision.
 • Treasure accountable community: Create an atmosphere where members can share spiritual struggles, receive
 counsel, be encouraged, corrected in love and strengthened without fear.
 • Include the children intentionally: Create a simple children’s segment where they can share what they learned
 from their Seed of Purpose manual, recite memory verses, lead worship or prayers.

 ~ 66 ~

(2) Plan with prayer and excellence in a busy church or campus environment: Excellence begins before the fellowship
starts. Strong intercession, advance planning and responsible coordination are critical. The goal is not to fill a calendar but
to create a rhythm that members can realistically follow without diluting the fellowship mandate.

Practical guideline for effective planning
 • Maintain a minimum one-month activity schedule: Publish the next four weeks of fellowship activities so that
 everyone leading worship, Word, prayer, children’s session, announcement or another assignment knows well in
 advance.
 • Confirm every facilitator during the same week: Follow up before the meeting to ensure the person is prepared,
 understands the assigned topic and has prayed. Always have a prepared back-up when the person selected is
 absent.
 • Intercede before every fellowship: Leadership should pray deliberately for the fellowship intentionally.
 Administration must never replace spiritual preparation.
 • Choose the most feasible meeting rhythm: Explore early morning before English Service, after service, a weekday
 physical meeting or complementary online sessions. One fellowship, for example, holds Sundays at 7am, a
 monthly post-service outreach in the main church at 2pm, and Monday at 9pm WhatsApp prayer meeting every
 week.
 • Plan campus fellowships around real campus life: Work with lecture timetables, examinations, and facility
 availability. Use semester calendars, shorter targeted meetings where necessary with specialized student focused
 events (e.g. Success Seminars, Examination Prayer).
 • Start and close responsibly: Punctuality, clear time allocation and disciplined moderation show respect for
 members and make it easier for people to participate when we keep to time.

(3) Shepherd people not just organise programme: A local fellowship becomes effective when leadership knows the
people and takes genuine interest in their spiritual life, welfare, progress and challenges. Attendance is important, but the
deeper task is to ensure that no member quietly drifts away from Christ or disappears under the weight of the pressures
of life and personal challenges.

Practical guideline for discipleship and member care
 • Know members by name and situation: Maintain an updated membership and contact register and deliberately
 know who is regular, new, absent, spiritually struggling, relocating, graduating, returning from school or needing
 practical support.
 • Follow up intentionally: Contact absent members during the week. Ask about prayer life, salvation, family,
 school, work, health and welfare, and provide or connect them to appropriate support.
 • Lead new people to Christ, not merely into TACEF: Every new member should be lovingly followed up with the
 intention of establishing a genuine relationship with Jesus and helping the person understand the fellowship’s
 revival vision.
 • Build one-to-one and small-group discipleship: Where possible, connect younger believers with mature brethren
 who can pray with them, answer questions, model Christian living and help them develop consistent spiritual
 disciplines.
 • Use welfare as part of shepherding: Pay attention to genuine needs without creating unhealthy dependency.
 Mobilise practical support, prayer, counsel and referrals within the fellowship and wider TACEF family.
 • Engage children and young people beyond Sunday attendance: Encourage regular participation in Seed of
 Purpose, Son of Purpose and other age-relevant TACEF platforms.

(4) Grow the fellowship through evangelism, soulwinning and revival impact: TACEF exists to be salt and light in
the local church, campus and community. Fellowship growth should therefore be intentional, but the aim is not to
increase numbers for their own sake. The goal is to bring people to Christ, disciple them and release them as
witnesses and agents of revival.

Practical guideline for growth and impact
 • Practise one-on-one invitation: Encourage every member to prayerfully invite friends, church members,
 classmates or colleagues and personally follow up those invitations.

 ~ 67 ~

• Build an evangelism rhythm: Schedule regular prayer for souls, personal evangelism, visitation and appropriate
 outreach rather than waiting only for large seasonal programmes.
 • Use innovative outreach platforms: Campus fellowships can use Catch-Them-Young initiatives, special teaching
 events and targeted engagements. Church-based fellowships can prayerfully use Sunday School, children’s
 ministry, or English Services as outreach opportunities where the church permits.
 • Remain a revival influence in the local church: Interact constructively with church leadership, support spiritually
 edifying programmes and organise Spirit-led outreach that strengthens salvation, discipleship, and biblical
 studies.
 • Watch for mission drift: If the fellowship becomes heavily occupied with general church activities while
 intercession declines, no disciples are being groomed and no souls are being won, the fellowship is losing the
 reason it was planted there.
 • Measure spiritual fruit: Look beyond attendance to conversions, restored prayer lives, discipleship progress,
 children growing in Christ and members becoming visible witnesses of Jesus.

(5) Run the fellowship with administrative and financial excellence: Spiritual vitality should be matched by orderly
administration. A fellowship that prays well but cannot account for money, attendance, information, assignments or
communication is not demonstrating kingdom excellence. Good systems protect trust, continuity and responsible
stewardship.

Practical guideline for administration, finance and communication
 • Keep complete financial records: Record every offering, gift, expense and approved commitment. Reconcile
 regularly with the zonal or central financial system for those who remit to the centralised bank account and retain
 supporting evidence for all transactions.
 • Maintain full bank-account visibility: Where the fellowship operates an account, ensure authorised leaders have
 appropriate visibility, approvals are documented and no single individual controls the fellowship’s money.
 • Report attendance every week: Capture attendance in the required format and submit promptly to the TACEF
 central reporting platform.
 • Manage information deliberately: Keep current records of members, leaders, programmes, attendance,
 outreach activities, follow-up needs, and significant fellowship decisions so that knowledge is not lost when
 leadership changes.
 • Use the Fellowship WhatsApp platform purposefully: Share weekly ministry trigger messages from the Sunday
 online fellowship and notices for relevant platforms such as Tuesday Prayer Meeting, Seed of Purpose session
 link for those who missed it, Sisters’ Tuesday Morning Prayer and other TACEF activities. Celebrate appropriate
 member milestones to keep healthy community engagement.
 • Control digital excesses: Do not allow incessant forwarding, unrelated debates, commercial promotions or
 distracting content to overwhelm the fellowship platform. Communication should strengthen fellowship,
 information, prayer and spiritual growth.

(6) Build leadership, alignment and succession for sustainability: An excellent fellowship must not depend on one
coordinator. It should continually raise people who can teach, evangelise, administer, care for members and eventually
carry responsibility. It must also remain connected to the subzone, zone and central ministry so that the local fellowship
does not become an isolated island.

Practical guideline for leadership and sustainability
 • Build a simple functional leadership team: Assign clear responsibilities for prayer, evangelism, discipleship,
 welfare, children, finance and communication according to the size of the fellowship.
 • Plan succession deliberately: Identify faithful members early, give them opportunities to lead sessions, involve
 them in planning and mentor them until there is a visible pipeline of people able to continue the fellowship.
 • Tap returning TACEF pipelines: Identify TACEFites returning from campuses, graduates coming home, NYSC
 members, members in boarding schools during holidays and others who can be reintegrated, discipled and
 gradually given responsibility.
 • Hold regular leadership prayer retreats: Use prayer retreats to renew the burden, resolve challenges, review
 members and prepare spiritually. The annual local fellowship end-of-year retreat should combine appraisal,
 thanksgiving, planning, review and readiness for the new year.

 ~ 68 ~

• Stay aligned to wider TACEF activities: Ensure members understand and participate in relevant subzone, zone
 and central activities and thematic platforms such as Seed of Purpose, Son of Purpose, MOTA, MICA, Mothers
 Fellowship, Ambassadors and Couples Chat Room.
 • Review the fellowship regularly: Ask whether the fellowship is growing disciples, winning souls, caring for
 members, raising leaders, maintaining sound records, aligning with the ministry burden and impacting the local
 church or campus for Christ.

Conclusion:
An effective TACEF local fellowship is a place of making. It is not a social group or an additional church programme. It is a
spiritual community where believers are intentionally discipled, prayed for, cared for, sent out to win souls and groomed
to become an army with a vision of revival.

Kingdom Excellence means protecting this spiritual purpose with prayerful planning, feasible meeting structures, strong
follow-up, evangelism, financial accountability, accurate reporting, disciplined communication, alignment with the wider
ministry and deliberate succession. Whether the fellowship is church-based or campus-based, it must learn to work wisely
within a busy environment without allowing competing activities to erase its identity.

The ultimate evidence of a thriving fellowship is not how many programmes it conducts but whether people are being
saved, disciples are being formed, intercession is increasing, members are growing in the character of Christ, new leaders
are emerging and the local church, campus and community are feeling the influence of a people who have been raised to
live as witnesses of Jesus.

TACEF 2026/2027
Weekly Bible Study
Annual Theme: An Exceeding Great Army

 ~ 70 ~

A 52-Week Journey through Joshua and Ephesians
Winning Territories, Advancing Christ’s Kingdom, Possessing the Land and Hearts of Men for the Lord in Local Churches,
Campuses, Communities, and Workplaces

Summary

The studies anchored on the theme, “An Exceeding Great Army,” are series of spiritual burden and prophetic call to raise a
consecrated, Spirit-led, Word-governed, and battle-ready people for the Lord. It is a call for the evolution of end-time revival
army rising from the dry bones.

Through Joshua, we see the practical journey of God’s army, vessels made, commissioned, led, tested, corrected, restored,
and sent to possess the land. Through Ephesians, we see our identity, inheritance, spiritual authority, and warfare posture
in Christ necessary to possess the land and hearts of men for the Lord.

This 52-week study calls TACEFites to move from personal encounter to kingdom responsibility, from inward formation to
outward possession, and from knowing God to enforcing His purpose in local churches, campuses, communities,
workplaces, families, and nations. It is a call for dry bones to live again, wounded soldiers to rise again, vision carriers to be
consecrated again, and the Lord’s army to stand as one revived, obedient, holy, and faithful people in Christ’s Kingdom.

Section 1: The Making of God’s End-Time Army -How God Forms Men Before He Entrusts Them with an Army
The journey of an exceeding great army does not begin with noise, numbers, platforms, titles, or visible exploits. It begins
with the hidden process of divine making of vessels whom God can trust. Before Joshua became the commander of Israel’s
conquest, he was first a servant, a minister, a disciple, a man under instructions, a man tested in battle, a man exposed to
the mountain of God, and a man who knew how to remain in the presence of God. Before God commits men, territories,
burdens, and assignments to a vessel, He first commits that vessel to a process of divine making.
God does not build His work on untrained passion, uncontrolled zeal, self-appointed burdens, or public noise. He first forms
the inner life of the vessel. He deals with pride, self-will, fear, unbelief, carelessness, impatience, and spiritual shallowness.
The vessel that will carry others must first be carried through God’s dealings. The life that will revive others must first be
revived. The soldier that will possess territories must first be possessed by the Lord.
Ephesians explains this process of divine making from the New Testament standpoint. We are God’s workmanship, created
in Christ Jesus unto good works which God has before ordained that we should walk in. Through this divine ordination, we
are perfected for the work of ministry, strengthened in the Lord, and equipped with the whole armour of God to stand
against every opposition to the will of God. As children of light, we are called to enforce the intention of God on earth, not
by human strength, but by the life, wisdom, Word, Spirit, and power of Christ working in us.
This first section therefore lays the foundation for the entire 2026/2027 study journey. If we must become God’s end-time
army, we must first become trusted vessels. If we must possess the land for the Lord, we must first allow the Lord to possess,
shape, correct, and send us.
 • Week 1: Becoming a Trusted Soldier in the Lord’s Army - Joshua in the School of Divine Making: The life of Joshua
 teaches us that discipleship is the pathway to becoming enlisted into the Lord’s army. He was shaped through
 obedience, the Word rehearsed into his ears, mountain encounter, and a personal altar. TACEFites must learn that
 God first makes the vessel before He sends the vessel. No one can carry divine territory safely if they have not first
 submitted to divine making process.
 • Week 2: Joshua - Kingdom Army Built in Courage, Wisdom, and the Spirit-Led Lifestyle: Joshua and Caleb showed
 us that God’s army must see through the eyes of heaven, not through fear, public opinion, or natural limitation.
 They saw the promised land through God’s promise while others saw only giants. They stood for God when the
 crowd chose unbelief and even risked being stoned by the people. TACEFites must therefore stand for the truth,
 holiness, and revival with Spirit-governed courage, not fleshly boldness, anger, pride, or ambition.
 • Week 3: Joshua’s Commissioning as God’s Army - Arising into God’s Ordained Assignment: Joshua’s
 commissioning reminds us that divine assignment begins with clear instructions, not emotion, pressure, or self-
 appointed burden. God said, “Moses my servant is dead; now therefore arise, go over this Jordan.” This means that
 the death of a season is not the death of God’s promise. We must arise from grief, failure, pain of the past, betrayal,

delay, disappointment, and unhealthy dependency. We must also discern “this Jordan,” the specific obedience,
 people, burden, or territory God is assigning to us.

Introduction
Our first study into how an exceeding great army is forged through the hand of God introduces us to the making of Joshua,
not first as a commander of an army, but as an ordinary vessel in the intense process of divine making. Before Joshua led
Israel across Jordan, divided territories, confronted kings, and possessed the land, he was first shaped and groomed to
become a trusted soldier of the Lord. Before he became the visible leader, he was hidden under Moses, trained through
service, sharpened by correction, exposed to battle, and drawn into the presence of God.

The first time Joshua appears in the battle narrative of Scripture, Moses gives him an instruction: “Choose us out men, and
go out, fight with Amalek.” The Bible immediately records, “So Joshua did as Moses had said to him.” This simple sentence
reveals the foundation of Joshua’s usefulness. He was teachable, available, responsive, and obedient. He did not argue,
delay, reinterpret the instruction, or insist on his own method. This is an important lesson to note that the Lord’s army is
not built with self-willed people who want to lead before they have learned to follow. A soldier who cannot take instruction
cannot be trusted with divine territory.

This opening study connects directly with our 2025/2026 spiritual year, where we learned that discipleship is not merely
learning about Christ but becoming like Christ. Joshua’s life brings this truth into a practical context. He was formed by
obedience, strengthened by the Word rehearsed into his ears, exposed to the mountain of prayer, and shaped by a personal
hunger that made him stay back in the tabernacle when others had gone.

Ephesians gives us the New Testament meaning of this divine making process. We are not self-made revival agents. We are
“his workmanship.” God is the divine Craftsman, shaping, correcting, pruning, repairing, preparing, and aligning us for the

 ~ 73 ~

good works He has ordained. He does not merely anoint people to work for Him; He first works on them. He does not only
give assignments; He forms the vessels that will carry the assignments. If He does not make us, He cannot trust us for His
use. Before God gives us territories, He must first possess our hearts. Before He sends us to carry others, He must first
shape us in His presence. Dear TACEFites, it takes a revived life to revive others. It takes a life that God has touched to touch
others for God.

Teachings
1. Discipleship Is the Pathway into the Lord’s Army: Joshua was not first introduced as a man with a personal vision,
platform, ambition, or ministry. He was introduced as a man under instruction. His first recorded act in battle was not self-
initiated but a response to instruction. Moses said, “Choose us out men, and go out, fight with Amalek,” and Joshua obeyed.
The first proof of readiness for divine assignment is not gifting, boldness, eloquence, or spiritual excitement. It is obedience.
Joshua could later command because he had first learned to submit. He could later lead because he had first been led. He
could later carry the burden of a nation because he first carried the instruction of his discipler without pride.
In our generation, many desire platforms without divine-making process. Many want to lead fellowships, run online
ministries, and start own outreaches, yet resist discipline, correction, and spiritual covering. This is not the Joshua pattern.
Ephesians 4:11-13 teaches us that God gives apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors, and teachers “for the perfecting of
the saints.” The word “perfecting” carries the idea of repairing, adjusting, and preparing. Discipleship serves this special
purpose of “perfecting” where self-will is broken, pride is corrected, character is repaired, obedience is tested, and Christ
is formed in us. A revival army that despises discipleship will become a crowd of untrained fighters. Joshua teaches us that
the person God will use tomorrow must be willing to be discipled today.

2. The Word Must Be Rehearsed until Truth Becomes Conviction: After the battle with Amalek, the Lord said to Moses,
“Write this for a memorial in a book, and rehearse it in the ears of Joshua.” The word “rehearse” means to repeat, recite,
remind, and reinforce until truth becomes conviction. God did not want Joshua merely to remember that Israel won a battle
but He wanted Joshua to understand the spiritual meaning of that victory. He wanted Joshua to see beyond the activities
but to understand the Word and the burden. Joshua had fought the battle and used the sword, but he also needed the
Word. Every revival army must be taught, not merely engaged in spiritual activities around us. We must not raise a
generation that only knows how to shout, sing, attend programmes, make quotable quotes, and engage in marathon fasts,
but lacks doctrinal depth and spiritual conviction.

We must learn to rehearse God’s Word into everyone around us. Fellowship leaders must rehearse the burden of revival
into younger TACEFites. Disciplers must rehearse sound doctrine into new converts. The great house of TACEF must rehearse
the vision of revival, holiness, soul-winning, prayer, discipleship, and kingdom service until it becomes the settled conviction
of the next generation. If the Word is not rehearsed, the work may be lost. If truth is not repeated, error will be normalised.

3. Mountain Encounter before Public Assignment: Exodus 24:13 says, “And Moses rose up, and his minister Joshua: and
Moses went up into the mount of God.” Joshua was not only trained in the valley of battle; he was also exposed to the
mountain of encounter. The “valley” represents the place of activity, service, responsibility, and visible assignment. It is
where Joshua fought Amalek, carried out instructions, served under Moses, and learned practical obedience. The
“mountain”, however, represents separation unto God, prayer, fasting, divine instruction, spiritual sight, waiting, and
personal encounter. The valley trained Joshua’s hands, but the mountain trained his heart. The valley taught him how to
serve, but the mountain taught him how to depend on God.

Every trusted soldier in the Lord’s army must understand both places. A believer who only knows the valley may become
active but empty, busy but dry, visible but shallow. Many can organise programmes, serve in fellowship, and carry out
assignments, yet they have no consistent secret place with God. They can fight in the valley, but they have no mountain
life. The mountain is where human noise reduces and the voice of God becomes clearer. It is where the vessel is shaped
before the assignment is enlarged.

For TACEFites, the mountain life means setting apart regular hours for prayer, fasting, meditation on the Word, and personal
retreats with God. It means deliberately creating uninterrupted time away from noise, phones, social media, entertainment,
and unnecessary conversations, so the heart can be trained in God’s presence. Beloved TACEFites, we must bring back the
mountain life. The dry bones of personal prayer must live again. The dry bones of fasting must rise again. The dry bones of
waiting on God must be restored. We cannot possess territories for Christ with empty hearts, prayerless lives, and distracted
spirits.

 ~ 74 ~

4. Personal Prayer Altar: Staying Back with God beyond Corporate Fire: Exodus 33:11 says that after Moses returned to
the camp, “his servant Joshua, the son of Nun, a young man, departed not out of the tabernacle.” This is one of the most
powerful pictures of personal hunger in Joshua’s life. Joshua followed Moses, but he did not depend on Moses’ fire. He
remained in the tabernacle. He stayed back with God. This is the foundation pf a life that will serve in the Lod’s exceeding
great army. Every kingdom soldier must have a personal altar of consistent fellowship with God. While corporate prayer is
good, whether at conventions, fellowship meetings, or online prayer gatherings, no believer can survive on corporate fire
alone. A person who only burns when others are praying will soon become cold when alone. A person who only studies the
Bible when there is a fellowship assignment will soon become shallow. A person who only responds to God during
programmes will struggle.

Joshua teaches us that a trusted soldier must learn the practice of staying back with God. Staying back means refusing to
rush away from God’s dealings. It means staying with the Word until it searches and purifies. It means staying under
conviction until repentance is complete. The Lord is calling us from crowd excitement into secret intimacy, and from
occasional encounters into daily fellowship.

Introduction
This week brings us to another mark of the trusted kingdom army: the courage to see as God sees, stand as God commands,
and walk as the Spirit leads. Joshua was not only formed in the school of obedience, Word rehearsal, mountain encounter,
and personal altar; he was also tested in the place of public pressure. When the spies returned from Canaan, all twelve saw
the same land, the same fruit, the same walls, and the same giants. Yet, they did not all see with the same eyes. Ten spies
interpreted the land through fear, unbelief, and natural limitation. Joshua and Caleb interpreted the same land through the
promise and faithfulness of God. The difference was not in what they saw physically, but in how they interpreted what they
saw spiritually.

This is a major burden for every TACEFite in this season of winning territories, advancing Christ’s Kingdom, and possessing
the land and hearts of men for the Lord. We cannot execute divine assignments with natural eyes. Natural eyes will always
see giants before God, walls before promises, impossibility before obedience, and death before revival. But spiritual eyes
see God first.

We must also note that spiritual perception does not deny the existence of challenges. The only difference is that it refuses
to magnify those challenges above the Lord. Therefore, we must see our local churches, campuses, communities,
workplaces, and The African Church the way God sees them. We do not see a dead church, but many souls waiting to know
the Lord. We do not see sinners as people destined for hell, but souls redeemed by the blood of Jesus whom we must reach
with the good news of Christ.

 ~ 78 ~

Teachings
1. Seeing Through the Eyes of Heaven: Joshua and Caleb saw the Promised Land differently because they saw through the
eyes of faith. The ten spies saw giants and concluded defeat. Joshua and Caleb saw the same giants and concluded victory
because God had spoken. Faith does not deny reality but interprets reality through God’s promise. This is what it means to
see through the eyes of heaven. It is to look at a dry and dying church and still believe revival can come. It is to see a sinful
campus and still believe souls can be saved. It is to see a difficult workplace and still believe Christ can be represented there.
It is to see a stubborn family member and still believe grace can reach them.

Many believers are defeated first by how they see. Before the children of Israel failed in action, they failed in perception.
Wrong sight produced wrong confession, and wrong confession produced wrong movement. They said, “We be not able,”
because they saw themselves as “grasshoppers”. Joshua and Caleb said, “The land is an exceeding good land,” because they
saw the land through God’s promise. A believer who does not see correctly will not speak correctly, pray correctly, serve
correctly, or move correctly. This understanding connects with the truth of our identity in Christ. A person who knows who
they are in Christ does not interpret life from fear, shame, inferiority complex, or public opinion. Ephesians 5:8 says, “For
ye were sometimes darkness, but now are ye light in the Lord: walk as children of light.” Our identity must shape our
perception. We are not grasshoppers. We are not abandoned. We are not hopeless. We are light in the Lord, created in
Christ for good works, and called to carry His light into dark places.

As a TACEFite, what do you see when you look at your local fellowship, The African Church, your campus, your workplace,
your family, or our nation? Do you see only dryness, impossibility, corruption, resistance, and weakness, or do you see a
harvest field waiting for labourers? We must pray for enlightened eyes until we see people, places, and battles the way
heaven sees them.

2. Standing Alone for God without Blending or Bending: Joshua and Caleb stood when the whole congregation turned
toward fear and rebellion. The people wanted to stone them, yet Joshua did not change his testimony to gain acceptance.
He did not dilute God’s promise to calm the crowd. He did not join unbelief because unbelief was popular. He stood with
God even when the majority stood against God. This is one of the greatest tests of a true revival army. Can you stand for
God when standing for God makes you unpopular? Can you speak the truth when everyone else prefers comfort? Can you
remain holy when immorality has become normal? Can you continue in obedience when obedience costs you acceptance?
Can you stand for revival in a place where people have become comfortable with spiritual dryness?

The fear of men is one of the greatest enemies of revival. Many know what is right, but they cannot stand because they
fear rejection, loneliness, mockery, or loss of opportunity. However, Joshua teaches us that divine trust is often built in
moments when we must choose between God and the crowd. The “stones” of men today may not be physical. They may
be gossip, false accusations, social media ridicule, workplace victimisation, or being misunderstood by people we love. Yet,
when the congregation wanted to stone Joshua and Caleb, “the glory of the LORD appeared.” When men gather stones
against those who stand for God, God releases His glory to defend His testimony.

As TACEFites, we must not blend or bend when the crowd chooses unbelief. We must stand for holiness and truth without
pride, rebellion, or harshness. Standing for God does not mean being rude. It does not mean becoming arrogant. It does
not mean dishonouring leadership or insulting others. It means holding the truth with humility, speaking with grace,
obeying God above fear, and refusing to join anything that contradicts the Word and Spirit of God.

3. Being Governed by the Spirit - Not Fleshly Boldness or Ambition: Numbers 27:18 gave another quality of Joshua as “a
man in whom is the spirit.” This is very important attribute of a member of the Lord’s army. Joshua’s courage was not
stubbornness, anger, ambition, or youthful arrogance. It was courage governed by the Spirit of God. A person may be bold
and still be proud. A person may be active and still be controlled by ambition. Therefore, not every boldness is spiritual
boldness, and not every courage is good courage. This is why the Lord told Joshua to be of “good courage” because there
is “bad courage”.

To be governed by the Spirit means that the Holy Spirit rules our motives, reactions, choices, speech, and service. It means
we do not simply do what we feel, say what we like, or react anyhow. A Spirit-led believer is led, corrected, restrained, and
empowered by the Holy Spirit.

 ~ 79 ~

In our daily lives, being governed by the Spirit may mean pausing before reacting, refusing to send an angry message,
apologising when convicted, speaking truth without bitterness, refusing to manipulate people in ministry, and allowing the
Holy Spirit to check our motives before we act.

4. Wisdom Is Required to Possess the Land for the Lord: Deuteronomy 34:9 further describes, “And Joshua the son of Nun
was full of the spirit of wisdom.” Joshua did not only need courage; he needed wisdom. Courage without wisdom can create
damage. Zeal without wisdom can scatter what God wants to gather. Passion without wisdom can become dangerous. This
is why we must remember the lesson from the 2025/2026 study that zeal must be according to knowledge. A believer may
be sincere and still be sincerely wrong if zeal is not governed by the wisdom and the Spirit of God.

Our call to possess the land and hearts of men as God’s exceeding great army require divine wisdom. Joshua had to lead
people, manage issues, confront enemies, divide inheritance, listen to God, handle crises, and maintain covenant orders.
These were not assignments for a man without a sound mind. He needed wisdom to know when to move, when to wait,
when to fight, when to listen, when to command, and when to seek God’s direction. Every revival army needs wisdom.
Wisdom is the correct application of what God has taught us through His Word and knowing when to act, how to act, and
how to serve without violating God’s order. We need wisdom to balance our spiritual life with the everyday demands of
our family life, academics, work demands, relationships, and other areas of our lives. For example, a student who neglects
lectures, assignments, and examinations in the name of fellowship activities has zeal, but not according to wisdom. An
employee who is careless at work, misses deadlines, and then claims to be persecuted for righteousness may actually be
suffering from irresponsibility. A believer who corrects others harshly in the name of holiness may have passion but lacks
the spirit of Christ.

Dear TACEFites, as God’s end-time army, we must become a people of wisdom. We must be wiser in how we plan our time,
manage our resources, prepare for the future, respond to crises, handle church administrative demands, and coordinate
the fellowship. We must be spiritually fervent and administratively precise. We must pursue revival and still excel
academically and professionally. We must win territories without damaging relationships, breaking order, or
misrepresenting Christ..
