Introduction
This week brings us to Joshua’s commissioning into the divine assignment of taking possession of the land for the Lord as
a member of the Lord’s exceeding great army. After years of discipleship, mountain exposure, staying back at the tabernacle
to pray, public testing, and spiritual formation, Joshua now hears the direct voice of God: “Moses my servant is dead; now,
therefore arise, go over this Jordan.” Divine-making process has now become commissioning. The vessel hidden in process
is now called into responsibility. The one who had been made in secret must now arise to a public assignment. We can see
clearly in our text of study that God’s commissioning begins with clear instructions, not emotion, pressure, or self-appointed
burden. Joshua did not assume his assignment but he received it from God.

 ~ 83 ~

This commissioning also begins with a painful reality: “Moses my servant is dead.” A familiar leader in Moses was gone, a
former season had ended, and a great chapter in Israel’s journey had closed. Yet, the death of Moses was not the death of
God’s promise. Joshua could not allow the painful loss of Moses, its grief, fear, or unhealthy dependency to weaken his
pursuit of what was ahead. In the same way, the fact that some people left the church, relocated, got married out, became
discouraged, or no longer stand with the fellowship must not stop the move of God in a location. TACEFites must arise in
clear instructions to do what the Lord has called them to do.

Teachings
1. Commissioning Begins with a Clear Instruction, Not Self-Appointed Burden: God said to Joshua, “Moses my servant is
dead; now therefore arise, go over this Jordan,”. The instruction was clear, direct, and specific. Joshua was not
commissioned by personal ambition, public pressure, or the desire to prove himself. He was commissioned by divine
command. This is important to note because many believers today enter spiritual activities because they feel moved,
challenged, provoked, recognised, or pressured, but not because they have received clear instructions from God. As we
learned at the convention, Ezekiel only spoke to the dry bones, as commended of the Lord.

Every army needs a command. No soldier fights correctly without instruction. No believer serves effectively without
direction. A revival army that moves without instruction will soon become exhausted. God’s assignment is specific. We do
not make assumptions about divine assignment but we must be fully persuaded through the Word, prayer, counsel, and
spiritual sensitivity. There is a difference between a burden that God gives and a reaction that comes from emotion. There
is a difference between divine commissioning and self-appointment. This is why Ephesians 2:10 is so important: “For we
are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in
them.” This verse reminds us that the works we are called to do are not self-appointed assignments but they are ordained
by God, and we are expected to discern them, embrace them, and walk faithfully in them. We do not create the assignment
and then ask God to bless it. We discover what God has ordained and then arise to obey. Therefore, before starting a work
for God, taking up a role in the church, launching an outreach, or making a major decision, we must ask: Is this God’s
command or my emotion? Is this divine burden, or personal pressure? Is this God’s timing, or my impatience?
Commissioning begins when God speaks clearly and the heart rises in obedience.

2. Arising from Seasons of Grief, Pain and Unhealthy Dependency: The first word of commissioning was “arise.” Joshua
had to rise from the weight of Moses’ death, the fear of responsibility, and the uncertainty of transition. God acknowledged
that Moses was dead, but He did not permit Joshua to build a tent around the grave of the past. The pain was real and the
loss was significant, yet, the purpose of God must continue to move forward.

Many believers remain stuck because a season has ended, but they refuse to arise. Some are sitting in grief because
something precious was lost. Some are sitting in disappointment because people they trusted hurt them. Some are sitting
in failure because they tried before and failed. Some are sitting in emotional pains because the admission, marriage, career
progress, family expectations, ministry opportunity, fruit of the womb or personal plans did not happen when expected.
Some are sitting in unhealthy dependency because the person they leaned on is no longer available. Others are discouraged
because a local fellowship has become weak after some well recognised members left, relocated, changed location, or
moved on.

We must know that the death of Moses was not the death of the promise, and the end of a season is not the end of God’s
purpose. We must not allow the past to weaken our search for what is ahead. The fact that a generation left the church,
some workers became weary, or a leader moved away must not stop the move of God in a local fellowship, church,
community or a generation. God does not deny the pain of the past, but He does not allow the past to become a prison.
He does not ignore the wound, but He calls us to live beyond the wound. There is a Jordan still to cross, a people still to
carry, a land still to possess, and an assignment still waiting. Dear TACEFites, arise.

3. Discerning “This Jordan” as the Specific Work or Territory God Is Assigning: God did not say to Joshua, “Go everywhere.”
He said, “Go over this Jordan.” The word “this” shows that God is always specific in divine assignments. There was a
particular river to cross before Joshua, a particular barrier between God’s people and their inheritance, and a particular
obedience required at that moment. Every believer, fellowship, and family must discern “this Jordan.”

There are many needs in the world, but God may assign a particular burden to a particular vessel. A person who does not
discern their Jordan may become busy, active, and everywhere, yet accomplish little or nothing for the Lord. Some people

 ~ 84 ~

are attracted to every activity but committed to no ordained assignment. Some move from tasks to tasks, ministries to
ministries and one online platform to another. Some admire the promised land from afar but never cross the specific Jordan
God has placed before them. Discerning and knowing “this Jordan” requires prayer, counsel, spiritual sensitivity, patience,
and obedient action. Until we cross the Jordan God has placed before us, we may keep discussing inheritance without
possessing it.

We must also remember that God said, “Go over this Jordan, thou, and all this people.” Joshua was not called to cross
alone. His assignment was not a private success; it was leadership that carried others into inheritance. Revival soldiers do
not cross alone. A selfish Christian is satisfied with personal progress, but a revival vessel asks, “Who else must cross with
me?” Who is weak and needs strengthening? Who is young in faith and needs discipleship? Who has missed the way and
needs guidance? Who is discouraged and needs encouragement? The true commissioned army carries others into God’s
purpose through prayer, discipleship, example, care, and leadership.

4. Being Strong in the Lord and Not in Personal Ability: God repeatedly told Joshua, “Be strong and of a good courage.”
This command was not a call to self-confidence but a call to total dependence on God. Joshua was not strong because
enemies were absent but was strong because God was present. God said, “I will not fail thee, nor forsake thee.” The promise
of God’s presence was the foundation of Joshua’s courage.

Ephesians 6 gives us the New Testament language of this strength: “Be strong in the Lord, and in the power of his might.”
We are not to be strong in ourselves, our titles, our experience, our certificates, our intelligence, our family background,
our past success, or expertise. Having a degree from a College of Theology, a mission training certificate, degrees abroad or
years of experience are good, but they are not enough. The commissioned army must be strong in the Lord and clothed
with the whole armour of God.
This is why Joshua was also commanded to keep the book of the law in his mouth and meditate therein day and night.
Courage without the Word of God is an error. Assignment without the Word becomes worthless. Warfare without the Word
becomes dangerous. The principle of the whole armour of God teaches us that we wrestle against spiritual forces, wrong
thoughts, corrupt systems, ungodly patterns, and every opposition that rises against the knowledge and purpose of God.
Therefore, TACEFites must put on truth, righteousness, the gospel of peace, faith, salvation, the Word of God, and prayer.
We must stand against systems that normalise sin, weaken discipleship, silence evangelism, and oppose revival. We must
reject fear, discouragement, prayerlessness, compromise, and unbelief.

 courage, decisions, speech, and kingdom service.

 trials, the Word in confession, and prayer in all situations.

 achievement, or human confidence. Be strong in the Lord, and in the power of His might.

Introduction
This week brings us to a very important truth in the life of Joshua and in the mandate of every revival army: what God gives
must still be possessed. The Lord said to Joshua, “Every place that the sole of your foot shall tread upon, that have I given
unto you.” The land had already been given by divine promise, yet it still required obedient effort, courageous action, and
practical possession. God’s promise did not remove Joshua’s responsibility. The inheritance was real, but Joshua and the
children of Israel still had to arise, tread upon the land, confront resistance, obey the Word, and move forward in the
assurance of God’s presence.

This same principle is confirmed in Ephesians. Paul declares that God “hath blessed us with all spiritual blessings in heavenly
places in Christ,” and that “we have obtained an inheritance.” In Christ, we are not trying to get an inheritance; we already
have it. Indeed, we are not begging for what heaven has not released but we are stepping into what God has already given.
This is how every revival army must see the souls of men. They are the inheritance of God, already purchased by the blood
of Christ, and we are called to reclaim them for the Lord. That troublesome child, that sinful adult, that corrupt community,
that idolatrous village, that perverse association, and every territory under the influence of darkness must be seen as part
of God’s inheritance to be reclaimed for its rightful Owner, as we go forth as the Lord’s army to possess thew land as our
inheritance in Christ.

Teachings

1. What God Gives Must Still Be Possessed: God told Joshua, “Every place that the sole of your foot shall tread upon, that
have I given unto you.” This statement brings together two important truths: divine gift and human responsibility. God had
given the land, but Israel still had to possess it. The promise was settled in heaven, but obedient action was required on
earth. A land can be promised but not occupied. A territory can be assigned but not taken. A soul can be paid for by the
blood of Jesus and still remained in the captivity of sin if those sent to reach that soul refuse to step out. This is a major

 ~ 88 ~

principle in the work of revival. God may give a burden, a promise, a territory, a people, or a ministry assignment, but His
people must still arise and possess it. A local church may belong to the Lord, but revival will not be experienced there if the
people God has sent refuse to pray, teach, disciple, evangelise, and serve. A campus may be full of souls Jesus died for, but
those souls will not automatically come to Christ if no one steps out to preach, pray, invite, counsel, and follow them up.

Many believers love promises but avoid possession. They can quote what God has said, but they do not move their feet in
obedience. They pray for revival but do not actively serve in their local churches. They ask God for souls but do not speak
to sinners. They desire growth in the fellowship but do not invite anyone. They want to see souls saved but do not make
themselves available in the children’s ministry, Sunday School classes, or any channel through which the lost can be
reached. Dear TACEFites, what God gives must be possessed. What Christ has paid for must be claimed.

2. Our Feet Must Tread from a Position of Victory in Christ: The promise in Joshua 1:3 was connected to the movement
of their feet. God did not say, “Every place you admire from afar.” He did not say, “Every place you discuss.” He did not
say, “Every place you complain about.” He said, “Every place that the sole of your foot shall tread upon.” This means
possession requires presence and active engagement. Many territories remain untouched because believers have refused
to tread upon them. However, our feet must tread from a position of victory, not fear. This means that we do not fight for
victory but we fight from victory. We do not step into our local churches, campuses, families, workplaces, or communities
as defeated people hoping to survive or win. We step in as children of God, complete in Christ, blessed in Christ, and sent
to enforce what Christ has already secured.

It is also to understand that the call to “tread upon the land” means we must show up where God has sent us. It means
being present, available, and responsible. It means going back to the local church with a burden, not as a critic, but as a
servant. It means going back to the campus with soul-winning fire, not merely as a student pursuing a certificate. It means
serving in children’s church with tears for the next generation, not just because the church listed our names in the roster
for the children church routine attendance. Possession cannot happen from a distance. New converts will not be discipled
from a distance. Backsliders will not be restored by distant wishes. Feet must tread upon the land. The land is possessed
when obedient feet begin to move from the confidence of what Christ has already won.

3. Souls Are the Lord’s Heritage by Creation and Redemption: When God spoke to Joshua, He spoke about land and
inheritance. In Ephesians 1:11, Paul declares that in Christ “we have obtained an inheritance.” In Joshua, the inheritance
involved land but in Christ, the inheritance is deeper, spiritual, eternal, and connected to God’s purpose in redeeming men
unto Himself. The souls of all men are the Lord’s heritage. They belong to Him first by creation, because all things were
made for His pleasure. No man was created for the devil. No child was created for darkness. No youth was created for sin.
No family was created for destruction. No community was created to be ruled by wickedness. Every soul was created for
God’s pleasure, God’s glory, and God’s purpose.

Beyond creation, souls also belong to Christ by redemption. Jesus has already paid for them with His blood. Therefore,
when we go out to win souls, we are not trying to purchase what has not been paid for but we are claiming for the Lord
what already belongs to Him. We are entering the field to recover divine inheritance. We are announcing to darkness that
these lives are not its lawful property because Christ has paid the full price. This understanding changes how we labour as
a revival army. The souls in our local churches, campuses, families, choir, children’s departments, communities,
workplaces, and church societies are precious to God. They are not mere numbers but are eternal souls. They are the
heritage of the Lord. Christ suffered, died, and rose again so that they may be reconciled to God.

When we see souls as the Lord’s heritage, we will not ignore the backslider. We will not despise the weak believer. We will
not abandon the new convert. We will not treat children as distractions. We will not treat youths as troublesome. We will
not treat unbelievers as enemies. We will see them as souls created for God and purchased by Christ, waiting to be
reclaimed through prayer, love, truth, evangelism, and discipleship.

4. The Word and Divine Presence Must Govern the Possessing Army: God tied Joshua’s success to the Word of God. He
said, “This book of the law shall not depart out of thy mouth; but thou shalt meditate therein day and night.” This means
possession is not sustained by human strategy but only by the Word of God. A revival army who will possess the land for
the Lord must be governed by the Word of God, not human excitement. We must know the Word, meditate on the Word,
speak the Word, and obey the Word.

 ~ 89 ~

Every kingdom soldier must be a Word-shaped army. We must not build revival on human opinions or emotional quotable
quotes. The Word of God alone must be our message, our weapon, and our guide. Meditation on the Word comes next as
the mean of taking the Word beyond reading into reflection, internalisation, obedience, and daily living. The Word of God
must enter our hearts until it shapes our minds, governs our tongues, directs our feet, and controls all our existence.

God also gave Joshua the assurance of His presence: “Be not afraid, neither be thou dismayed: for the LORD thy God is with
thee whithersoever thou goest.” Divine presence is the cure for fear and discouragement. Fear is natural when the
assignment is bigger than our strength, but God’s answer to fear is His presence. We do not go out for the Lord on our own
charge. The Lord goes with us. His presence gives courage, wisdom, protection, and fruitfulness. The land may be hard, but
God is with us. The people may resist, but God is with us. The assignment may be heavy, but God is with us. Therefore, we
must arise, tread, and possess for the Lord.

Section 2: The Harvest, Leading, Memory, and Consecration of God’s Army - How God Prepares His People to Enter,
Preserve, and Possess New Territories

The journey of God’s end-time army is not only about divine making; it is also about entering the land with the right eyes,
the right leading, the right memory, and the right consecration. After God has made a vessel, He begins to show that vessel
the harvest hidden inside difficult territories. Jericho was not only a city of walls, resistance, and judgement; it was also the
place where Rahab was waiting for mercy. Jordan was not only a river to be crossed; it was a place where God’s presence
had to lead the people into a new season. The memorial stones were not ordinary stones; they were witnesses of divine
acts that must be preserved for the next generation. Gilgal was not merely a campsite; it was the place where the reproach
of Egypt had to be rolled away before the army could move into victory.

 ~ 92 ~

God does not send His army into the land with natural eyes, careless movement, forgetful hearts, or unbroken flesh. He
first teaches them to see harvest where others see only sin, to follow His presence rather than rush ahead in assumptions,
to preserve His works through remembrance and testimony, and to cut away the old life before entering new inheritance.
The army that will possess the land must understand that conquest is not only about outward activity; it requires mercy for
souls, sensitivity to divine leading, remembrance of God’s dealings, and a life separated unto the Lord.

Ephesians explains this meaning through the analogy of how those who were once far off are made nigh by the blood of
Christ. Through Him, we have access by one Spirit unto the Father and are built together for an habitation of God through
the Spirit. We are called to live to the praise of His glory and commanded to put off the old man and put on the new man
in righteousness and true holiness. Therefore, God’s army must not only move; it must move by redemption, divine leading,
remembrance, and consecration.
This second section therefore calls TACEFites to see the land beyond its walls, challenges, and limitations. God has Rahabs
in Jericho, hidden harvests in hard places, testimonies that must be preserved, and old reproaches that must be rolled away
as we submit to the circumcision of the heart that cuts away the flesh before conquest.

 • Week 6: Rahab and the First Fruits of the Land - The Power of Redemption to Save All Men: Rahab teaches us
 that God has souls in unlikely places, and that redemption reaches people whom men have written off. She was an
 outsider in Jericho, yet, she responded by faith to what she heard about the God of Israel. The scarlet cord became
 a sign of rescue, mercy, and redemption, pointing us to the blood of Christ that brings the far off near. We must
 not despise so-called sinners, difficult youths, morally broken people, or communities that appear hard.
 • Week 7: Crossing Jordan - Moving by Divine Leading into New Territories: The crossing of Jordan teaches us that
 God’s army must never move ahead of His presence. Before Israel crossed, Joshua commanded the people to
 sanctify themselves, and the ark had to go before the army. The waters did not part while the priests stood at a
 distance; they opened when obedience stepped into the river. TACEFites must not enter new seasons without
 spiritual direction. We must ask: Has God led this? Is it consistent with His Word? Is there peace in the Spirit?
 • Week 8: Memorial Stones - Preserving Revival Testimonies for the Next Generation: The memorial stones teach
 us that God’s works must be remembered, explained, documented, and passed on. Divine encounters are not only
 to be celebrated; they are to become teaching tools for covenant continuity. If testimonies are not preserved,
 future generations may become detached from the source of the vision. TACEFites must therefore develop the
 discipline of remembrance, documenting personal encounters, answered prayers, convention burdens, prophetic
 instructions, and testimonies of God’s faithfulness.
 • Week 9: Gilgal and the Circumcised Army - Consecration Before Victory: Gilgal teaches us that the old life cannot
 possess new inheritance. The flesh cannot carry what God has prepared. Ephesians calls us to put off the old man

Introduction
This week brings us to the story of Rahab, the first fruit of mercy in the land that Israel was about to possess. Before the
walls of Jericho fell, before the armies of Israel marched around the city, and before the land was taken in battle, God had
already identified a soul inside Jericho who would respond to faith. Rahab was a woman of Jericho, a city marked for
judgement. She was also described as a harlot, carrying a reputation that many people would have used to condemn her
or conclude that nothing good could come out of her life. Yet, when the two spies came into Jericho, Rahab received them
into her house, hid them from danger, and protected them at her own personal risk. If she had been discovered, she could
have paid dearly for standing with the people of God. But her heart had already been touched by what she had heard about
the God of Israel.

Rahab did not merely hide the spies because she was afraid of Israel; she confessed faith in the Lord. She said, “I know that
the LORD hath given you the land” (Joshua 2:9), and also declared, “for the LORD your God, he is God in heaven above, and
in earth beneath” (Joshua 2:11). Rahab heard and believed. Her faith moved her to action. She protected the spies, pleaded
for mercy for herself and her household, and asked for a true token that they would be spared when Israel returned to take
over the land. The spies promised her that if she bound the scarlet line in her window and gathered her family into her
house, they would be preserved when judgement came upon Jericho.

This is why Rahab’s story is so important. She lived in an unlikely place, carried an unlikely reputation, and belonged to an
unlikely people, yet grace found her. Rahab represents the outsider brought near by faith. Ephesians explains this gospel
mystery clearly: those who were once far off are made nigh by the blood of Christ. This means redemption is wider than
human bias, deeper than social shame, and greater than the labels people put on others. Rahab’s past did not stop the
mercy of God. Her location did not stop the purpose of God. Her reputation did not stop the grace of God. She heard,
believed, acted, and was saved. This is the heart of the gospel. Jesus died for all men, not only for those who already look
religious or morally acceptable. Therefore, we must not despise the so-called sinners, difficult youths, backsliders,
unsupportive elders, morally broken people, or communities that appear hard and idolatrous. God desires all men to be
saved. Our mission field includes people others have written off. We must stop seeing The African Church, our campuses,
and our communities only through the lens of obvious challenges and limitations. We must see a harvest waiting to be
claimed for the Lord.

1. God Has Souls in Unlikely Places: Joshua sent two spies to view the land, but God used that journey to reveal a soul
prepared for mercy inside Jericho. Rahab was not in Israel. She was not among the covenant people. She did not have the
background, reputation, or outward appearance that many would have expected from a person God would save. She was
a prostitute and a chronic sinner, yet she became the first fruits of the land. This is the wonder of redemption. God is able
to find a soul in a house on the wall, in a city marked for judgement, and in a life carrying terrible moral history.

This is important for every revival army. We must not allow a person’s past, appearance, weakness, age, behaviour, social
reputation, or present resistance to make us conclude that such a person is beyond redemption. Many people we call
difficult may simply be waiting for the light of the gospel. Some children we call troublesome may be future vessels in God’s
hand. Some youths we call stubborn, may become candidates of discipleship. Some adults we call hardened may be carrying
silent fears, hidden convictions, and unanswered questions. Some backsliders we avoid may be waiting for someone to
restore them in love.
Ephesians 2 reminds us that we also were once strangers, without hope, and without God in the world. If grace brought us
near, grace can bring others near. A true revival army must never look at people only through the lens of their sins. We
must see them through the blood of Christ. We must believe that God still has souls in unlikely places.

2. Rahab’s Faith Responded to What She Heard: Hearing Can Become Saving Faith: Rahab told the spies, “We have heard
how the LORD dried up the water of the Red sea for you.” What she heard became the doorway through which faith entered
her heart. She had not seen the Red Sea open. She was not physically present when Israel defeated Sihon and Og. Yet, the
testimony of God’s works travelled to Jericho, and Rahab believed. She confessed, “For the LORD your God, he is God in
heaven above, and in earth beneath.”

This shows the power of hearing. A soul may be far from God, but a testimony, a message, a Bible study, a simple invitation,
a personal witness, or a loving conversation can awaken faith. If Rahab believed because she heard, then how shall others
hear if we do not speak? How shall difficult youths hear if nobody patiently teaches them? How shall backsliders hear if
nobody follows them up? How shall the morally broken hear if the church only condemns them from afar? How shall our

 ~ 95 ~

campuses hear if we remain silent? How shall our communities hear if we refuse to preach the love, mercy, holiness, and
saving power of Christ?

The gospel must be heard before it can be believed. Scripture says, “So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the
word of God” (Romans 10:17). This means that saving faith is awakened when the message of Christ is clearly declared and
received by the heart. Many people are not yet saved, not because they are beyond redemption, but because no one has
explained the love of God to them with clarity, compassion, and conviction. Some have seen church activities, attended
religious programmes, heard spiritual songs, or watched believers from afar, yet they have not truly heard the saving
message of the cross. Rahab’s faith began with what she heard. She said, “For we have heard how the LORD dried up the
water of the Red sea for you” (Joshua 2:10). What she heard created fear, conviction, faith, and a cry for mercy. In the same
way, someone around us may be waiting to hear the gospel in a way that opens their heart to God. Someone we think does
not qualify for the mercy of God like Rahab, may be closer to salvation than we think, if only someone will lovingly and
patiently speak to them about the love of God and the new life available in Christ.

3. The Scarlet Cord Represents Redemption and the Blood that Brings the Far Off Near: The spies instructed Rahab to bind
the scarlet line in the window as a sign, so that she and her household would not be destroyed when they came to attack
the city of Jericho. That scarlet cord became the visible mark of rescue, the sign of covenant mercy, and the boundary
between destruction and preservation. Rahab’s house was inside a city appointed for judgement, yet, the scarlet cord
marked her household for deliverance. This points us to the greater redemption we have in Christ. Ephesians 2:13 says,
“But now in Christ Jesus ye who sometimes were far off are made nigh by the blood of Christ.” As the scarlet cord
distinguished Rahab’s house in Jericho, the blood of Jesus brings the sinner near to God, marks the redeemed for mercy,
and delivers those who believe from judgement.

Rahab was far off by nationality, lifestyle, history, and location. But mercy brought her near. In the same way, the blood of
Jesus brings the far off near. It can bring the sinner near. It can bring the backslider near. It can bring the broken near. It can
bring the idolater near. It can bring the corrupt adult near. It can bring the rejected, wounded, ashamed, and morally
entangled near. The blood of Christ does not merely cover respectable people; it saves sinners who repent and believe.

This must shape how we evangelise. We are not sent to announce that people are too far gone. We are sent to announce
that the blood of Jesus is powerful enough to bring them near. The scarlet cord also reminds us that redemption requires
a response. Rahab had to bind the line in the window. She had to gather her household inside. She had to act on the
promise. In the same way, those who hear the gospel must respond by faith, repentance, and obedience. True salvation
produces visible turnaround. Rahab did not just admire the message; she acted on it. Repentance must move from hearing
to obedience, from conviction to action, and from fear of judgement to faith in God’s mercy.

4. Every Revival Army Must Discern Harvest and See People beyond Their Sins: The spies went to view the land, but what

Introduction
This week brings us to the crossing of Jordan, a major turning point in the journey of Israel and in the making of God’s end-
time army. God’s people had come to a boundary between promise and possession. Behind them were years of wilderness
journeying; before them was the land God had sworn to give. Yet, before they could step into new territory, they had to
learn a crucial lesson: God’s people must not move without divine leading. We do not live our lives by assumptions,
pressures, competitions, trends, or human calculations. Joshua did not tell the people to rush forward because the land
was so close. He commanded them to watch for the ark of the covenant and follow it. The presence of God had to go
before the Lord’s great and exceeding army.

 ~ 99 ~

Jordan represents every new season, new assignment, new territory, new responsibility, and new level of obedience that
God brings before His people. It may be a new burden in the local church, a campus outreach, a family altar to be rebuilt,
a career decision, a ministry step, a marital decision, a financial decision, a business move, a change of location, a home
decision, or a call to serve in a new role. The principle is the same: do not enter new territories without spiritual directions.
Before taking major steps, we must ask: Has God led this? Is this consistent with His Word? Is there peace in the Spirit? Are
we following the ark, or are we following assumptions?

Joshua Chapter 3 also teaches that consecration precedes possession. Before the miracle of Jordan, Joshua said, “Sanctify
yourselves: for to morrow the LORD will do wonders among you.” God’s wonders are not to be handled by an unclean army.
The people had to be set apart and ready to follow God’s presence. Israel was also commanded to keep a space between
themselves and the ark so they could clearly see the way. This teaches careful spiritual sensitivity, not careless rushing.
God’s presence must be more important than speed. It is better to move slowly with God than to run quickly outside His
leading.

Teachings
1. Consecration Precedes Possession: Before Israel crossed Jordan, Joshua commanded the people, “Sanctify yourselves:
for tomorrow the LORD will do wonders among you.” This shows that the miracle of possession required a sanctified people.
Crossing Jordan was not an ordinary movement from one riverbank to another. It was a sacred transition into covenant
inheritance. The people were about to step into a land that God had promised, but they could not step into it casually. The
vessel that enters new territory for the Lord must first be separated unto the Lord.

Consecration means being set apart for God. It means allowing the Lord to cleanse our motives, desires, relationships,
habits, and hidden life through His Word and continued fellowship of the Holy Spirit. We cannot desire God’s wonders
without God’s dealings. We cannot want open doors without clean hands. We cannot long for new territories of divine
lifting in life and career without renewed hearts.
For TACEFites, consecration must precede every major life cycle. Before taking a leadership role, there must be heart-
searching. Before starting a new work, there must be surrender. Before entering a new season in academics, career,
business, marriage, ministry, or family life, there must be a renewed separation unto God. An army that will cross Jordan
must first allow God to purify its camp.

2. The Ark Must Go Before the Army Because God’s Presence Must Lead Every Effort: Joshua commanded the people
that when they saw the ark of the covenant of the LORD and the priests bearing it, they should remove from their place
and go after it. The ark represented the presence and leading of God among His people. Israel was not to move because
the river was so close or because the people were anxious. They were to move when the ark moved. God’s presence had
to lead the army.

This is a vital lesson for us. The fact that an opportunity is attractive does not mean the ark is going before us. The fact that
others are rushing to exploit a business trend does not mean we must rush. Israel was told to keep a distance from the ark
so they could clearly see the way, because they had not passed that way before. New territories require fresh leading.
Yesterday’s method is not be enough for today’s crossing. Familiar experience must be replaced with present guidance.
Therefore, God’s presence must lead every effort: academics, career, ministry, marriage, finance, business, home,
investment, relocation, and everyday decisions. Even something as simple as praying over a meal should not be empty
religion, but a practical acknowledgement that the Lord leads all actions. Before taking major steps, we must ask: Have I
prayed? Have I received godly counsel? Am I following the ark.

3. Spiritual Leadership Carries Responsibility Before the People: The priests who carried the ark entered Jordan first
before the people, and they stood firm in the river until all Israel passed over to the other side. This is a powerful picture
of spiritual leadership. Leaders do not merely give instructions from a safe distance; they carry responsibility before the
people. The priests had to step into the river first and they had to remain in position until everyone crossed.

Every leader at home, in the workplace, in school, in the church, and in fellowship must understand this principle. Our call
to lead is not a title to display, but a burden to carry. Leadership is not sitting in front, giving instructions, being recognised,
or enjoying respect. True leadership is sacrificial responsibility. It means carrying people in prayer, bearing burdens that
others may not see, taking responsibility before others are ready, and standing firm until those entrusted to us are helped

 ~ 100 ~

to cross. The priests did not send the people into Jordan while they watched from a safe distance. They entered first, stood
in the midst of the river, and remained there until all Israel passed over.

This speaks to every kind of leader. A father must not only provide money; he must go first in prayer, discipline, love,
patience, integrity, and spiritual example. A mother must not only organise the home; she must model faith, sacrifice,
watchfulness, and godly affection. Parents must not demand from children what they are unwilling to practise. A class
captain, school prefect, fellowship executive, subgroup leader, choir leader, children’s church teacher, business manager,
team lead, or church worker must understand that leadership requires extra sacrifice. Leaders may need to arrive first and
leave last. They may need to sacrifice meals to ensure others are cared for. They may need to give up personal comfort,
sleep, convenience, and leisure so that the people under their care are guided, protected, encouraged, and established. A
leader cannot be late and expect punctuality from others. A leader cannot be prayerless and expect spiritual fire in the
fellowship. A leader cannot be unserious with assignments and expect excellence from the team. A leader cannot be selfish
and expect sacrifice from others. Those who lead must go first in consecration, prayer, punctuality, humility, responsibility,
sacrifice, and faithfulness. Their lives must become a pattern others can safely follow.

4. God Opens the Way When His People Obey: Jordan did not divide while the priests were still standing at a distance.
The waters parted when the feet of the priests that carried the ark touched the edge of the river. This shows that obedience
is the place where God confirms His promise. Many people want the river to open before they move, but God requires
obedient movement before the way becomes clear. Faith does not wait for every difficulty to disappear before obeying
God. Faith steps forward because God has spoken.
Jordan was overflowing its banks at the time of harvest. Naturally, it was not the easiest time to cross. We can imagine the
force of the waves at Bar Beach in Lagos, or the frightening movement of any major river anywhere in the world when the
waters are high and restless. Yet, this was the very moment God chose to display His power. The overflowing river did not
stop the living God. The challenge before the people became the stage on which God revealed His presence. This teaches
us that difficult seasons do not cancel divine instructions. When God commands, He also makes a way. When His people
obey, He confirms His presence with them. God who parted Jordan is still able to make a way for His people.

 zonal officer, carry people in prayer, example, follow-up, patience, and sacrifice.
 • Take the first obedient step: Once God has clearly led, do not remain permanently at the riverbank. It is time to
 act. Send that CV or business proposal, start the prayer altar, make the restitution, or take the specific step of
 obedience in response to the Lord.

Introduction
This week brings us to the memorial stones taken from the midst of Jordan after the children of Israel crossed over on dry
ground. God did not want Israel merely to enjoy the miracle and move on. He commanded Joshua to appoint twelve men,
one from each tribe, to take twelve stones from the place where the priests’ feet stood firm in Jordan. These stones were
to be carried along into the new land and set up as a memorial. The miracle was not to be forgotten and the place of divine
intervention was not to be treated casually. The story of God’s mighty hand was not to end with the generation that
experienced it.

In essence, the memorial stones were not ordinary stones. They were teaching stones, witness stones, memory stones,
testimony stones, and covenant stones. They were physical reminders of a spiritual encounter. This shows that God’s acts
must not only be celebrated; they must be explained. If a generation only celebrates divine encounters but does not explain
their meanings, the next generation may inherit activities without understanding the God behind them. They may inherit
programmes without burden, vision statements without conviction, history without encounter, and fellowship without fire.

This is a major burden for TACEF in this season. We must not become forgetful in our journey with God. We must not forget
how the Lord has helped us, corrected us, preserved us, revived us, instructed us, and carried us in different seasons. The
culture of remembrance, reflection, and testimony must become part of our personal and collective walk with God. Every
answered prayer, every convention encounter, every prophetic instruction, every visitation of God, every local fellowship
story, every personal deliverance, every divine leading, and every testimony of God’s faithfulness must be preserved with
reverence. God’s acts are teaching tools for covenant continuity.

Teachings
1. God’s Works Must Be Remembered: After the crossing of Jordan, God immediately instructed Joshua to raise a
memorial. This shows that God does not want His people to forget His works. In everyday life, we naturally preserve
important memories. We save pictures, record videos, back up files, and even buy extra memory cards so that precious
moments are not lost. If we take such care to preserve human memories, how much more should we preserve the acts,
instructions, and testimonies of God? The same God who opened Jordan also commanded Israel to remember the opening
of Jordan. The miracle was not complete until it became a memorial. The testimony was not to remain only with those who
saw it; it had to be preserved for those who would come after them.

Forgetfulness is dangerous in the journey of faith. A people who forget what God has done may soon complain when new
challenges arise. A believer who forgets past mercies may become fearful before new battles. A fellowship that forgets the
sacrifices, prayers, tears, instructions, and visitations that shaped its beginning may become casual with the vision. A revival
army that forgets its source will soon become detached from the fire that gave it life.

This is why the act of remembrance is actually a form of spiritual warfare. When we remember rightly, faith is strengthened.
When we remember God’s faithfulness, fear loses its power. When we remember answered prayers, we gain courage to
pray again. When we remember divine instructions, we avoid careless wandering. When we remember how the Lord helped
us before, we are strengthened to trust Him for what is ahead.

2. Encounters with God and Foundational Truths Must Be Explained to the Younger Generation: The memorial stones
were designed to provoke questions from children. Joshua said, “When your children shall ask their fathers in time to come,
saying, What mean these stones?” The answer was not to be, “These are old stones.” The answer was to explain the mighty
act of God: “Israel came over this Jordan on dry land.” This teaches us that testimonies must be interpreted, not merely
displayed. Divine encounters must be explained, not merely celebrated.

Every generation has a responsibility to explain God’s dealings to the next generation. Children, teenagers, youths, new
converts, and younger believers must not only see our activities and vague testimonies without details; they must
understand our convictions, commitments and consecrations. They must not only attend conventions; they must
understand the burden of the convention. They must not only hear about revival; they must understand the price, purpose,
purity, and power of revival. They must not only join fellowship; they must understand the vision, doctrine, sacrifice, prayer,
holiness, evangelism, discipleship, and burden that shaped the fellowship.

 ~ 105 ~

A generation that inherits activities without explanation may continue the form but lose the fire. They may repeat the
language but miss the essence. They may attend the meetings but miss the meaning. This is why discipleship-based
knowledge-sharing is important. We must intentionally explain the foundational truths that shaped the vision. Parents must
explain God’s faithfulness to their children. Fellowship leaders must explain the burden of the fellowship to new members.
As a fellowship, we must therefore raise ‘explainers’, not only organisers. We need people who can explain why we pray,
why we preach holiness, why we labour for souls, why we serve, why we honour the Word, why we focus on local
fellowships, and why we do not do certain things even when many other believers do them. What is not explained may be
misunderstood. What is misunderstood may be neglected. What is neglected may be lost.

3. Memorials Strengthen Future Faith by Connecting Present Obedience to Past Divine Acts: The stones from Jordan
connected the present generation to what God had done. They were reminders that Israel did not cross Jordan by human
strength. They crossed because the Lord dried up the waters. Joshua also connected Jordan to the Red Sea during the time
of Moses when they left Egypt, saying that the Lord dried up Jordan “as the LORD your God did to the Red sea.” This means
that God wanted Israel to see continuity in His works. The God who made a way before was still the God who made a way
again. Memorials strengthen faith because they remind us that God has a record of faithfulness. When we face a new
Jordan, remembrance tells us that He has opened waters before. When we face new resistance, remembrance tells us that
He has delivered before. When we face new responsibilities, remembrance tells us that He has strengthened before. When
we face new seasons of uncertainty, remembrance tells us that He has led before. The memory of past divine acts becomes
fuel for present obedience.

This is why testimonials, such as the TACEF Stories Series shared as part of TACEF at 30, must not be treated as
entertainment. A carefully curated testimony is not merely a story that makes people clap; it is a weapon of faith. It is a
reminder of God’s nature, a witness of His faithfulness, and a declaration that the God who did it before can do it again
according to His will and purpose. Every TACEFite must therefore learn to build personal memorials. Keep records of
answered prayers. Write down instructions received during conventions, retreats, Bible studies, personal prayers, and
moments of conviction. Please document how God led you, corrected you, delivered you, helped you, and provided for
you. When future battles come, you can return to those memorial stones and say, “The Lord helped me before, and He is
still faithful.” Through such remembrance, we war a good warfare.

4. Forgetfulness Weakens Revival Continuity and Makes New Generations Vulnerable to Spiritual Decline: One of the
greatest enemies of the continuity of the move of revival and personal life progress is forgetfulness. When a generation
forgets God’s works, it begins to lose reverence for God’s ways. When people forget the source of the fire, they may start
depending on structures, marketing strategy, titles, noise, numbers, social media trends and human strength. When future
generations do not understand how the Lord led, they may assume that the work can continue without the same
consecration, prayer, sacrifice, purity, and obedience that originally birthed it. Forgetfulness makes new generations
vulnerable to spiritual decline. It creates room for compromise, error, and detachment. A generation that does not know
the sacrificial cost of raising an altar of revival on a campus or a local church may easily despise the altar. A generation that
does not understand the burden of soul-winning may reduce fellowship to social gathering. A generation that does not
know the Word may be moved by trends and shallow excitement.

This is why disciple-makers must build others through their lives. We must not only document testimonies and stories of
encounters in books, files, pictures, recordings, and archives; we must also become living memorials. Our lives must explain
what God has done. Our lifestyles must preserve the truth we preach. Our sacrifices must show younger believers that
revival is not a quotable quote. Our consistency must teach them faithfulness. Our sacrificial giving must show them that
nothing is too big to be laid down for the Lord. Dearly beloved TACEFites, we must pass on the burden, not only the brand.
We must pass on the fire, not only the format. We must pass on the doctrine, not only the documents. We must pass on
the mandate, and the best channel is our own lives.

5. Step-by-Step Applications and Practical Implications
 • Develop a personal memorial journal: Begin to document your personal walk with God. Buy a special jotter or
 create a virtual journal on your phone with cloud back-up to write down answered prayers, divine instructions,
 Bible study insights, convention encounters, warnings, corrections, testimonies, and moments of clear leading.
 • Explain testimonies clearly and in details: Do not only say, “God did it.” Explain what God taught, how He led, what
 obedience was required, what faith was exercised, and what the testimony should produce in the next generation.

 ~ 106 ~

• Build archives of God’s faithfulness: Keep records of convention burdens, prayer themes, prophetic instructions,
 local fellowship stories, campus outreaches, and ministry milestones.
 • Use testimonies as teaching tools: Let testimonies lead to discipleship, obedience, and renewed faith. Do not
 reduce testimonies to emotional excitement or public applause.
 • Remember every instruction and leading: Revisit what the Lord has spoken to you personally and collectively. Ask
 yourself whether you have obeyed and passed on what God entrusted to you.
 • Become a living memorial: Let your life preserve the testimony of God’s grace. Let everyone see in your sacrificial
 living, prayer life, holiness, faithfulness, and love the truth of the God you speak about.

Questions for Discussion

without teaching their meanings? Am I preserving the burden of revival through my words, lifestyle, and discipleship? Am
I a living memorial of God’s grace, or am I a broken link in the chain of revival continuity? Am I using those testimonies to
war a good warfare?

Title: Gilgal and the Circumcised Army: Consecration Before Victory

Bible Texts: Joshua 5:1-9; Ephesians 4:22-24; Ephesians 5:1-8

Key Extracts from the Bible Texts to Remember and Reflect On
 • Make thee sharp knives, and circumcise again the children of Israel the second time.
 • This day have I rolled away the reproach of Egypt from off you.
 • Put off concerning the former conversation the old man.
 • Be renewed in the spirit of your mind.
 • Put on the new man, which after God is created in righteousness and true holiness.
 • For ye were sometimes darkness, but now are ye light in the Lord: walk as children of light.

Introduction
Our study this week introduces us to the encounter at Gilgal, the place where God dealt with the inner condition of His
army before they moved deeper into the path of victory. Israel had crossed Jordan by divine leading. The waters had parted
into two for them to walk through the dry land. The priests had stood firm. The people had entered the land. The fear of
the Lord had already fallen upon the kings of the Amorites and the Canaanites. Naturally, this looked like the perfect time
to move quickly into battle and take over the land completely. But God stopped the army at Gilgal before they moved to
Jericho. They had to go through a process of circumcision. Before the conquest of the land that is ahead of them, there had
to be consecration. Before public victory, there had to be private cutting away of the flesh.

 ~ 109 ~

Gilgal teaches us that we cannot possess the new while still carrying the old life. The people had crossed Jordan, but the
reproach of Egypt still had to be rolled away. They had entered the land geographically, but they needed covenant identity
spiritually. This is a serious lesson for every TACEFite. It is possible to be in the right place and still carry the wrong identity.
It is possible to be among God’s people and still be uncircumcised in heart. It is possible to be active in fellowship, church,
choir, children’s ministry, campus work, or leadership, and still carry old appetites, secret sins, worldly habits, pride,
bitterness, lust, and compromise.

Ephesians explains the demand of Gilgal when Apostle Paul says we must put off the old man, be renewed in the spirit of
our mind, and put on the new man, which after God is created in righteousness and true holiness. The flesh cannot inherit
what God has prepared. The old life cannot possess new inheritance. Unbroken flesh cannot win a generation for the Lord.
If God cannot win our lives, He cannot win other lives through our lives.

Teachings
1. The Reproach of Egypt Must Be Rolled Away Because Old Identities Cannot Possess New Inheritance: Joshua 5:9 says,
“This day have I rolled away the reproach of Egypt from off you.” Egypt was behind them, but the reproach of Egypt still
needed to be rolled away. They had left Egypt physically, crossed the Red Sea, journeyed through the wilderness, and
crossed Jordan, yet God still addressed something connected to their old identity. This teaches us that a person can leave
a place outwardly but still carry its lifestyle inwardly. A believer can leave the world physically, yet still carry worldly desires,
worldly language, worldly values, worldly friendships, worldly dressing, worldly humour, worldly ambition, and worldly
appetite.

In essence, the reproach of Egypt represents every old identity, shame, bondage, habit, mindset, appetite, and lifestyle that
contradicts the new life God has given His people. God did not bring Israel into Canaan so that Egypt could continue living
inside them. In the same way, Christ does not save us so that the old life can continue ruling us. He saves us to make us
new.

This is why the truth of our identity in Christ is important. A person who does not know who he is in Christ may continue
to live according to who he was in Egypt. A believer who still sees himself mainly through past sin, old friends, former habits,
family background, social pressure, or secret shame may struggle to walk in the authority of the new life. But in Christ, old
things are passed away. Dear TACEFites, God is calling us to Gilgal. We cannot possess new inheritance while still living in
old habits. We cannot become revival vessels while still embracing the identity of the old life. The Lord wants to remove
the smell of Egypt, the language of Egypt, the pride of Egypt, the lust of Egypt, the compromise of Egypt, and the unbelief
of Egypt, so that we may stand as His covenant army in the land.

2. Possession Requires Covenant Identity: Many children were born among the children of Israel after they left Egypt and
journeyed through the wilderness. These children belonged to the travelling company, grew up among the covenant people,
crossed Jordan with the congregation, and were physically present in the camp. Yet, they had not been circumcised. They
had not personally received the covenant mark that separated Israel unto the Lord. This is a serious warning. Being in the
camp is not the same as bearing the mark of covenant. Being around God’s people is not the same as belonging wholly to
God. Association is not transformation and fellowship attendance is not consecration. Being around the brethren is not
personal encounter and being in church is not the same as salvation because religious presence is not the proof of covenant
identity.

We live in a time when many people are near the things of God outwardly, but far from God inwardly. In our study on
knowing God last year, we learned about the sons of Eli, who served around the altar but were called sons of Belial. They
were close to sacred things, but their lives were far from God. This same danger still exists today. Some people attend
fellowship, join several online prayers daily, sing in the choir, serve in ministries (subgroups), follow Christian conversations,
and may even hold positions, yet their hearts have not been separated unto the Lord. Every soldier must personally bear
the mark of belonging to the Lord. Every member of the revival army must encounter the Commander of the army in the
place of genuine salvation, personal surrender, and covenant identity.

This is why Ephesians calls us to “put off concerning the former conversation the old man” and to “put on the new man,
which after God is created in righteousness and true holiness.” The proof of covenant identity is not that we are counted
among the people of God, but that our lives are being changed by the power of God.

 ~ 110 ~

3. Circumcision of the Heart Is Separation unto the Lord: Circumcision did not begin at Gilgal. It was first established by
God as His covenant with Abraham, a visible mark that Israel belonged to Him and was separated from the nations for His
divine purpose (Genesis 17). Every male in Israel was required to bear this covenant sign in his flesh as a continual reminder
that they were God's chosen people. When Israel entered the Promised Land, however, a new generation had not been
circumcised during their wilderness journey. Before they could possess their inheritance, God commanded Joshua to
circumcise them at Gilgal (Joshua 5). The act was painful, personal, and costly. It involved cutting away part of the flesh with
a knife, bringing pain and temporary weakness. Yet this outward act was far more than a physical procedure but a covenant
renewal and a public declaration that Israel belonged wholly to the Lord.

Even under the Old Testament, God made it clear that physical circumcision alone was never His ultimate desire. He
repeatedly called His people to "circumcise the foreskin of your heart" (Deuteronomy 10:16; Jeremiah 4:4), revealing that
the greater issue was an inward separation from sin and wholehearted devotion to Him. This reaches its fulfilment in the
New Testament, where circumcision is no longer of the body but of the heart, accomplished by Christ through the Holy
Spirit (Colossians 2:11). Circumcision of the heart is God's inward work of cutting away the rule of the flesh, breaking the
power of sin, and separating every believer unto Himself. The flesh must be dealt with because unbroken flesh cannot safely
carry divine assignments. A believer who has not allowed God to deal with the flesh may have passion, but that passion
will still be polluted by self. He may preach, sing, lead, organise, or pray fervently, yet remain defeated by lust, anger,
bitterness, jealousy, greed, competition, unforgiveness, or rebellion. The danger is not only that such a person may fall, but
that he may wound others while appearing to serve God.

4. Consecration Precedes Conquest, and Holiness Protects the Army from Fleshly Warfare: God brought Israel to Gilgal
before Jericho. This order is important. Jericho which is the land to be possessed, was ahead, but circumcision came first
at Gilgal. The walls would soon fall, but God first dealt with the army because winning the inner battle against sin, as we
learned at the last convention is more important than the outside war. This also teaches us that God does not want an
unclean army fighting holy battles. He does not want fleshly men carrying spiritual weapons. He does not want people who
are defeated in secret trying to win publicly. Holiness protects the army from fleshly warfare. When holiness is absent, the
army becomes vulnerable, prayer becomes weak, discernment becomes dull, leadership becomes polluted, service
becomes performance, evangelism becomes powerless, and fellowship becomes social gathering.

Clean hands and a pure heart are not optional for those who want to ascend into God’s purpose. We cannot win for the
Lord when our lifestyles are lost in secret sins. We cannot call people out of darkness while walking in darkness ourselves.
Therefore, every revival army must return to holiness. TACEFites must confront besetting sins, weights, compromises, old
habits, worldly appetite, lust, bitterness, pride, and every secret thing that weakens our walk with the Lord. For if the Lord
wins our lives, He can win other lives through our lives. If God conquers our private battles, He can make us vessels of public
victory. Gilgal must come before Jericho.

5. Step-by-Step Applications and Practical Implications
• Ask God to reveal your Egypt: Prayerfully identify the old habits, old appetites, old mindsets, old relationships, old
 language, and old compromises that still follow you. Do not excuse them. Bring them honestly before God.
• Allow the reproach to be rolled away: Declare before God that the identity of the old life will not define your new life
 in Christ. Refuse to carry Egypt into inheritance.
• Check your covenant identity: Do not depend on church attendance as an indication of genuine salvation. Genuinely
 ask yourself whether your heart truly belongs to the Lord.
• Submit to circumcision of the heart: Allow God’s Word, Spirit, correction, and godly accountability to cut away pride,
 lust, bitterness, rebellion, anger, and secret compromise.
• Put off the old man practically: Delete what feeds sin. Stop that ungodly association. End that subscription what
 weakens holiness. Stop what pollutes your mind.
• Put on the new man daily: Choose righteousness in everyday living, true holiness in secret life, purity in relationships,
 truth in speech, and light instead of darkness.

 • There stood a man over against him with his sword drawn in his hand.
 • but as captain of the host of the LORD am I now come.
 • Joshua fell on his face to the earth, and did worship.

Introduction
This week's study brings us into one of the most important leadership encounters in the life of Joshua. Israel had crossed
River Jordan. The memorial stones had been set. The reproach of Egypt had been rolled away at Gilgal through the cutting
away of the flesh. The people had been circumcised, consecrated, and prepared to possess the Promised Land. Jericho, the
first great fortified city waiting to be conquered, now stood before them. Everything appeared ready for battle. Yet before
Israel could confront Jericho, Joshua himself had to undergo one final lesson. He had to discover that he was not the true
commander of the army.

Joshua lifted up his eyes and saw a Man standing before him with His sword drawn. Thinking as a military leader, Joshua
asked, "Art thou for us, or for our adversaries?" The answer completely changed his understanding of spiritual warfare:
"Nay; but as captain of the host of the LORD am I now come." The issue was never whether God had come to support
Joshua's plans. The issue was whether Joshua was willing to lay down his own authority and submit completely to the
Commander of the Lord's army. The battle did not belong to Joshua. The army did not belong to Joshua. The victory would
not come through Joshua's military ability. Everything belonged to the Lord, and Joshua could only succeed by receiving
and obeying divine command. His first act was therefore not to fight but to fall on his face in worship and ask, "What saith
my Lord unto His servant?"

This is a foundational lesson for every TACEFite and every revival army. Before God entrusts us with His battles, He first
teaches us that we do not own the work, the ministry, the fellowship, the platform, the vision, or the results. We are not
commanders asking God to bless our plans. We are servants receiving His instructions. Every outreach, leadership
responsibility, ministry assignment, relocation plans, financial plans, career decision, and act of service must begin with the
same posture of surrender: "What saith my Lord unto His servant?" Only an army that has first submitted to the Captain of
the Lord's host can be trusted to advance His kingdom and fight His battles.

 ~ 115 ~

Teachings
1. God’s Army Must Surrender to the Commander Before Conquest: Joshua had already been commissioned by God. He
had crossed Jordan by divine leading. He had witnessed the power of God in opening the river. He had obeyed the
instruction to circumcise the people at Gilgal. Yet, before Jericho, he still had to learn that he was not the ultimate
commander of the battle. Joshua led Israel under God, but he did not own the army. He carried responsibility, but he did
not carry final authority. He was a mere servant under the Captain of the Lord’s host.

This is a deep lesson for every leader and every believer. The more God entrusts to us, the more surrendered we must
become. Divine assignments must not create a sense of personal control. Spiritual responsibility must not turn into self-
importance. Leadership must not make us forget that Christ alone is the Head. Joshua had to bow before the Captain before
he could lead the people to win Jericho. The commander of Israel had to become a worshipping servant before the
Commander of heaven.

In addition, we must understand that the battle belongs to the Lord. The battle for souls belongs to Him. The battle for
revival belongs to Him. The battle for The African Church, our campuses, local churches, families, communities, workplaces,
and nations belong to Him. We are not owners; we are servants. We are not commanders; we are soldiers under divine
command. This is why the first posture Joshua took after hearing the identity of the Captain was worship. “Joshua fell on
his face to the earth and did worship.” Surrender begins when the heart bows. Before our business strategies, financial
plans, meetings, outreaches, career assignments, and service platforms, there must be a total submission because the Lord
must win the leader before the leader can lead others into victory.

2. The Army Must Ask, “What Saith My Lord?” Before Every Battle: Joshua’s question changed after the Captain spoke. At
first, he asked, “Art thou for us, or for our adversaries?” But after the Captain revealed Himself, Joshua asked, “What saith
my lord unto his servant?” This is the question of a surrendered soldier. It is the question of a man who no longer wants
God to bless his own plan, but wants to hear and obey God’s command.
This question must become the governing question of every revival army. Before we organise an outreach, we must ask,
“Lord, what are You saying?” Before we take up a church responsibility, we must ask, “Lord, what are You saying?” Before
we start a new business venture, enter a relationship, pursue an opportunity, relocate, begin a business, or make a major
decision, we must ask, “Lord, what are You saying?” This is the proof that we are not running our lives by assumptions.

A major danger in our time is that many are busy without being led. A leader can push an idea because it looks attractive,
not because the Lord has spoken. A business owner can start a new venture out of pressure, not from divine instruction. A
husband can force a family into a relocation or investment decision just because it is trending. In essence, we must learn to
submit to the Commander of our lives because we have no plans outside His. This does not mean we should not plan but
every plan must originate from Him and we intentionally submit every of our plans to the Lord for guidance. It does not
mean we should not strategise. It means strategy must bow to divine instruction. It does not mean we should not use
wisdom. It means wisdom must remain under the rule of Christ.

3. Holiness in Spiritual Warfare - Holy Ground Requires Surrendered Shoes: The Captain of the Lord’s host said to Joshua,
“Loose thy shoe from off thy foot; for the place whereon thou standest is holy.” This instruction shows that spiritual warfare
is not first about weapons, but about holiness. Joshua saw a drawn sword, yet the first command he received was not
“fight,” but “remove.” Before Jericho could be confronted, Joshua’s shoes had to be loosed. Before the battle could be
entered, the servant had to recognise the holiness of the ground and the holiness of the Commander.

“Shoes” in this context represent contact with the old ground, worldly patterns, works of the flesh, and self-directed steps.
To remove the shoe is to surrender our way of walking, our pride, our self-dependence, our old methods, our personal
control, and anything unfit for holy ground. The Lord was teaching Joshua that the battle ahead was not an ordinary military
effort, but a holy assignment under a holy Commander.
This connects with the pattern of Moses, who also had to remove his shoes before the burning bush. A holy encounter
demands surrendered shoes. God does not only call us first to fight in spiritual warfare for souls of men; He calls us to bow,
remove, surrender, and be purified. Every time we encounter the Commander of the Lord’s army, we must be willing to
remove old shoes. The shoes of self-will must be removed. The shoes of secret compromise must be removed. The shoes
of bitterness, lust, anger, envy, prayerlessness, carelessness, worldliness, and old habits must be removed. We cannot fight
spiritual battles with unclean hands. We cannot confront darkness while keeping darkness in our private lives.

 ~ 116 ~

4. Christ Is Head Over All Things, and Every Army Must Submit to His Rule: Ephesians 1 reveals the exalted position of
Christ as our Commander and Head. God raised Him from the dead and set Him at His own right hand in the heavenly
places, “far above all principality, and power, and might, and dominion.” This means Christ is not one power among many
powers. He is far above all. Every principality, power, dominion, name, system, idol, fear, resistance, and opposition is under
His feet. The same passage says God “gave him to be the head over all things to the church.” Christ is Head over all things
to the church. The church is His body and He is the Head. The body must receive direction from the Head. The body must
move when the Head commands. The body must not run ahead of the Head or act independently of the Head. A body
disconnected from the head becomes lifeless, confused, and dead.

In this regard, if Christ is the Head, then our opinions must bow to His at all times. Our traditions must bow. Our preferences
must bow. Our strategies must bow. Our ego must bow. Our fear must bow. Our ambition must bow. Our timing must bow.
Our titles must bow. Our platforms must bow. Every plan must pass through His authority. The question is not, “Will Christ
support what I want?” The question is, “Am I submitted to what Christ commands?”

5. Step-by-Step Applications and Practical Implications
 • Surrender the battle before you enter it: Before confronting any challenge, whether in family, school, work, ministry,
 fellowship, or personal life, pause and declare that the battle belongs to the Lord.
 • Ask the Joshua question daily: Before major actions, ask: “What saith my Lord unto His servant?” Do not act
 because you are angry, excited, pressured, or confident.

 family plan unto the Lord and prayerfully submit it to the Lord. Ask Him to correct, redirect, purify, or confirm it.

 • Practise holiness in warfare: Do not try to fight for God while hiding from God. Let your private life, online life,
 relationships, speech, appetite, and motives come under the searchlight of the Holy Spirit.
 • Live under Christ’s headship: In every decision, ask whether Christ is truly ruling. Is His Word directing you? Is His
 Spirit restraining you? Is His character being formed in you?
