Introduction
This week takes a further deep dive into the battle that began when the five kings gathered themselves against Gibeon.
After the Lord discomfited the enemies before Israel and fought for His people, the five kings fled and hid themselves in a
cave at Makkedah. Their armies had been defeated, but the kings were still alive and hidden. Joshua did not ignore them
or pretend that the battle was fully over. He ordered that great stones be rolled upon the mouth of the cave where the
kings were hidden and that men should keep them there, while Israel continued to pursue the remaining enemies. Later,
Joshua commanded that the kings be brought out of the cave and dealt with openly.

This principle in spiritual warfare teaches us that we must not start celebrating victory when the battle is not yet fully over.
Every remaining threat must be dealt with completely. The hidden kings represent strong forces that are behind the scene
who sustain the open opposition. A battle may appear to have been won outwardly, while the deeper rulers of that spiritual
battle remain untouched. This is why the Lord’s army must not be satisfied with partial victory. God does not call us to
manage what He has commanded us to conquer. Joshua did not allow the five kings to remain hidden in the cave. He
brought them out and ended their influence. In the same way, TACEFites must not allow any “king” of immorality,
covetousness, unforgiveness, bitterness, lust, pride, dishonesty, spiritual laziness, wrong relationships, or secret
compromise to rule over our lives.

Ephesians explains this clearly with two clear warnings. First, “Neither give place to the devil.” This means believers must
not create openings, spaces, footholds, permissions, or access points through which the enemy can operate and sustain
their influence. Second, “Have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness, but rather reprove them.” This means
darkness must not be tolerated, managed, excused, entertained, or covered. It must be exposed by the light of Christ and
judged by the Word of God.

Teachings
1. Hidden Kings Must Be Brought Out and Not Allowed to Hide: The five kings fled and hid themselves in a cave at
Makkedah. Their armies had been scattered, but the rulers behind the attacks were still alive. If these kings had been left
hidden, they could have become a future source of renewed attack and war against Israel. Joshua understood that the
battle was not complete simply because the visible enemies had been defeated. The hidden kings had to be brought out.

This is a very important spiritual lesson for all TACEFites. Many people fight outward symptoms while leaving inward rulers
untouched. A person may stop a visible habit for a while, but still leave the root of lust, pride, bitterness, greed, fear,
unforgiveness, or rebellion hidden in the heart. A fellowship may address outward disorder but fail to deal with the hidden
spirit of offence, prayerlessness, worldliness, or disunity operating underneath. A family may settle arguments on the
surface but leave unresolved anger, pride, wounds, and unforgiveness hidden in the cave. We must identify and destroy
these root causes because if these “kings” remain hidden, they will continue to influence decisions, weaken consecration,
and reopen doors the Lord wants closed.

Ephesians says, “Neither give place to the devil.” A place can be a small opening, but if it is not dealt with, it can become a
stronghold. The devil does not need full ownership to cause damage; he only needs a small access, a crack or a small gap.
Therefore, we must not keep hidden spaces where darkness can operate. We must bring such areas into the light through
repentance, confession, godly counsel, discipline, and obedience to the Word. Beloved, we must not allow hidden kings to
remain in the cave. Ask the Lord to search your heart and bring hidden sin, bitterness, careless habits, wrong relationships,
secret compromises, and unfinished obedience into the light for correction. The Lord’s army cannot possess territory while
secret enemies are still ruling within.

2. Victory Must Be Completed, Not Celebrated Too Early: Joshua did not stop the battle when the five kings hid in the cave.
He told the people, “Stay ye not, but pursue after your enemies.” This means he understood that victory required

 ~ 152 ~

completion. He did not allow the army to be distracted by the captured kings while other enemies were escaping. He
secured the cave, continued the pursuit, and later returned to deal with the kings. This was discipline, focus, and
thoroughness. Many believers lose lasting victory because they celebrate too early. They rejoice after one breakthrough
but stop praying. They overcome one temptation but relax their guard. They attend one powerful programme but do not
continue in sustaining the encounter. They confess one sin but do not build new spiritual disciplines not fall again. They win
one soul but do not follow up. They start a revival prayer siege for their local fellowship but do not sustain it.

Victory must be completed. A student who has begun to overcome laziness must continue until discipline becomes a
lifestyle. A believer who has broken away from wrong relationships must also delete all the memories of the ungodly
relationship while building an accountability layer. A fellowship that has experienced revival must continue in the teaching,
discipleship, and intercession. The Lord’s army must learn to finish what God has started. Spiritual victory is not only an
event but a continued walk. Deliverance must be followed by discipline. Repentance must be followed by obedience.
Restoration must be followed by watchfulness. Revival must be followed by discipleship.

3. Partial Obedience Is Future Danger: Joshua’s victory in this text of our study this week is marked by thoroughness and
attention to details. Again and again, the Bible says that he left none remaining and acted as the Lord God of Israel
commanded. What God commands must not be obeyed halfway. What God says must be judged must not be preserved
secretly. Partial obedience is dangerous because it leaves seeds for future trouble. A small secret sin today can become a
stronghold for the future. A small offence can become tomorrow’s bitterness. A small secret habit can become bondage of
a lifetime. A careless casual relationship with an opposite sex outside marriage can become a source of permanent spiritual
damage. A tolerated wrong association in business can become a destiny destroyer. What is not dealt with today may rise
stronger tomorrow.
As revival army, we must understand that lasting revival requires complete obedience. Revival must be protected by
discipline, truth, correction, and obedience. If we keep excusing what God has condemned, we will weaken spiritual grace
upon the mandate and if we keep negotiating with the flesh, we will lose boldness to walk in the Spirit. This applies to our
personal and corporate lives. In personal life, TACEFites must not give room to hidden sin, ungodly entertainment, wrong
relationships, bitterness, pride, laziness, dishonest practices, or get-rich-quick schemes like betting because they are seeds
that destroy a glorious future. As a group, we must not tolerate doctrinal errors, gossip, immorality, rebellion, careless
leadership, or spiritual shallowness. What is wrong must be corrected in love, truth, and spiritual maturity. Beloved, be
thorough in your spiritual walk. Do not manage what God says must die. Do not pamper what God says must be judged.

4. The Revival Army Must Give No Place to the Devil: Ephesians 4:27 gives a direct command: “Neither give place to the
devil.” This is one of the clearest warnings to believers. The devil looks for a place. He looks for an opening, a little crack
and a careless moment. He looks for a foothold. That place may be unresolved anger, secret sin, bitterness, pride, lies, lust,
unforgiveness, disobedience, careless friendship, corrupt communication, prayerlessness, or compromise. Once a place is
given, influence begins. Ephesians 5:11 adds, “And have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness, but rather
reprove them.” This means that we must not be friendly with darkness. We must not condemn sin in others while hiding it
in ourselves. We must not excuse what God calls unfruitful works of darkness. Darkness must be brought into the light and
reproved by truth.

This calls for honest personal examination. Is there any king hiding in the cave of my heart? Is there a habit that has not
been surrendered? Is there bitterness being protected? Is there a secret sin weakening my prayer life? Is there an ungodly
relationship that keeps pulling my heart away from God? Is there a form of entertainment, conversation, appetite, or online
behaviour that is opening a door to the enemy?
The Lord Jesus has redeemed us to walk in light, not darkness. We must refuse every foothold of the enemy and submit
every area of life to Christ. We must give no place to the devil. Close every door. Bring every hidden king into the light. Have
no fellowship with darkness. Walk in truth, purity, discipline, and complete obedience. The army that will possess the land
must not be ruled by hidden kings.

SECTION 5: How God’s Army Must Grow in Consecration, Endurance, Testimony, and Expanding Burden for More Land
The journey of God’s end-time army now enters a wider and deeper phase of possession. After Jericho, Ai, the Gibeonite
deception, the southern coalition, and the hidden kings, Israel was not permitted to relax as though the work was finished.
A new and larger northern coalition arose against them. Joshua also had to fight a long war, record the defeated kings, and
later hear from the Lord that there still remained very much land to be possessed. This teaches us that spiritual progress
does not remove the need for vigilance. Bigger victories can attract bigger battles. Greater enlargement requires deeper
consecration. Early success must not become the burial ground of future obedience.

 ~ 156 ~

As God enlarges His army, He also deepens its dependence on Him. The battle that came after earlier victories required
fresh courage, fresh obedience, and fresh leading. The long war required endurance beyond seasonal excitement. The list
of defeated kings became a written testimony of God’s power over named enemies and specific territories. Yet, the
reminder that there remained very much land taught Israel not to confuse progress with completion. God’s people must
not measure the mandate only by what has been achieved; we must also be burdened by what remains unfinished.
This series of four studies calls TACEFites to mature beyond early excitement into sustained kingdom responsibility. We
must not relax after early success, because the enemy does not easily give up territories. We must not abandon our duty
posts because results appear slow. We must remember and document the victories of the Lord, because testimonies
strengthen future faith and teach the next generation. We must not settle too early, because there are still souls to win,
youths to disciple, children to nurture, local churches to strengthen, campuses to recover, families to restore, and
communities to reach. The land belongs to the Lord, but there remains very much land to be possessed.
Week 21: The Northern Coalition - Deeper Consecration for Bigger Battles: After Jericho, Ai, and the southern kings,
another coalition gathered against Israel. This teaches that progress often attracts resistance, and bigger victories can bring
bigger battles. When God begins to enlarge a life, fellowship, career, business, marriage, prayer altar, or soul-winning
burden, increased pressure should not surprise us. TACEFites must not relax after early success.
Week 22: Joshua’s Long War - Endurance in Labouring for Lasting Revival: Joshua 11:18 reminds us that Joshua made war
a long time with those kings. Possession is not always instant, and lasting revival is not sustained by short term momentum.
Some mission assignment, local church challenges, campus fields, family situations, academic goals, career journeys, and
spiritual growth processes require long path to victory. Ephesians teaches us to stand after doing all, while Galatians
reminds us not to be weary in well doing. TACEFites must not abandon their duty posts too early, even when transformation
is slow, results delay, or labour feels hidden.
Week 23: The Defeated Kings - Remembering the Victories of Christ Over Every Power: Joshua 12 is not merely a historical
list; it is a written testimony of conquest and a theological record of God’s sovereignty. The naming of kings and territories
shows that God defeats specific enemies, both small and great. In the light of Ephesians, these defeated kings point us to
Christ, who is exalted far above all principality, power, might, dominion, and every name. TACEFites must learn to record
and remember victories, souls saved, youths discipled, prayers answered, families restored, fellowships revived, and battles
overcome, because testimonies strengthen future faith and become teaching tools for the next generation.
Week 24: There Remaineth Yet Very Much Land - The Danger of Settling Too Early: Joshua 13:1 teaches that age,
experience, and past success do not mean the work is finished. Israel had truly advanced, but advancement was not the
same as full possession. Ephesians calls believers into the fullness of God, reminding us that God’s purpose is larger than
our present achievement. TACEFites must not settle into celebration while there are still unreached souls, weak local
churches, neglected campuses, undiscipled children, wounded families, and communities waiting for the light of Christ. The
unfinished work should not make us hopeless; it should drive us back to prayer, planning, evangelism, discipleship, and
renewed obedience.

Introduction
As we progress into our studies into the making of an exceeding great army, our study this week explores another major
battle in Israel’s journey of possession. After Jericho, Ai, the southern kings, and the hidden kings had been defeated,
another group of cities formed a coalition and rose from the north against Israel. Jabin king of Hazor gathered many kings,
many people, horses, and chariots in very great number. The Bible says they were “much people, even as the sand that is

 ~ 158 ~

upon the sea shore in multitude.” This was not a small battle. It was a larger, more organised, and more intimidating
opposition. The progress of God’s people had attracted more enemies on their journey to their Promised Land. The victories
of yesterday had not ended the battles of tomorrow.

This study into the northern coalition teaches us that bigger victories often attract bigger battles. As God enlarges a life,
fellowship, family, career, business, ministry, or revival mandate, new levels of challenges, temptations and oppositions may
also arise. When God begins to use a person, the demands of consecration increase. When a fellowship begins to grow, the
need for watchfulness increases. When a believer moves into new responsibility in his career or gets promoted, the battle
also expands. This does not mean God is absent but it shows the need to grow deeper in Christ.

Ephesians deepens this lesson by commanding believers to be strong in the Lord and in the power of His might. It does not
say we should be strong in our past victories, titles, intelligence, strategies, achievements or confidence. It says we must be
strong in the Lord. As battles become more complex, the whole armour of God becomes necessary. Truth, righteousness,
the gospel of peace, faith, salvation, the Word of God, prayer, watchfulness, perseverance, and supplication in the Spirit are
required for every new level of warfare and life demands. Spiritual advancement brings new dimensions of warfare, and
new battles demand deeper roots in Christ. This study teaches TACEFites how to seek God afresh for every season because
God gives specific strategies for new levels, not mere repetition of old methods. Every lifting we receive comes with a
greater responsibility, deeper dependence on God, and renewed submission to the Holy Spirit.

Teachings
1. Bigger Victories Attract Bigger Battles, Requiring Deeper Roots in Christ: After many victories had been won, Israel faced
another combined enemy from the north. Jabin king of Hazor did not come alone. He sent to many kings, and they gathered
with much people, horses, and chariots. Their number was described as the sand upon the sea shore in multitude. This
shows that the battle had moved to another level. Israel had progressed, and the attacks by the enemy had also intensified.
We must therefore understand that when God begins to enlarge a life in his career, local church, community, campus, or
workplace, the demands and pressure will also increase.

For example, a firebrand local church or campus fellowship doing great work in discipleship may suddenly face distractions,
offences, leadership pressures, and spiritual attacks. A brother who has just been promoted to a managerial role at work
may begin to have less time for quiet time or fellowship with the brethren. Another brother who has started a new business
or start-up may spend most of his time building the business, managing staff, and carrying the pressure of paying salaries,
and this can create great spiritual tension. A sister whose singing ministry has been favoured by the Lord may become so
busy with different invitations to the extent that she becomes detached from accountable spiritual oversight and no longer
maintains a consistent prayer life. A brother appointed as a Church Warden may also become so occupied with multiple
church meetings that he no longer has time to join the local fellowship, spend time with his family, follow-up converts or
sustain personal quiet time of prayer and study of the Word of God.

2. Courage Must Grow with Kingdom Assignment: When the northern coalition gathered with much people, horses, and
chariots, the situation could have intimidated Israel. They had seen victories before, but this battle looked bigger and more
organised. Yet, the Lord spoke to Joshua again, saying, “Be not afraid because of them.” This shows that fear can return
even after earlier victories if the heart begins to focus on the size of the opposition rather than the faithfulness of God.
Therefore, our boldness in the Lord must mature with assignment. The courage needed at Jericho was real, but the courage
needed at Merom to meet this bigger battle also had to be renewed. Every new level demands fresh courage. A believer
who trusted God yesterday must still trust Him today. A brother or sister who was strong in his or her day on campus must
remain stronger even during youth service or when in the workplace or marriage. No season of life must diminish our
consistent courage in our walk of faith because courage is not something we use once and abandon but something that
must grow as the assignment grows.

Fear often comes back when we face a new kind of battle, one that is different from what we have faced before. Israel had
fought Jericho, Ai, and the southern kings, but now they were facing horses, chariots, many kings, and a multitude like the
sand of the sea. New kinds of opposition can awaken old fears. New responsibilities can expose hidden anxieties. New
seasons can make people feel unprepared. But the Word of the Lord remains the same: “Be not afraid.” A brother who
maintained a strong level of discipline as a single person may face a new demand after marriage, as he learns to adjust to
his wife’s style, builds a new rhythm together, and embrace their future without fear or unnecessary tension. A firebrand
sister on campus may also face unfamiliar battles during National Youth Service (NYSC), especially when she is posted to a

 ~ 159 ~

heavily compromised workplace where integrity, purity, and faith are constantly tested. She must now learn to maintain
spiritual discipline when no one is watching, stand for Christ without the support structure she enjoyed on campus, and
remain faithful in prayer, holiness, and witness in a new environment.

Also, someone who has always enjoyed perfect health may begin to notice new health issues as age increases, and fear
may begin to whisper thoughts of serious or terminal disease every day. Every symptom searched on the internet may
deepen that fear and make the person imagine the worst. Such a person must learn to trust God in a new season, seek
proper medical care without fear, avoid feeding anxiety through constant online searches, and refuse to allow fear to
replace faith, peace, and daily dependence on the Lord. As a member of the Lord’s exceeding great army, we must not be
controlled by fear when new battles come. Always remember that the God who brought you through earlier battles can
carry you through new ones.

3. God Gives Fresh Strategy, but His Army Must Not Adopt the Enemy’s Methods: The Lord gave Joshua a specific
instruction for this new battle: “You must cut the legs of their horses so that they cannot run well. You must also burn their
chariots.” (Easy Bible Version). This was a precise strategy for the kind of battle before them. God did not only promise
victory; He also gave instruction on what to do with the instruments of enemy strength. The horses and chariots
represented the speed, strength, confidence, sophistication, and military advantage of the enemy. Naturally, Israel could
have thought, “These are powerful tools and valuable technologies. Let us keep them for future battles.” But God
commanded them to destroy the horses and burn the chariots. This teaches us that the Lord’s army must not adopt or
adapt the enemy’s methods simply because they look sophisticated, attractive, or useful. God was teaching Israel not to
transfer confidence from Him to captured strength. In the same way, we must be careful when the methods of the world
look exciting to us. Always remember that our exposure to the enemy’s sophistication and knowledge must not become
permission to yield our dependence on them.

This applies in many practical ways. A fellowship may begin to copy worldly entertainment methods to attract youths, until
it gets to a point that holiness message, prayer, holiness, doctrine, and discipleship are pushed aside. A music minister may
accept every platform because it gives visibility and access to collect honorarium, but slowly lose his prayer life and and the
fear of God. A preacher may adopt motivational language that excites people but removes the cross and sound doctrine of
salvation. A business owner may adopt a strategy that promises growth but requires exaggeration, manipulation, bribery,
or dishonest positioning. A professional may begin to copy workplace politics, flattery, compromise, and ungodly
networking because “that is how things are done.” These are horses and chariots that look useful, but can become paths
of backsliding. Beloved, when the Lord gives instructions on what must be rejected, destroyed, and not carried into the
next battle, do not try to keep the enemy’s chariots because they look advanced. Do not preserve what God has
commanded you to burn.

4. Obedience Must Remain Complete Even When Battles Become Complex: Joshua obeyed the Lord fully in the northern
battle. The Scripture says, “So Joshua did to them as the LORD had told him.” It also says, “He left nothing undone of all that
the LORD commanded Moses.” These are powerful statements as we learned how Joshua remained obedient to what God
said. Complexity did not become an excuse for partial or no obedience. The presence of advanced enemy resources did not
make Joshua adjust God’s instruction.

When battles become complex, the temptation to modify God’s instruction becomes strong. People may want to use
natural wisdom to manage what God has commanded them to let go. They may want to obey only the convenient part of
divine instruction and keep what seems useful to them. This was the danger before Israel. The horses and chariots looked
valuable, but God said they must be destroyed. If Israel had kept them, what looked like military advantage could have
become spiritual danger. Like Achan, who saw, desired, took, and hid what God had forbidden, believers can also begin to
treasure what God has clearly condemned because it looks profitable, attractive, modern, or strategic.

This lesson is very relevant to us all as revival army today with many everyday temptations to want to adapt to the horses
and chariots of the world. A young professional may be told to “package” false experience on a CV, inflate results, or
manipulate reports in order to advance quickly and a Christian minister may begin to use emotional manipulation, heavily
funded social media deceptions or celebrity culture to build influence instead of focusing on the Word, prayer, discipleship,
and the Spirit of God. Beloved, be careful when new methods, platforms, relationships, technologies, networks, or
opportunities begin to reduce your dependence on God. Do not adjust divine instruction to satisfy personal interest. Always
keep your confidence in the Lord, not in the horses and chariots of the enemy.

Week 22: Monday, 25 January 2027 to Sunday, 31 January 2027
Title: Joshua’s Long War: Endurance in Labouring for Lasting Revival
Bible Texts: Joshua 11:18; Ephesians 6:13; Galatians 6:9

Bible Texts
Joshua 11:18: 18 Joshua made war a long time with all those kings.
Ephesians 6:13: 13 Wherefore take unto you the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to withstand in the evil day,
and having done all, to stand.
Galatians 6:9: 9 And let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not.

Key Extracts from the Bible Texts to Remember and Reflect On
 • Joshua made war a long time with all those kings.
 • Take unto you the whole armour of God.
 • That ye may be able to withstand in the evil day.
 • Having done all, to stand.
 • Let us not be weary in well doing.
 • In due season, we shall reap.
 • If we faint not.

Introduction
Our study this week x-rays one of the shortest but deepest statements in the book of Joshua: “Joshua made war a long
time with all those kings.” After the fall of Jericho, the defeat and restoration at Ai, the southern coalition, the hidden kings,
and the northern coalition, the journey of possession still required time, patience, discipline, and endurance. The land was
promised, but it was not possessed in one day. The battles were real, the enemies were many, and the process was long.
Joshua had to continue until the work assigned to him was accomplished.
This study teaches us that accomplishing things for God is not always instant. Some victories come suddenly, but some
labour in His vineyard require long season of obedience. Some battles will fall quickly like the wall of Jericho, but some
require years of faithfulness, patience, perseverance, and repeated obedience. This means that the transformation we hope
to see in our church, campus, family or community may take time. A family situation we are been trusting God for may
require long sustained prayer, such as all your desired academic goals, career growth, business development, and total
health recovery may all demand long season of endurance. As a revival army, we must learn that revival is not a sprint for
a short time but a marathon for a long-term.

Ephesians deepens this lesson by teaching us that after we have done all, we must stand. Standing is part of warfare.
Sometimes victory is not only seen in moving forward quickly but it is also seen in remaining faithful under pressure, abiding
during delay and holding strong in God even when we do not understand what is happening. “To stand” means to refuse
to abandon one’s duty post. It means to continue trusting God in prayer even when results are slow and circumstances are
contradicting our hope. This is when we hope against hope and we do not become weary in well doing, because in due
season we shall reap if we faint not. This lesson teaches all TACEFites to remain faithful even when transformation looks
slow, labour seems unrecognised, and breakthrough results do not come as quickly as expected.

Teachings
1. Possession Is Not Always Instant, and Long Warfare Requires Endurance: Joshua 11:18 says, “Joshua made war a long
time with all those kings.” This verse reminds us that even though God had promised Israel the land, possession still
required persistent long season of warfare. The promise was real, but the process was long. The inheritance was certain,
but the battles had to be fought. God had spoken, but Joshua still had to endure. Many believers struggle because they
expect every divine promise to manifest immediately and easily. We want instant transformation, instant growth, instant
answers, instant revival, instant change in people, instant open doors, and instant harvest. But the ways of God often require
patience. Some prayers require continued faith. Some people require patient discipleship. Some fields require years of
sowing before harvest becomes visible.

Long warfare is not a sign that God has failed. Delay is not denial. Slow transformation does not mean the work is useless.
The fact that a local church has not changed quickly does not mean the prayer labour of many years is wasted. The fact that

 ~ 163 ~

a campus field is difficult does not mean the Lord is absent. The fact that a family situation remains challenging after many
days of fasting does not mean God is not working. The fact that a business or investment is not picking us as expected does
not mean God did not lead us into them.

The Lord often forms endurance in His soldiers through long battles. This is why every revival army must grow in patience
and longsuffering as fruits of the Spirit. We must not only be excited when there is visible result but also learn to remain
obedient when results are hidden and delayed. Possession requires endurance. Dear TACEFites, do not give up because the
transformation is slow. Do not abandon the labour of revival or the divine leading to pursue an entrepreneurial path
because the result is delayed. Do not leave your duty post because the battle is long. If God has assigned the work, receive
grace to continue.

2. Longsuffering for Long Battles - Sustaining Grace for a Long Journey: Longsuffering is the fourth fruit of the Spirit, and
it means more than ordinary patience. It carries the idea of being able to “suffer long,” to remain steady under pressure,
to endure delay without giving up, and to continue in obedience even when the process is demanding. It is the grace to
stay faithful when results are slow, when the burden is heavy, when people are difficult, and when the promise appears
delayed. Therefore, seasonal excitement is not enough for the pursuit of divine purpose. Many people begin well when the
atmosphere is charged, when programmes are fresh, when leaders are present, when public attention is strong, or when
testimonies come quickly. But the fruit of longsuffering helps us to continue when excitement reduces and the work
becomes hard. It keeps a believer serving after the crowd has gone. It keeps a soul-winner following up even when converts
are slow to grow. It keeps a leader standing when criticism, fatigue, pressure, and discouragement come.

Joshua did not make war for a short time; he made war a long time. Sarah also waited for the promise. This demand of
longsuffering applies to our everyday lives. A local fellowship may start the journey of discipleship with energy, but it takes
longsuffering to keep teaching, mentoring, correcting, praying, and visiting people month after month. A young professional
may start a career with big dreams, but it takes longsuffering to learn, fail, improve, serve under authority, receive queries
and grow without bitterness or grudges. A couple may love each other deeply, but it takes longsuffering to understand
differences, forgive quickly, adjust patiently, and build a peaceful home. A person working on health recovery process may
begin with motivation, but it takes longsuffering to continue with treatment, exercise, rest, diet, and prayer when progress
is slow.

Longsuffering also refines our knowledge of God. Through prolonged labour, delay, pressure, and affliction, God teaches
His army to know Him beyond excitement. We learn His faithfulness when results are not immediate. We learn His strength
when our own strength is small. We learn His patience when our timetable is not fulfilled. We learn His comfort when the
journey is difficult. So, when the Bible speaks of longsuffering as a fruit of the Spirit, it means the Holy Spirit forms in us the
capacity to suffer long without losing love, faith, obedience, purity, or hope.

3. Weariness Is a Real Challenge: Galatians 6:9 warns us, “And let us not be weary in well doing.” This means it is possible
to become weary while doing what is right. A person can become tired in prayer, tired in service, tired in giving, tired in
discipleship, tired in waiting, tired in leadership, tired in intercession, and tired in carrying people. Weariness is a real threat
to every revival army. Weariness comes when results are slow, when people do not appreciate the labour, when those being
helped resist correction, when resources are limited, when prayers seem delayed, when the local church that you know
you are giving all of yourself into is abusing you, or when personal needs remain unresolved.

This is why every revival army must know how to renew strength through prayer, fasting, and fellowship. Prayer brings the
heart back into communion with God. Fasting disciplines the flesh and sharpens spiritual sensitivity. Fellowship strengthens
weary soldiers through encouragement, accountability, shared burden, and corporate prayer. No soldier should carry the
battle alone. Isolation can multiply weariness, but fellowship can restore courage.
Dear TACEFites, do not pretend that weariness is not real. Take it to God. Renew your strength in prayer. Fast when your
spirit needs fresh fire. Stay connected to fellowship. Share burdens with mature believers. Encourage one another. The long
war requires a renewed army.

4. Standing Is Part of Warfare, Because Faithfulness under Pressure Is Victory:
Ephesians 6:13 says, “Having done all, to stand.” This means that after praying, obeying, serving, fasting, teaching, giving,
and labouring, the command is still to stand. Standing means refusing to fall, refusing to retreat, refusing to compromise,
and refusing to abandon the place God has assigned. We live at a time when many people define victory only as visible

 ~ 164 ~

progress, but this is not always so. In long warfare, standing itself is already a victory. When a believer remains holy under
pressure, that is a great victory. It is also victory when a leader continues faithfully despite discouragement; when a parent
keeps praying for a child even when the child’s behaviour seems to be getting worse; and when a worker remains honest
in a corrupt workplace despite demotion, rejection, or a poor annual review.

Faithfulness under pressure is precious to God. The Lord does not only reward visible success; He honours steadfast
obedience. He sees hidden labour. He sees tears in prayer. He sees consistent service. He sees the believer who continues
when nobody claps. He sees the fellowship that remains faithful in a difficult field. He sees the TACEFite who refuses to
abandon the duty post. Dear TACEFites, after doing all, stand. Stand in prayer. Stand in holiness. Stand in doctrine. Stand in
your duty post. Stand in love. Stand in patience. Stand in faith. In due season, we shall reap if we faint not.

5. Step-by-Step Applications and Practical Implications
 • Accept that some victories take time: Do not become discouraged because transformation, growth, or harvest is
 slow.
 • Refuse to abandon your duty post: Remain faithful in your family, local church, campus, workplace, mission field,
 fellowship assignment, business leading, and personal consecration.
 • Build endurance beyond excitement: Do not depend only on the programme atmosphere, public applause,
 leadership presence, or emotional momentum. Keep serving when no one is there.
 • Renew strength regularly: Use prayer, fasting, the Word, and fellowship to recover strength when weariness begins
 to rise.
 • Stand after doing all: When there is no immediate result, keep standing in faith, holiness, truth, obedience, and
 service.
 • Encourage weary soldiers: Strengthen those who are tired, discouraged, delayed, or labouring without visible
 results.
 • Trust God’s due season: Do not measure God’s faithfulness only by your preferred timetable. In due season, we
 shall reap if we faint not.

 4. How should believers manage the pressure and emotional pain that come when other believers appear to flaunt

 6. How can standing under pressure also be a form of victory, especially in life, career, academic pursuit, business
 growth, and ministry labour?

Personal Reflection
Am I willing to continue when results are not coming on time? Do I give up when transformation is slow or results are
delayed? Is my service built on conviction or seasonal excitement? Do I depend on public recognition of men, leadership
presence, or programme momentum before I remain faithful? Am I becoming weary in well doing? Am I already allowing
the so-called results or success of others to affect my service unto the Lord? Do I renew my strength through prayer, fasting,
the Word, and fellowship? Have I abandoned any duty post too early? Am I still standing in faith, holiness, obedience, and
service after doing all?

Introduction
This week brings us to Joshua 12, a chapter that may appear at first to be only a historical list of conquered kings. Yet this
list is beyond just a catalogue of listing but a written testimony of how God enabled victory for His people. It records the
kings defeated by Moses on the other side Jordan and the kings defeated by Joshua in the land of Canaan. It names
territories, kings, cities, and victories. It reminds Israel that the Lord defeated named enemies, gave specific victories, and
brought His people into real victory. Joshua 12 teaches that victories must be remembered so that the Lord’s revival army
does not lose confidence in God. The list includes great kings, small kings, fortified cities, known territories, and repeated
battles. Each name is a witness that God ruled in the affairs of His people. Each conquered king points to God’s superior
authority. The listing of all the defeated kings is also a reminder that our God is the Lord over all the “satanic kings” like

 ~ 167 ~

personal struggles, family crisis, campus disappointments, local church challenges, career pressures, business failures,
relationship collapses, spiritual opposition, and territorial forces that seek to have dominion over our lives.

We also learn from this detailed listing the act of recording God’s work in our midst, which must be elaborate,
comprehensive and not shallow. We must keep record of when God answers prayer, saves souls, restores families, revives
fellowships, strengthens weak believers, heals broken lives, gives a contract, opens doors for relocation, expands a business,
grants an unexpected promotion, or gives examination success when hope seems lost. The Lord’s works in the midst of His
people must be remembered, named, documented, and passed on.

Ephesians deepens this lesson by lifting our eyes from Joshua’s earthly conquest to Christ’s supreme victory. Joshua
subdued earthly kings, but Christ defeated all principality, power, might, dominion, and every name that is named. The
defeated kings in Joshua point us to the higher victory of Christ over every spiritual power, every dominion, every throne,
every name, and every authority that opposes God’s purpose. The same mighty power that raised Christ from the dead is
working in all revival army. Therefore, our testimonies are not merely records of human survival; they are witnesses of
Christ’s authority and victory in our lives.

Teachings
1. Victories Must Be Recorded, Reflected on and Remembered: Joshua 12 records the victories God gave His people. It
names the kings defeated on both sides of Jordan and reminds Israel of their journey of victory. This was not for information
but for gratitude and appreciative remembrance. God’s people needed to remember what the Lord had done so that they
would not lose confidence in Him as the work continued. One danger in the journey of faith is forgetfulness as we studied
in week 8. A believer may forget past divine interventions when facing a present challenge. A family may forget how God
once made a way when another crisis comes. When memory becomes weak, faith can become unstable.

Remembering victories strengthens confidence in God, and it also reminds us that the God who helped us before can help
us again. The God who opened a door before can open another and the same God who gave strength in one season can
supply grace in another. This is why testimonies must not be treated casually. They are weapons against fear,
discouragement, doubt, and unbelief. When we rehearse the works of God, our hearts become strong again. These acts of
reflection also help us to remember that our journey is sustained by the faithfulness of the Lord. Dear TACEFites, do not
forget the victories of God. Remember how He saved you, kept you, corrected you, restored you, led you, provided for you,
and used you.

2. God Defeats Specific Enemies, Showing His Authority over Named Strongholds: Joshua 12 does not only say that God
gave victory. It names kings. It mentions territories. It lists Jericho, Ai, Jerusalem, Hebron, Jarmuth, Lachish, Eglon, Gezer,
Debir, Hazor, and many more. This is important because it shows that God’s victory was specific, definite and documented.
This act of specific naming takes us into a deeper dimension of spiritual warfare where we engage in direct confrontation
and dethronement of the satanic forces or what we call “strongman” behind a life, family, city, campus, village, lineage, or
destiny. Jesus taught that “except we first bind the strong man,” his house cannot be destroyed. This means that some
battles are not only about scattered symptoms; they are connected to a ruling influence that must be named, identified,
confronted, and displaced by the authority of Christ. In some families, there may be repeated patterns of delay, immorality,
untimely death, marital collapse, poverty, addiction, idolatry, or rejection of the gospel. In some campuses, there may be a
ruling atmosphere of lust, cultism, confusion, rebellion, intellectual pride, or spiritual coldness. In some villages or cities,
there may be ancient altars, blood covenants, idolatrous traditions, occult networks, or territorial powers that have shaped
the behaviour, bondage, and resistance of many people over time.

This is why taking over territories for the Lord sometimes requires more than general prayer. The Holy Spirit may lead the
revival army to trace the root of a bondage, discern the pattern behind a repeated battle, and confront the ruling influence
in the name of Jesus. This must not be done through fear, superstition, curiosity, or carnal boldness, but through revelation,
discernment, and spiritual authority in Christ. When the strongman is bound, his influence is broken; just as when the root
is destroyed, the fruit begins to dry up. This is why warfare prayers must sometimes specifically name and confront the
spirit of bondage, divination, infirmity, fear, lust, rebellion, idolatry, death, confusion, or deception operating in a place or
family.

However, this warfare must remain Christ-centred and Word-governed. We are not called to glorify demons, magnify
ancestral battles, or become obsessed with hidden names and dark histories. Our confidence is not in knowing the enemy’s

 ~ 168 ~

name but in the name of Jesus, which is above every name. The purpose of revelation, when God chooses to give it, is not
to make us fearful, but to make our warfare accurate. Therefore, TACEFites must learn to pray with understanding: asking
God to expose the strongman, break genealogical bondages, silence ancestral voices, overthrow territorial altars, destroy
inherited patterns of sin, and establish the government of Christ over families, campuses, villages, cities, careers, marriages,
and destinies.

3. Kingdom Documentation Teaches Attention to Detail and Excellence: Joshua 12 teaches us that the work of God must
be recorded with accuracy, detail, and excellence. The chapter does not only mention the major battles that had already
been narrated in detail, such as Jericho, Ai, the southern coalition, and the northern coalition. It also records many kings
and territories whose battles were not fully explained in the earlier story that we have studied. We saw new names like
Bethel, Geder, Hormah, Arad, Adullam, Tappuah, Hepher, Aphek, Lasharon, Taanach, Kedesh, Jokneam, Dor, Tirzah, and
others, which were not forgotten when the final summary was written. This means that what may look small in the daily
story still matters in the final record. This is a major lesson for TACEFites. Kingdom work must not be handled carelessly. We
must pay attention to details in documentation, reporting, planning, organisation, welfare, communication, and service
delivery. Excellence is stewardship with respect for the Lord. For example, sleeping arrangements for campers must
consider age, gender, safety, privacy, and comfort. Feeding arrangements must consider timing, quantity, quality, and the
kind of food that will help participants remain alert and not distracted. Weather forecast can affect travel, outdoor sessions,
seating, equipment, and emergency planning. Technical teams must master sound, projection, livestreaming, lighting,
recordings, backup devices, and internet stability. Welfare teams must know who is ill, who needs support, who arrives
late, who has special needs, and who must not be left behind. These “little things” are not little before God because they
affect the overall fruitfulness of His work.

In the same vein, it is very sad today that many people miss very important programme details, and many do not even
submit proper reports, such as weekly local fellowship report, ministry report, post-event report, kingdom financial reports,
converts’ reports, and other necessary records. This is contrary to biblical excellence because documentation is proof of
the value we attach to kingdom work. These act of documentation are now even easier, as we can use voice notes to record
updates and later convert them to text with many free tools. If the fathers of faith who used ink to write the Bible had lived
on excuses as many of us do today, we would not have the written records that now guide our faith. This excellence in
documentation also applies to personal life, marriage, and private business. Many people struggle to find important
documents because they have not been properly filed or archived. Some have lost important business meeting records that
could have helped their competitive advantage.

4. Kingdom Documentation Must Preserve Continuity, Not Promote Self Glory: Joshua 12 also teaches that kingdom
documentation is not about personal glory. The chapter records both the victories under Moses and the victories under
Joshua. Joshua was the leader who brought Israel into the land, yet his record did not erase Moses. The victories on the
other side of Jordan were named first and Moses was honoured as “the servant of the LORD.” This shows that the work of
God is bigger than one man, one generation, one leader, or one season. God’s work is continuous, and no servant should
rewrite the story in a way that removes those who laboured before. This is an important lesson for every revival army.
When God begins to move through us, we must not behave as if the work began with us. We must not name God’s move
after ourselves, exaggerate our roles, or diminish the labour of others in order to appear more important. We must not
erase past sacrifices, older leaders, hidden intercessors, supportive parents, senior disciplers, alumni labour, village
missionaries, and quiet supporters whose labour prepared the ground.

Blowing out someone else’s candle will not make yours shine brighter. Honour given to others does not reduce what God
is doing through us but only makes the testimony more truthful.
Of a truth, Moses planted certain victories before Joshua completed others. Joshua’s series of victories did not cancel
Moses’ labour, instead they built on it. In the same way, a present fellowship leader may be harvesting from prayers sown
by past leaders. A present revival move may have been prepared by many generations of mothers, fathers, and elders who
prayed for years. A convention may succeed because many unseen people planned, cooked, cleaned, carried chairs, paid
bills, drove buses, hosted guests, managed the media, and interceded quietly. Therefore, when we document kingdom
achievements, we must write in a way that gives glory to God and give honour to all vessels He used. The story must not
be self-centred. It must not become “my ministry, my vision, my achievement, my platform.” It must remain the Lord’s
work. We must record contributions honestly, acknowledge those who went before, and make it clear that no man owns
the move of God.

 ~ 169 ~

5. Step-by-Step Applications and Practical Implications
 • Record your testimonies with detail: Write down answered prayers, souls saved, victories over sin, divine
 provisions, healings, restorations, instructions, divine encounters, open doors, examination success, business
 breakthroughs, and family deliverances.
 • Name the battles God has conquered: Avoid vague thanksgiving. Mention the specific fears, temptations, delays,
 strongholds, family patterns, local church challenges, career pressures, and spiritual battles the Lord has helped
 you overcome.
 • Pray with spiritual understanding: Ask God to expose and dethrone every strongman, hidden influence, ancestral
 voice, territorial altar, inherited pattern, and spiritual force resisting Christ’s rule over lives, families, campuses,
 churches, villages, cities, careers, marriages, and destinies.
 • Practise kingdom documentation with excellence: Keep proper records of local fellowship reports, ministry reports,
 converts’ reports, post-event reports, financial reports, welfare records, testimonies, lessons learnt, challenges
 faced, decisions taken, and follow-up needs.
 • Do not despise details in kingdom service: Pay attention to planning, feeding, accommodation, welfare,
 communication, transport, media, sound, livestreaming, backup arrangements, safety, and follow-up. These details
 affect the fruitfulness of God’s work.
 • Use simple tools to improve documentation: Voice notes, shared documents, spreadsheets, photos, forms, Google
 Drive, Google Form for feedback, and free transcription tools can help preserve important records and reduce
 excuses.
 • Preserve continuity, not self-glory: When documenting God’s work, honour those who laboured before, those who
 served quietly, and those who supported behind the scenes. The story must glorify God, not promote personal
 importance.
 • Let every record lead to worship and future obedience: Documentation should not end in archives; it should
 strengthen faith, guide decisions, improve service, fuel intercession, and preserve revival continuity.

Questions for Discussion
 1. Why is Joshua 12 more than a historical list of defeated kings but an important lesson in kingdom excellence,
 attention to detail, reporting, documentation, and excellence in kingdom service?
 2. Why must the Lord’s army record, reflect on, and remember past victories?

 4. Why is it important to identify and confront the strongman behind repeated negative patterns in lives, families,
 campuses, communities, and territories?
 5. How can poor documentation weaken continuity, accountability, planning, follow-up, and future learning in
 fellowship work?
 6. Why must kingdom documentation preserve continuity instead of promoting self-glory?

Personal Reflection
Do I remember the victories God has given me, or do I easily forget the goodness of God in my life? Have I documented the
specific ways God has helped, corrected, restored, provided, delivered, strengthened, and used me? Do I give vague thanks,
or do I name the specific battles the Lord has conquered for me intentionally? Are there repeated patterns in my life, family,
fellowship, campus, workplace, or local church that require deeper prayer and spiritual understanding? Do I treat kingdom
documentation as important, or do I handle reports, testimonies, follow-up records, welfare records, financial reports, and
meeting notes carelessly? Am I faithful in small details, or do I miss important things because I am disorganised or casual?
When I document God’s work, do I give glory to God and honour all vessels He used, or do I present the story as though it
is about me? Do I acknowledge those who prayed, served, gave, led, taught, supported, cooked, cleaned, followed up,
organised, and laboured before me?

Prayer Points

Week 24: Monday, 8 February 2027 to Sunday, 14 February 2027
Title: There Remaineth Yet Very Much Land: The Danger of Settling Too Early

Bible Texts: Joshua 13:1; Ephesians 3:14-21

Bible Texts
Joshua 13:1: 1 Now Joshua was old and stricken in years; and the LORD said unto him, Thou art old and stricken in years,
and there remaineth yet very much land to be possessed.

Ephesians 3:14-21: 14 For this cause I bow my knees unto the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, 15 Of whom the whole family
in heaven and earth is named, 16 That he would grant you, according to the riches of his glory, to be strengthened with
might by his Spirit in the inner man; 17 That Christ may dwell in your hearts by faith; that ye, being rooted and grounded in
love, 18 May be able to comprehend with all saints what is the breadth, and length, and depth, and height; 19 And to know
the love of Christ, which passeth knowledge, that ye might be filled with all the fullness of God. 20 Now unto him that is
able to do exceeding abundantly above all that we ask or think, according to the power that worketh in us, 21 Unto him be
glory in the church by Christ Jesus throughout all ages, world without end. Amen.

Key Extracts from the Bible Texts to Remember and Reflect On
• Joshua was old and stricken in years.
• There remaineth yet very much land to be possessed.
• Strengthened with might by his Spirit in the inner man.
• Filled with all the fullness of God.
• Able to do exceeding abundantly above all that we ask or think.
• According to the power that worketh in us.

Introduction
Our text of study this week is a sobering moment in the life and ministry of Joshua. Joshua was declared old and stricken in
years. He has advanced in age and has grown very old. He had seen the wilderness, followed Moses, crossed Jordan,
conquered Jericho, recovered from Ai, defeated southern and northern coalitions, endured long warfare, and led Israel
through many seasons of possession. Yet the Lord said to him, “You are old, advanced in years, and there remains very
much land yet to be possessed.” This statement teaches that growth in age, experience, past victories, and visible
achievements do not always mean the work is finished. Israel had truly advanced, but advancement was not the same as
full accomplishment of the mandate the Lord set for them.
This is a deep warning to every revival army. The danger after progress is the temptation to settle too early. A people can
celebrate what God has done and forget what remains undone. A fellowship can rejoice over past growth and lose burden
for unreached souls. A leader can remember former labours and become satisfied while the next generation remains
unprepared and unmotivated to continue the labour. Beloved, it is very possible to become thankful for what God has done
and yet become careless about what He is still demanding. The Lord measures not only the completed work but also points
to the remaining work yet to be done.

Ephesians deepens this burden by calling believers into the fullness of God – not half or even ninety nine percent of
attainment. Paul bows his knees in prayer that the saints may be filled with all the fullness of God. This means God’s purpose
is larger than our present experience. There is always more of Christ to know, more of His love to comprehend, more of His
power to experience, more of His life to express, and more of His fullness to carry. We must not confuse progress with
fullness.

Teachings
1. Age or Past Success Does Not Mean the Work Is Finished: The Lord’s word to Joshua is striking and worrisome: “You are
old, advanced in years, and there remains very much land yet to be possessed.” Joshua’s age was real. His labour was real.
His victories were real. His faithfulness was commendable, yet the remaining work that has not been done was also real.
God acknowledged Joshua’s condition, but He still pointed to the unfinished land.
This understanding brings to light that a believer may have served faithfully for years, but there may still be more souls to
reach, more disciples to raise, more prayers to pray, more instructions to obey, more lives to strengthen, and more
territories to cover for the Lord.

 ~ 172 ~

In essence, growth in age, experience, position, and past sacrifice must not become excuses for spiritual retirement from
the mandate and assignment of the Lord. Even when physical roles or titles change, the burden of revival must continue.
Older or past fellowship executives may not carry the same daily activities as before, but they must continue to labour. They
can still pray, mentor, counsel, teach, encourage, support, and preserve the integrity of the vision. In the same vein, younger
brethren must not wait until they are old before they become serious. Every season of life carries responsibility before God.

Dear TACEFites, a successful handover is not the same as the completion of the assignment. Transitioning the day-to-day
leadership of a local fellowship, subzone, zone, ministry/subgroup or the Central Executive Council to new executives does
not mean that the burden of raising an exceeding great army has ended or reduced. Like Joshua, who became old while
much land still remained to be possessed, every outgoing leader must recognise that the work continues, even when the
nature of their responsibility changes. For there remains very much land and lives to be possessed for the Lord.

2. Unpossessed Land Must Still Burden the Heart of Every Revival Army: God did not only tell Joshua what had been
achieved; He showed him what remained. The unpossessed land still mattered to God. The remaining territories were not
forgotten because Israel had already won many battles. This means that the heart of the revival army must continue to
carry the burden of unpossessed land because they represent every territory where Christ is not yet fully known, honoured,
obeyed, and glorified. It includes unsaved souls, weak local churches, unreached campuses, undiscipled children, broken
families, neglected communities, compromised workplaces, and believers who have not yet come into maturity.

The vision of God is for all men to be saved. His purpose is that the earth shall be filled with the knowledge of the glory of
the Lord, as the waters cover the sea. Therefore, revival must keep expanding. It must move into homes, campuses,
communities, markets, schools, offices, families, and local churches. It must touch children, youths, parents, ministers,
workers, students, professionals, artisans, traders, and the elderly. The Lord wants His knowledge to spread. A revival army
must therefore not lose the burden and passion for what remains. If we only celebrate those already attending fellowship
and forget those outside, we are settling too early. If we only care for strong members and ignore weak ones, we are settling
too early. If we only focus on central programmes and neglect local fellowship and other grassroot activities, we are settling
too early.

3. Complacency Is an Enemy of Inheritance: Celebration is good when it leads to thanksgiving and renewed obedience but
it becomes a concern when it creates a feeling of self-satisfied contentment with one’s current status, achievement or
situation
Celebration becomes dangerous when it makes us feel we have arrived and have done all that is expected of us. Israel had
many reasons to rejoice, but the Lord still reminded Joshua that much land remained and so much has not yet been done.
This shows that thanksgiving must not blind us from seeing the unfinished assignment. The feeling of “I have arrived” while
we are still in the middle of the journey does not always look like a problem at first. It may appear as satisfaction, comfort,
routine, nostalgia, or self-congratulation. A believer may say, “At least I am better than before,” while refusing important
call to consecration. A fellowship may say, “At least we are doing well,” while neglecting the core mandate of revival and
discipleship. A career person may say, “I am now certified,” while neglecting the need to build practical skills beyond
certification. A student may say, “At least I passed,” while refusing to improve study discipline, deepen understanding, or
prepare better for future opportunities.

We must also be careful about what we celebrate or call progress. We can celebrate numerical growth and ignore spiritual
depth. We can celebrate positions and forget responsibility. This is why every testimony must lead us back to God’s
unfinished work. We must thank God for what He has done, but we must also ask, “Lord, what remains?” Which souls
remain unreached? Which children remain undiscipled? Which campuses remain untouched? Which communities remain
without witness? Which areas of my life remain incomplete? Dear TACEFites, celebrate with humility, not complacency.
Thanksgiving must lead to renewed consecration. Past success must become fuel to go farther and further, not an excuse
to stop halfway.

4. God’s Fullness Is More than Present Experience, So Do Not Confuse Progress with Completion: Ephesians 3 shows Paul
praying for believers to be strengthened in the inner man, rooted and grounded in love, and filled with all the fullness of
God. This prayer was not for unbelievers; it was for saints. They already belonged to Christ, yet Paul prayed that they would
enter deeper fullness. This means that present experience is not the end of God’s intention.
The journey of knowing God is continuous and never ending. We may know Him, but there is still more of Him to know. We
may have seen His power, but there is still more of His fullness to experience. We may have witnessed revival move in one
place, but there are still more territories to cover for the Lord.

 ~ 173 ~

This is why we must not confuse progress with completion. Israel had advanced, but the land was not fully possessed. We
need to know that God measures the remaining work, not only the completed work. He sees what has been done, but He
also sees what is yet undone. He receives our thanksgiving for what has been done, but He also gives fresh burden for the
work that remains undone. He honours our labour, but He calls us into greater fullness. Dear TACEFites, do not stop at the
present experience. There is more of Christ to know, more of His love to comprehend, more of His fullness to carry, and
more land to possess for Him. Thank God for the current lifting in your career, the expansion in business, the global
platforms to showcase what He has put in your hands, the peace in your marriage, the growing stability in your home, the
consistency in your local fellowship, the permission given to TACEF by the church to run programmes, the expansion of
campus ministry, the souls being saved, and the new doors opening before us. However, we must also remember that there
is still more ahead.

5. Step-by-Step Applications and Practical Implications
• Thank God for past victories, but ask what remains: After every testimony, breakthrough, programme, convention, or
 season of progress, ask, “Lord, what land is still unpossessed? and “what more have I left undone?”
• Do not settle into spiritual comfort: Refuse to let past success, age, experience, title, or history become an excuse for
 reduced burden.
• Identify the unpossessed land around you: Look at your family, local church, campus, workplace, community, and
 fellowship. Where is Christ not yet fully known and obeyed?
• Turn unfinished work into prayer: Let remaining needs push you into intercession, fasting, evangelism, follow-up, and
 discipleship.
• Resist complacency hidden under celebration: Celebrate what God has done, but do not allow celebration to stop you
 from advancing further.
• Pursue the fullness of God: Keep seeking deeper knowledge of Christ, deeper love, deeper obedience, deeper
 consecration, and deeper manifestation of His life.
• Continue even when roles change: Whether old or young, visible or hidden roles or titles, leading or supporting, keep
 carrying the burden for souls, discipleship, prayer, and revival.

Questions for Discussion

What land remains unpossessed in my family, local church, campus, workplace, community, or personal life? Have I
confused progress with completion? Am I celebrating what God has done while ignoring what He is still asking me to do?
Do I still carry burden for children, youths, local churches, families, campuses, and communities? I am reaching out for the
next level in my career, business, academics and family life? Am I pressing into the fullness of God, or am I living only on
past experiences?

Prayer Points

Introduction
Our year-long study into the making of an exceeding great army brings us to the critical phase of dividing the land among
the tribes of Israel. After many battles had been fought and much land had been subdued, God instructed Joshua to divide
the land for inheritance. The land was not to be shared through competition, personal ambition, or tribal jealousy. It was
to be distributed by divine order. Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh had already received their possessions on
the eastern side of the Jordan, while Levi’s inheritance was different because the Lord God of Israel Himself was their
inheritance. This teaches us that God assigns portions according to His will, and every portion must be received with
gratitude and stewarded faithfully.

The division of the land also teaches that possession is not only about winning battles; it is about taking responsibility for
what God has given unto us. Every tribe had a portion, but not every tribe had the same portion. The difference in size or
portion did not mean inferiority. The fact that Levi did not receive land like the other tribes did not make Levi useless or
less than others. Their portion was unique and sacred. In the same way, every believer has a place in the body of Christ. No
believer is useless. No assignment is accidental. No grace is too small when it is yielded to the Lord because the divine order
is that “every joint must supply,” as we always say in the great house of TACEF.

Ephesians deepens this lesson by showing that in Christ, we have obtained an inheritance according to the purpose of God,
who worketh all things after the counsel of His own will. It also teaches that grace is given to every believer according to
the measure of the gift of Christ. These gifts are not given for status, superiority, self-display, or personal importance. They
are given for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, and for the edifying of the body of Christ. The body
grows when every joint supplies its measure and every part works effectually. In this regard, every TACEFite must know that
they have a portion of divine assignment in God. Like we said at the convention, everyone have a duty post, that is, the
place of primary assignment. Everyone must serve in their respective postings. Nothing is small when used for the Lord.
The mandate of revival will grow stronger when each part supplies its measure faithfully, committedly, consistently, and in
love.

Teachings
1. Inheritance Must Be Distributed by Divine Order, Not Competition: When God instructed Joshua to divide the land,
inheritance was not left to personal preference, influence, or ambition. The land was not to be taken by the tribe that could
argue best, fight hardest, or position itself most strongly. It was to be divided according to divine order. God had a portion
for each tribe, and each tribe needed to receive and steward what God assigned.
This understanding teaches us that an assignment in the Lord’s army is not a contest for visibility, titles, or recognition. A
believer does not become important because his role is public, and another does not become unimportant because his role
is hidden. God distributes portions according to His purpose, and every portion matters when it is used faithfully.

Competition becomes dangerous when it enters spiritual service because it makes people compare their portion with
another person’s portion. It makes gifted people seek attention instead of service and it makes hidden workers feel useless
and unrecognised. The grace given to another person should not make you despise your own grace, and the fact that
someone teaches, sings, leads, gives, organises, or prays in a visible way does not mean your own portion is small. What

 ~ 178 ~

matters is whether you are faithful in what God has committed into your hands. Dear TACEFites, do not fight for another
person’s portion. Do not despise your own giftings and never serve from envy, rivalry, or the desire to be noticed.

2. Every Tribe Has a Portion, and Every Believer Has a Place in the Body: Joshua 13 that we are studying this week carefully
describes the inheritance of two and a half of the tribes – tribes of Reuben, Gad, and the half tribe of Manasseh. Their
borders, cities, families, villages, and territories were recorded. These details show that God was specific about their
portion. God knew where each tribe belonged and what each tribe was expected to manage. This is very important for the
body of Christ. Ephesians says, “But unto every one of us is given grace according to the measure of the gift of Christ.” This
means grace is not given only to pastors, teachers, or fellowship leaders. Every TACEFite irrespective of age, gender,
background or spiritual experience has received grace and carries something from God that can build, strengthen,
encourage, equip, or bless others. We all have a specific duty post as we heard at the last convention.

This understanding means everyone has something to offer. No believer is useless. Some people may have visible
assignments, while others may serve in hidden ways. Some may be strong in teaching, while others may be strong in prayer,
hospitality, administration, music, writing, counselling, mentoring, follow-up, evangelism, children’s ministry, visitation,
media, technical support, or practical care. The problem begins when believers do not know their place or refuse to function
in it. The body of Christ becomes weak when parts are present but inactive, dormant and doing nothing. A fellowship
becomes weak when many members receive but only few make effort to contribute and supply. The household of TACEF
will mature when every part begins to function especially when we realise that everyone of us has a place in God and we
have something special to offer. Do not say, “I am not needed.” Do not say, “My role is too small.” Do not bury what God
has placed in you. Find your place, grow in grace, and supply your measure.

3. Assignment Differs, but Purpose Is One in Christ: The tribes of Israel did not all receive the same land, but they still
belonged to the same, one covenant people of Israel. Their portions differed, but their purpose was one. Each tribe had its
boundaries and inheritance, yet all were part of God’s larger plan for Israel. This means that difference in assignment was
not meant to create division but to complement one another so that we can complete the corporate inheritance. This is
the same principle in the body of Christ. Ephesians 4 shows different gifts and graces, but one purpose of building up of the
body of Christ. Christ gave apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors, and teachers for the perfecting of the saints, for the
work of the ministry, and for the edifying of the body. These gifts were not given to create personality centres, spiritual
competition, or private kingdoms. They were given so that the whole body may grow into Christ.

Therefore, each of us as God’s end-time revival army must walk in the understanding that though our gifts and assignments
differ, our purpose is one in Christ. We all need one another for the sake of winning more hearts for the Lord. We are not
competing on assignments, but manifesting different expressions of one purpose, which is that Christ may be formed in His
people and His body may be built. As we learned in our annual study last year, this is why serving God with other believers
requires humility, love, honour, and understanding. If we do not understand the unity of purpose, we may begin to compare,
criticise, isolate ourselves, or compete. A person who teaches must not despise those serving in administration. A person
who sings must not despise intercession. A person who leads must not despise those who serve quietly in the kitchen or
clinic. Every part matters because the mandate is bigger than any single person.

4. Understanding the Five-Fold Ministry as Distributed Grace for Building the Body:
Ephesians 4 teaches that Christ gave gifts unto men for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, and for the
edifying of the body of Christ. These gifts are not titles for show-off, ranks for superiority, or platforms for self-display. They
are distributed graces given by Christ to build, equip, strengthen, and mature His body, as explored below:
• Apostolic grace: This helps to lay foundations, open new territories, establish order, strengthen doctrines, and raise
 people into kingdom assignment. It carries a burden to build beyond one season and ensure that the work of God is
 properly planted and sustained.
• Prophetic grace: This helps the body to hear God clearly, discern His mind, expose compromise, call the people back to
 holiness, and remain sensitive to divine direction. It must bring the saints into alignment with God’s will.
• Evangelistic grace: This carries a burden for souls and those who are far from God. It stirs the body to go beyond church
 walls, preach Christ, win the lost, and bring men into the saving knowledge of the Lord Jesus.
• Pastoral grace: This nurtures, feeds, guides, protects, and cares for the flock of God with patience and love. It carries
 the burden of stability, follow-up, restoration, encouragement, and the spiritual wellbeing of the people.

 ~ 179 ~

• Teaching grace: This explains truth, grounds believers in sound doctrines, corrects errors, and helps the saints
 understand and apply the Word of God. It protects the body from shallowness, confusion, deception, and every wind
 of doctrine.

5. Step-by-Step Applications and Practical Implications
• Receive your portion with humility: Stop comparing your assignment with another person’s assignment. Ask God to
 show you your place and serve there faithfully.
• Honour the portions of others: Celebrate the grace of God in other people without envy, criticism, jealousy, or
 competition.
• Discover your measure: Identify the area where God has given you special grace, ability, opportunity, or spiritual gift,
 and begin to develop it.
• Serve beyond visibility: Do not serve because you want to be seen. Hidden service before God is precious.
• Use your gifts to build others: Let your teaching, singing, leadership, giving, writing, organising, mentoring, intercession,
 welfare, visitation, digital skills and follow-up strengthen the body of Christ.
• Steward your resources: Use your time, talent, treasure, knowledge, relationships, and spiritual gifts for the
 advancement of God’s purpose.
• Function as part of the body: Do not isolate yourself or behave as though your grace is independent of others or better
 than others. Serve in love, humility, and accountability.
• Supply your measure in TACEF: The mandate will grow stronger when every TACEFite serves faithfully, committedly,
 consistently, and in love.
