Introduction
Our study this week x-rays the life of Caleb, one of the strongest examples of long-standing faith, inner strength, disciplined
courage, and wholehearted following in the book of Joshua as we continue to learn the characters of an exceeding great
army. Caleb was forty years old when Moses sent him from Kadeshbarnea to spy out the land with Joshua when twelve
spies were sent out. While the other ten spies returned with fear and made the heart of the people melt, Caleb with Joshua
brought back a good report, because of their personal relationship with God which made them see through the lens of
heaven and not human sight. Forty-five years later, at the age of eighty-five years, Caleb did not come to Joshua asking for
the easiest land or the most convenient inheritance. He boldly said, “Now therefore give me this mountain.”

Caleb’s request is deeply instructive. The mountain he asked for was not an easy territory. The huge and dangerous Anakims
were still there, and the cities were great and fenced. Yet Caleb did not run from difficulty. He did not use age as an excuse
for smallness. He did not settle for comfort because he had waited long. He did not say, “I have tried enough.” Instead, he
looked at a difficult territory and asked for it because he trusted the God who had promised.

 ~ 182 ~

Ephesians expands this lesson by showing us that true strength begins in the inner man. Paul prays that believers may be
strengthened with might by the Spirit in the inner man. This means the deepest strength of a believer is not physical energy,
youthful appearance, or natural capacity but also the inner man. The outer man may face age, pressure, tiredness, delay,
affliction, responsibility, and weariness, but the inner man must be renewed day by day, strengthened by the Spirit, and
rooted in Christ. When the Spirit strengthens the inner man, believers can continue to believe, obey, serve, endure, and
take on difficult assignments beyond natural limitations. This study also reminds us that we have to manage our bodies well
in good health so that at old age we can do much more for the Lord like Caleb.

Teachings
1. Faith Can Remain Alive after Long Delay: Caleb waited forty-five years for the promise God gave concerning his
inheritance. Many people would have allowed time, age, delay, disappointment, wilderness seasons, or leadership
transitions to weaken their confidence. But Caleb’s faith remained alive. Time did not bury the promise, and long waiting
time did not destroy his conviction. This teaches us that divine promises can mature in waiting because some promises
from God require seasons of testing, endurance, discipline, preparation, and continued obedience before fulfilment comes.
Caleb did not forget what the Lord said and he did not treat the promise as an old story. He carried it in his heart until the
appointed time came.

However, Caleb did not only remember the promise; he claimed it with courage. He said to Joshua, “Thou knowest the thing
that the LORD said unto Moses the man of God concerning me and thee.” He then added, “Now therefore give me this
mountain.” This was not arrogance but a covenant confidence. Caleb knew what God had spoken, and he came in the right
order to receive what had been promised. The promise of God did not remove his responsibility. Waiting did not lead to
inactivity. Caleb came forward with courage because he trusted the faithfulness of God. He had seen the Lord keep him
alive up to eighty-five years, and he believed that the same God who preserved him could still help him possess the land.

Dear TACEFites, thirty-two years of revival pursuit must not make us become tired of the burden. Time must not weaken
the mandate. Years must not reduce our passion for souls, discipleship, prayer, holiness, and genuine revival in our local
churches, campuses and communities. If God has called us to turn the hearts of men unto Him, then we must keep the
promise alive from one generation to another.

2. Taking Mountains for the Lord Requires Inner-Man Renewal: Caleb asked for the mountain where the dangerous
Anakims lived and where the cities were fenced. He did not ask for the easiest portion. He did not seek the most convenient
inheritance. He did not say, “I have tried enough; give me anything that is available.” Instead, he looked at a hard territory
and said, “Give me this mountain.” This mindset shows that Caleb’s strength was not merely physical; it was the strength
of faith, conviction, courage, and inner renewal. The book of Ephesians teaches us that true strength begins in the inner
man, that is, the hidden part of us where our convictions, character, faith, desires, and relationship with God reside. It is
the control centre of our spiritual life, shaping how we think, respond, endure trials, and walk with God even when the
outward man is weak or under pressure.

Apostle Paul therefore prayed that believers may be “strengthened with might by his Spirit in the inner man.” The outer
man can face age, pressure, delay, and weariness, but the inner man must be renewed by the Spirit of God day by day. We
need inner strength for the work of revival because it can become a hard territory of difficult souls, neglected children,
frustrating systems, broken families, and resistant communities. The outer man may grow tired, but the inner man must
not collapse. The body may feel pressure, but the spirit must remain alive. It is also important to note that the inner-man
renewal is daily. A yesterday’s encounter cannot sustain today’s walk. We must return daily to the Word, pray continually,
fast with understanding, maintain fellowship, guard the heart, and remain rooted in the love and fullness of Christ. The
mountain is not possessed by outward boldness but by inward strength that has been renewed by God.

3. The Mountain Belongs to Those Who Seek Hard Territories and Follow the Lord Wholeheartedly: Caleb’s request, “Give
me this mountain,” reveals the spirit of a wholehearted follower. He did not ask for what was easy, safe, comfortable, or
already settled. He asked for a place where the Anakims were and where the cities were difficult and tough. He was not
looking for convenience and was not trying to avoid difficulty. He was determined to possess what God had promised. Even
at eighty-five years old, Caleb was still speaking the language of faith and responsibility. While others might have been
looking for a place to rest, Caleb was asking for a mountain to possess. His focus was not on his age, limitations, or the
strength of the enemy, but on the faithfulness of God. This disposition of Caleb is a major kingdom principle where every
revival army must not always look for the easiest assignment, the most comfortable environment, or the place where

 ~ 183 ~

everything is already formed with the right spiritual atmosphere. Sometimes, God calls His soldiers to remain in difficult
places until His light breaks forth there.

This principle is equally applicable to our personal lives. We must not settle for less when God has given us the capacity
and grace for much more. Caleb teaches us that spiritual vitality is not determined by age but by vision, faith, and purpose.
Why should a formal retirement age of sixty years stop a believer from remaining productive? Retirement from a profession
should never become retirement from purpose. There are still mountains to possess, lives to impact, disciples to raise,
books to write, businesses to build, communities to transform, and nations to influence. In the same way, a professional
should not settle into complacency when there are greater opportunities in God’s will for leadership, innovation, and
impact as a potential business owner.

4. As Thy Days, So Shall Thy Strength Be: Preserving the Body for the Fulfilment of God’s Promise: Caleb said, “I am as
strong now as I was when Moses sent me on that journey, and I can still travel and fight as well as I could then” NLT version.
At eighty-five years old, Caleb still had strength for war, to go out and to come in. This does not mean that age had no effect
on his body, but it shows that Caleb had been preserved by God and had lived in such a way that he could still respond to
divine assignments even at old age. His testimony reminds us that long life, health, and usefulness are blessings that should
be stewarded for the fulfilment of God’s promise.

There is a spiritual principle here. The inner man must be renewed daily and the outer physical bodies must also be
managed wisely. We need the body to serve God on earth. We need strength to pray, travel, teach, mentor, work, visit,
evangelise, attend fellowship, raise children, support the church, and carry responsibilities. If we constantly abuse our
bodies through careless eating, unhealthy habits, poor rest, unmanaged stress, and lack of self-control, we may weaken
our ability to fulfil long-term assignments. Therefore, every revival army who seeks to go far for God must embrace the
principles of wellness and healthy living. We must avoid excessive sugar, sugary drinks, late-night eating, and unhealthy
indulgence. We should eat with wisdom, take enough water, maintain good rest, practise regular body movement or
exercise, and emotional wellness. We should avoid bitterness, anxiety, anger, hidden stress, and tensions that weaken the
body.

It is also important to note that healthy living and wellness are not vanity when they are submitted to God’s purpose. We
are not preserving the body for appearance or selfish comfort. We are preserving strength so that we can serve long, finish
well, and accomplish the promise of God.

5. Step-by-Step Applications and Practical Implications
• Keep old promises alive: Write them down and revisit the promises, instructions, prophecies, burdens, and convictions
 God has given you. Do not allow time, delay, or changing seasons to bury them.
• Claim promises with courageous obedience: Do not only remember what God said. Take responsible steps through
 prayer, planning, sacrifice, and faith.
• Renew the inner man daily: Feed on the Word, pray in the Spirit, worship, fast, meditate, repent quickly, and remain
 rooted in fellowship with God.
• Ask for mountains, not ease alone: Do not always choose the easiest way out. Be willing to serve in hard fields, difficult
 fellowships, demanding ministries, unreached places, and burdensome responsibilities.
• Manage the body for long-term usefulness: Eat wisely, reduce sugary drinks and excessive sugar, take water, exercise
 regularly, rest properly, and avoid destructive habits.
• Care for mental and emotional wellness: Bring anxiety, bitterness, anger, pressure, disappointment, and hidden stress
 to God in prayer. Seek godly counsel and support when needed.
• Do not retire from the vision of revival: Past excos, alumni, leaders, and older believers should continue to serve,
 mentor, counsel, teach, give, encourage, and model faithfulness.
• Preserve strength for divine assignment: Do not live carelessly with the body God gave you. Ask for grace to live long,
 serve well, finish strong, and accomplish God’s promise.

Week 28: Monday, 8 March 2027 to Sunday, 14 March 2027
Title: The Daughters of Zelophehad: Claiming Covenant Inheritance with Boldness
Bible Texts: Joshua 17:3-6; Numbers 27:1-11; Ephesians 1:11-14

Bible Texts

that ye believed, ye were sealed with that holy Spirit of promise, 14 Which is the earnest of our inheritance until the

Key Extracts from the Bible Texts to Remember and Reflect On
 • Zelophehad had no sons, but daughters.
 • Give unto us therefore a possession among the brethren of our father.
 • Moses brought their cause before the LORD.
 • The daughters of Zelophehad speak right.
 • The LORD commanded Moses to give us an inheritance among our brethren.
 • In whom also we have obtained an inheritance.
 • Predestinated according to the purpose of him who worketh all things after the counsel of his own will.

Introduction
Our study this week explores the remarkable story of the five daughters of Zelophehad (Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and
Tirzah). To fully appreciate the significance of their story, we must understand that it did not begin in the book of Joshua.
Their story began during the days of Moses, long before Israel crossed the Jordan. In Numbers 27:1–11, these daughters
appeared before Moses, Eleazar the priest, the princes, and the congregation to make a case concerning their inheritance.
Their father had died in the wilderness and had no sons. Under the customary practices of that time, this could have meant
that their father’s name, family line, and inheritance would disappear from among his brethren. Yet these women
understood that God's covenant purposes were greater than human customs. They refused to allow ignorance, fear, or
cultural limitations to rob them of what God intended for their family. What makes their story even more instructive is
Moses' response. Moses did not dismiss them because they were women and neither did he make a hasty personal
judgment. Instead, he brought their case before the Lord (Numbers 27:5), and God Himself declared, “The daughters of
Zelophehad speak right.” Their request therefore became more than a personal appeal; it became a divine statute in Israel.

 ~ 187 ~

The background above is critical because when we arrive in Joshua 17 and find the daughters of Zelophehad standing before
Joshua, Eleazar, and the leaders to claim their inheritance, they were not making a new request. They were standing upon
a promise already established and a covenant matter already settled before the Lord through Moses. Joshua's positive
disposition towards them was therefore not merely an act of kindness but an act of faithfulness to a divine precedence. He
honoured what God had already spoken through Moses and ensured that a previous revelation became a present reality.
This act of the daughters of Zelophehad teaches us that we do not need to fight, manipulate, complain, or create tension
in the house of God to gain attention. They approached the matter through the proper channels and respectfully reminded
the leaders of God's established word. Their request was bold but respectful. They did not speak against the leadership,
form a pity party, or create division among the people. They respectfully engaged the leadership and communicated their
intention clearly within order.

This teaching also helps us understand the biblical place of women in God's purposes. The daughters of Zelophehad
demonstrate that women have a covenant portion in God's inheritance and can serve His purposes meaningfully while
maintaining the spirit of submission, order, and teachability required in the household of faith. The book of Ephesians
further highlights this study by showing us that in Christ we have obtained an inheritance according to the purpose of God,
and this inheritance is not determined by gender, social class, background, age, or human evaluation. It is secured in Christ
and sealed by the Holy Spirit of promise. Therefore, no TACEFite should allow gender, age, family background, or past failure
to define their destiny.

Teachings
1. Inheritance Must Be Claimed Because Ignorance Can Lead to Loss: The daughters of Zelophehad understood that they
had a legitimate inheritance. If they had remained ignorant, their father’s name could have disappeared from among his
family. If they had silently accepted the situation as unavoidable, they would have lost what God was willing to give them.
Their knowledge of covenant inheritance gave them the confidence to speak. They knew enough to ask, and their asking
resulted in a righteous judgment that benefited not only them but future generations of Israel. This teaches us that we
must know enough to access what God has made available to us in our faith and life journey. Many opportunities in life are
not lost because they do not exist, but because people do not know they exist. Many workplace benefits often go unclaimed
because employees never take time to understand their entitlements. Many young professionals are unaware of legitimate
opportunities for professional certifications, internships, grants, fellowships, entrepreneurship support, and career
development programmes. Students miss bursaries, scholarships, exchange programmes, research opportunities,
government supported student loans, and academic grants because they never search for them. Small business owners
sometimes struggle unnecessarily because they do not know about available intervention funds, non-interest financing
schemes, business support programmes, mentorship platforms, or market access opportunities through many non-profits.
Around the world, there are countless opportunities for learning, leadership development, holiday employment, and
enterprise creation, many of them freely available to those who are willing to seek, learn, and apply. However, all of these
searches must always remain within the boundaries of God’s will and leading,

As kingdom-minded believers, we must not live in ignorance of either spiritual truth or practical life knowledge because
ignorance can result in significant loss. A believer who does not know what God has provided in Christ may live far below
the provisions of grace. A believer who does not understand their identity may accept rejection, fear, shame, condemnation,
limitation, or inferiority as destiny. A believer who does not know their gifts and calling may watch others serve effectively
while burying their own grace and potential. Dear TACEFites, study the Word until you know what God has given you in
Christ. Do not allow ignorance to rob you of your inheritance. Know your identity, portion, calling, and your place in the
body of Christ and in the mandate of revival. At the same time, pursue knowledge diligently in every legitimate area of life,
learn new skills, understand available opportunities, explore avenues for growth and development, seek wisdom
concerning your career, finances, education, business, family, and ministry. What you do not know, you may never claim
and what you do not understand, you may fail to access.

2. Bold Faith Can Make a Claim without Rebellion or Disorder: The daughters of Zelophehad were bold, but they were
respectful and orderly. They did not speak in secret rebellion, murmur or create any form of tension within the camp. They
did not gather a faction. They did not insult leadership but they approached through the right channel and presented their
cause with clarity. As modern-day believers, we must know that boldness is not the same as rebellion. A believer can
respectfully make a claim without dishonouring authority, age and leadership. A youth can ask questions without arrogance.
The lesson here is that we learn to walk in humility, wisdom, and submission to godly process.

 ~ 188 ~

This principle is highly relevant in everyday life. As children relating with parents, employees interacting with employers,
students engaging with teachers, TACEFites relating with ministers in charge of our local churches, or even believers
interacting with one another, there will be moments when we need to speak up, seek clarification, request opportunities,
challenge assumptions respectfully, or present a legitimate concern. However, how we pursue these things matters as much
as the things themselves. Some people lose opportunities because they approach them with impatience, accusation, or a
sense of entitlement. Others remain silent and miss their inheritance because they are afraid to ask. As believers, we must
learn to communicate clearly, ask respectfully, and pursue God's promises courageously while maintaining the spirit of
Christ. As a member of God’s exceeding great army, we must be bold but remain respectful. We must seek clarity, do not
manipulate people. We must learn to present our case and not cause division.

It is also important to learn from the response of Moses when the daughters of Zelophehad asked about their inheritance.
He did not dismiss them because they were women. He did not silence them because their case was unusual. He did not
judge them by tradition and culture. He brought their cause before the Lord. This is a pattern for spiritual leadership.
Leaders must be careful not to reject people on things that we do not yet understand clearly. When a matter is unclear, it
must be brought before the Lord, tested by the Word, and handled with spiritual maturity.

3. Women Also Have Covenant Portion -Biblical Inclusion, Ministry, Submission, and Order: The daughters of Zelophehad
show clearly that women also have covenant portion in God because God has purpose, grace, and assignment for women
as well as men. The wider testimony of Scripture confirms that women have been used by God in significant ways. Miriam
led the women of Israel in worship after the crossing of the Red Sea. Deborah judged Israel and gave prophetic leadership
in a difficult season. Huldah the prophetess was consulted concerning the book of the law in the days of Josiah. There were
women who followed Jesus and ministered to Him of their substance. Philip had daughters who prophesied. Junia was
described by Paul as someone "prominent among the apostles”. He also commended Phoebe as a servant of the church
and recognised many other women who laboured in the gospel. These examples show that God’s work has never been
without women who believed, served, witnessed, taught, supported, prayed, prophesied, and laboured faithfully.

At the same time, biblical inclusion must always operate within biblical order in the home, the church, and the household
of faith. This context helps us understand difficult passages such as 1 Corinthians 14:34–35 and 1 Timothy 2:11–12, which
are sometimes interpreted as though women have no spiritual voice or place of service in God's kingdom. Such an
interpretation would be difficult to reconcile with the broader testimony of Scripture. In the same Corinthian letter, Paul
already acknowledges that women prayed and prophesied in the assembly under proper authority and order (1 Corinthians
11:5). Therefore, the issue in Corinth and Ephesus is not a universal prohibition against all forms of female participation in
ministry. The historical and cultural context of these verses are important. In both Corinth and Ephesus, the early church
was ministering within societies where many women had limited access to formal religious instruction and theological
training. The churches were also dealing with false teachings, disorderly conduct that were carried over by women from
their past lifestyle before they became believers which Paul needed the church to manage for order in public worship.

Therefore, we must see our mothers and sisters as vital members of the great and exceeding army that God is raising. We
must encourage our sisters to pray, serve, disciple believers, lead initiatives, coordinate kingdom projects, engage in
evangelism, and fully deploy the graces that God has entrusted to them. Our TACEF Mothers Fellowship should continue to
grow into a battalion of intercessors, nurturing mothers who carry the burden of revival, discipleship, and kingdom
influence. Likewise, our weekly Tuesday morning Sisters Programme and general Sisters Fellowship should be treated with
intentional commitment and seriousness, serving as strategic platforms for spiritual growth, leadership development,
mentorship, discipleship, and preparation for kingdom service.

4. Silence Can Lead to Loss Due to Ignorance: The daughters of Zelophehad could have remained silent. They could have
accepted their situation simply because their father had no sons. They could have concluded that nothing could be done
and allowed their family's inheritance to disappear. But they understood enough about God's covenant and His promises
to speak up. Their holy boldness preserved their inheritance, secured their father's name, and established a righteous
precedent for future generations. Many believers today lose ground because they do not fully understand who they are in
Christ or the opportunities that God has made available to them in various spheres of life. They remain silent when they
should pray, seek counsel, ask questions, apply, volunteer, or step forward in faith. They withdraw when they should pursue
opportunities. More painfully, many believers settle for far less than God's purpose for their lives because they assume
certain opportunities are beyond their reach while others bury their gifts in silence because of fear, low self-esteem, societal
limitations, cultural expectations, background, or status.

 ~ 189 ~

Step-by-Step Applications and Practical Implications
• Know your inheritance in Christ: Study the Word to understand your, identity, spiritual blessings, calling, gifts, access to
 God, and place in the body.
• Do not allow ignorance to rob you in life: In life generally, learn to ask questions, seek contemporary knowledge, be
 abreast of facts, and grow in understanding.
• Make righteous claims with humility: When you have a burden, request, concern, or conviction, approach through the
 right channel with wisdom, respect, and order.
• Be bold without rebellion: Do not confuse confidence with pride or courage with disorder. Speak truth with humility
 and honour.
• Encourage women’s ministry with biblical order: Sisters should be encouraged to serve faithfully within sound doctrine,
 submission, holiness, and godly structure.
• Do not silence God-given portions: Leaders must not suppress sisters, converts, quiet workers, or less-visible members
 whom God is calling to serve.
• Claim your portion responsibly: Do not use inheritance for self-promotion. Use your grace to serve, build, strengthen,
 and edify the body.
• Reject limiting labels: Do not allow background, fear, age, gender, past failure, or human rejection to define your
 destiny.

Key Extracts from the Bible Texts to Remember and Reflect On

 • How long are ye slack to go to possess the land?

Introduction
This week’s study brings us to a serious moment in Israel’s journey of possession the land and winning their territory for
the Lord as a reference example of an exceeding great army. The whole congregation assembled at Shiloh, and the
tabernacle of the congregation was set up there. The land had been subdued before them, yet seven tribes out of the
twelve had not received their inheritance. This means that the promise had been given and the land had been brought
under control, but many of the people had still not moved into what God had apportioned to them. Joshua therefore asked
a searching question: “How long will you delay going out to take possession of the land that the LORD, the God of your
ancestors, gave you?” (CSB version).
Joshua’s question is a prophetic charge to every TACEFite, every family, fellowship, local church, campus, business, career
and believer who has received divine promises but remains passive, delayed, distracted, or laid back. God’s promise does
not cancel man’s responsibility. Divine provision must be met with timely action. The land may be available while people
remain slack. Access may be granted while souls remain unclaimed. A door may open for youth Sunday outreaches in our
local churches or opportunity to run the children church, yet the work may still be delayed because people refuse to pray,
arise in the spirit, plan, act, and follow through.

The book of Ephesians further elaborates on this by calling believers to awake out of sleep and to redeem the time because
the days are evil, and therefore time must not be wasted. Spiritual laziness often hides under excuses, busyness, fear, poor
planning, lack of discipline, and endless postponement. It is possible to attend programmes but remain slack in personal
obedience. It is possible to talk about revival but fail to plan, pray, follow up, disciple, and possess the souls God has placed

 ~ 192 ~

within our reach. Therefore, our Week 29 calls all TACEFites, as true revival army to arise from delay into timely God-
initiated actions. Joshua did not only rebuke the seven tribes on being slack, but he also went further to give them a
practical approach of what needs to be done. He asked them to select men, survey the land, describe it, return with
findings, and divide the land into parts.

Teachings
1. Slackness Delays Inheritance Even When the Land Has Already Been Provided: Joshua 18 shows a painful reality when
the Promised Land had been subdued before Israel, but seven tribes had not yet received their inheritance. The problem
was not that God had failed or that the land was unavailable. The problem was that the people had become slack,
comfortable, lazy and unwilling to take the necessary steps to possess what had already been provided. The promise was
available, but possession was delayed because responsibility was neglected. This teaches us that God may open great doors
and God’s people may never walk into it. He may provide access that people never utilise and bring many opportunities
our way that we may never pursue. God may bring a person into a season of favour, yet fear, procrastination, poor
planning, lack of discipline, distraction, or complacency can prevent them from entering fully into what He has prepared.
This is because divine provision never eliminates the need for human responsibility. God gives the land, but we must still
rise and possess it.

Many believers live in this condition today. They know what God has been prompting them to do, yet they keep postponing
action. They know they need to restore their prayer altar, reconcile with someone, follow up on souls, let go of the pains
of the past, join a service unit, teach children, support the fellowship, or grow deeper in the Word, but they keep saying,
“I will do it later.” The same pattern extends into everyday life. Some know they should obtain a professional certification,
learn digital skills, improve their communication and social skills, pursue an advanced degree, update their CV, start a side
business, write a proposal, apply for a scholarship, seek a mentor, improve their health, or develop leadership capacity,
yet they continually postpone taking action. Others spend years talking about what they hope to do while watching
opportunities pass by. They become stale in their skills, outdated in their knowledge, and limited in their impact. Beloved,
do not postpone action until the opportunity is gone. When God provides the land, rise and possess it. The time to act is
now, as the Lord leads.

2. Spiritual Laziness Hides under Excuses: Joshua's question, “How long are ye slack?” reveals that the delay had persisted
for far too long. Slackness does not always appear as open rebellion but hides behind seemingly reasonable excuses and
endless postponement. Sometimes it disguises itself as busyness, because we can always find genuine reasons why we
have not yet done what God has instructed us to do. At other times, it hides behind fear, uncertainty, over-analysis, lack
of confidence, or waiting for the “perfect time.” Yet delayed obedience remains delayed obedience, no matter how
convincing the excuse may sound. Indeed, slackness can sound religious. It may say, “We are waiting on God,” when God
is actually waiting for us to obey and act. It may say, “The time is not yet right,” when fear is the real problem. It may say,
“We are very busy,” when the issue is wrong priority. It may say, “There is no money,” when the real issue is lack of
planning.

Ephesians warns us, “Awake thou that sleepest.” This means some people can be spiritually asleep while surrounded by
many opportunities, even while pretending to be overwhelmed in spiritual activities. They may speak the language of
revival but lack the discipline of doing the right thing at the right time and in the right way. They may rejoice over promises
but remain laid back and irresponsible to act on time. This is the time for us to press a pause and examine our excuses.
Beloved, it is time to awake, arise, and possess the land.

3. Possession Requires Structure, Practical Actions and Territorial Mapping: Joshua did not merely rebuke the tribes for
their slackness; he went further and provided a practical framework for action. This is an important lesson for every leader.
It is not enough to identify a problem; effective leadership must also provide a clear pathway toward a solution. Joshua
instructed the tribes to appoint representatives to survey the land, describe it according to its territories, document their
findings, return with a report, and then proceed with the allocation and occupation of the inheritance. This reveals a
powerful kingdom principle: possession requires more than desire or good intentions. It requires structure, planning,
execution, accountability, and follow-through. Joshua's six step process can be summarised as: (1) define the territory; (2)
understand the landscape; (3) document the realities; (4) assign responsibility; (5) establish a plan; and (6) take action.
The men did as instructed and returned with a report. In doing so, they transformed a promise into a practical pathway for
possession.

 ~ 193 ~

This same principle applies to every area of life. In our spiritual lives, we should not merely desire spiritual growth; we must
create structures that support it. A believer who desires a stronger prayer life should have a prayer schedule and create an
accountability structure. A local fellowship that desires growth must identify new converts, engage inactive members, and
create outreach programmes for new members. A campus fellowship should understand its campus environment, map
faculties, hostels, departments, and student groups, identify where students are concentrated, and how best to maximise
programmes like “Catch Them Young” during new session for growth. The same principle applies to career development,
business growth, and personal advancement. Many people desire promotion but have never honestly assessed their
current competencies, identified skill gaps, or developed a learning plan. A professional should periodically survey their
career landscape, do skills audit, identify areas requiring improvement, build relevant skills, strengthen professional
networks, and create measurable development goals. A business owner should understand the market, study customer
needs, analyse competitors, identify growth opportunities, review financial performance, and create deliberate plans to
increase value and sales. A student should periodically review academic performance, identify weak subjects, improve
study habits, seek mentorship, and establish learning goals. In every case, growth begins with understanding the territory
before attempting to possess it.

4. Time Must Be Redeemed through Kingdom Focus and Planning: Ephesians says, “Redeeming the time, because the days
are evil.” This means time is a spiritual resource that can be invested, wasted, lost, abused, delayed, misused, or redeemed.
A believer who does not manage time well may miss seasons, lose opportunities, delay divine lifting, and become unfruitful.
Redeeming time requires thorough planning. Every revival army must ask: What has God assigned to me in this season?
What must I do now? What must not be postponed? What skill must I build now? What certification must I complete
before year-end? What spiritual discipline must I maintain now? What relationship must I build? What soul must I follow
up? What local church assignment must I carry? What opportunity is time-sensitive? What door may not remain open
forever?

It is a sad reality that many believers delay doing the right things at the right time. They postpone personal development
opportunities until the season for advancement has passed. Some remain in the same career position for years because
they never prepared themselves for the next level. Others pray for business growth but never study their customers,
understand the market, improve their products, or develop the skills required to compete effectively. Some desire financial
increase but never learn budgeting, investment, or financial stewardship. Others dream of ministry enlargement but
neglect prayer, study, and discipleship. They become stale in their skills, outdated in their knowledge, and limited in their
influence while praying for enlargement. This explains our text of study from Ephesians which calls us to walk “not as fools,
but as wise.” Wisdom helps us recognise opportunities, prepare for them, and act when God opens the door.

Time must also be redeemed by avoiding the waste of precious hours on endless social media browsing, consuming
irrelevant videos, pictures, and content that add little or no value to our lives. Much of that same time can be invested in
learning new skills, acquiring knowledge, improving professional competence, deepening spiritual understanding, or
developing practical capabilities through the countless free learning resources available online. Platforms such as YouTube,
online courses platform like Coursera, digital libraries, and professional learning communities provide unprecedented
access to knowledge for those who are intentional about growth.

5. Step-by-Step Applications and Practical Implications
• Identify where you have been slack: Write down areas where you have being slack, avoided responsibility, postponed
 growth, or refused to act.
• Separate access from possession: Ask whether the doors God has opened have produced real fruits, such as souls
 saved, people discipled, members restored, children taught, or families strengthened.
• Practise territorial mapping: List the people, families, church units, campuses, departments, businesses, homes,
 communities, and groups that need divine encounter.
• Describe the land clearly: Do not keep the assignment vague. Write names, needs, locations, challenges, opportunities,
 possible actions, and follow-up plans for both spiritual and your career or business efforts.
• Break vision into action: Convert every assignment to be done into steps, timelines, responsibilities, resources needed,
 and accountable reporting.
• Redeem time for kingdom tasks: Set weekly time for every activity and hold yourself accountable.
• Plan your life wisely: Identify skills development programmes, certifications, advanced degrees, professional skills,
 business disciplines, health routines, financial habits, and spiritual disciplines that must not be delayed.

• Avoid becoming stale or obsolete: Keep learning, reading, training, and improving so that your usefulness in God’s hand
 is not diminished by outdated knowledge or poor preparation.
• Stop hiding behind excuses: Replace “I will do it later” with a clear decision, a first step, and a date for action.
• Review progress regularly: Like the men who returned to Joshua with a written description, report progress, learn
 lessons, adjust plans, and keep moving until the land is possessed.

SECTION 7: How God’s Army Preserves Order, Extends Ministry, and Trusts God’s Faithfulness

The journey of God’s end-time army now moves from possessing inheritance into preserving order, extending ministry,
building healthy communities, and resting in the faithfulness of God. After the land had been divided and the inheritance
allocated, Israel still needed structures that would sustain covenant life across generations. Boundaries had to be defined,
cities of refuge established, the Levites distributed among the people, and the nation continually reminded that every
promise God had spoken would surely come to pass. This section therefore explores how God’s people must move beyond
receiving blessings to building systems, relationships, and ministries that preserve His purposes in every territory.
Possession is not complete until what has been received is properly ordered, protected, stewarded, and passed on.

There is also a pattern of divine administration throughout this section. Every tribe had boundaries that defined its portion.
Every city of refuge reflected God’s balance of justice and mercy. Every Levitical city ensured that no territory was left
without spiritual influence. Every fulfilled promise reminded Israel that God’s faithfulness is the foundation of covenant

 ~ 197 ~

inheritance. This teaches us that God’s work thrives where there is order, responsibility, accountability, spiritual coverage,
and faithful stewardship. Confusion, rivalry, isolation, and lack of structure weaken what God has built. The army that has
received inheritance must now learn to preserve unity, distribute ministry, restore the wounded, and maintain covenant
order across every territory.

Week 31: Setting the Boundaries – Serving God Faithfully in Your Assigned Portion: The division of the land teaches that
every tribe had boundaries and every assignment had a defined territory. Boundaries are not restrictions but provisions
for fruitfulness, order, and effectiveness. Ephesians teaches that every part of the body must supply its measure. TACEFites
must learn to serve faithfully within their God-given assignments without comparison, competition, jealousy, or
unnecessary interference in another person’s portion. The mandate advances when every member knows their place,
respects godly boundaries, and serves with wisdom, focus, and accountability.

Week 32: Cities of Refuge – Building Communities of Mercy, Healing, and Restoration: The cities of refuge reveal the
heart of God for justice, mercy, restoration, and protection. They remind us that Christ is our ultimate refuge, whose
atoning work secures our salvation and inheritance. TACEFites must learn to build fellowship cultures where truth and
mercy walk together, where correction seeks restoration rather than humiliation, and where wounded, struggling,
repentant, and recovering believers can find healing. God’s revival army must neither crush people through harshness nor
excuse sin through careless tolerance.

Week 33: The Levites Among the People – Distributing Ministry Across Every Territory: The Levites were scattered among
the tribes so that every territory would have access to spiritual instruction, worship, counsel, and covenant guidance.
Ephesians teaches that ministry gifts are given to equip the saints for the work of ministry. TACEFites must therefore carry
revival beyond central programmes into local churches, campuses, homes, workplaces, communities, and families. No
territory should be left spiritually uncovered. The burden of ministry must be shared so that every believer becomes both
a recipient and a distributor of kingdom life.

Week 34: The God Who Fulfils Every Promise – Trusting God’s Faithfulness Over Every Inheritance: Joshua concludes this
section with one of the strongest testimonies in the Scripture that not one good thing failed of all that the Lord had spoken.
Israel possessed the land because God remained faithful to His covenant. Ephesians reminds us that the Holy Spirit is the
earnest of our inheritance and that God is able to do exceeding abundantly above all that we ask or think. TACEFites must
therefore learn to trust God beyond delays, opposition, uncertainties, and changing circumstances. Every promise,
inheritance, and assignment rests upon the faithfulness of God, who never fails and whose Word cannot fall to the ground.

 • The whole body fitly joined together.
 • Every joint supplieth.
 • According to the effectual working in the measure of every part.
 • Maketh increase of the body unto the edifying of itself in love.

Introduction
As we continue to learn the principles of becoming a great and exceeding army, our study this week brings us to the setting
of boundaries among the tribes of Israel. Joshua 19 gives detailed descriptions of the inheritances of Simeon, Zebulun,
Issachar, Asher, Naphtali, Dan, and finally the inheritance given to Joshua himself. The chapter may look like a list of names,
cities, borders, and territories, but it teaches a deep principle of divine order. God did not only give Israel the land generally
but also assigned portions specifically to each tribe. Each tribe had its place, its boundary, its cities, and its responsibility.

We can also learn that the setting of boundaries teaches that God is a God of order, placement, and purpose. He does not
only call people generally, but He also assigns them specifically to tasks and assignments. A tribe could not simply take
another tribe’s portion because it looked better and a tribe could not abandon its portion because another field appeared
more visible. Some tribes received large territories, some smaller. Some were near the sea, some inland. Some were in
strategic areas, some in ordinary-looking places. Yet every portion mattered because it came under the instruction of God.

Ephesians expands this principle by using it to show us how the body of Christ grows when every part supplies its portion.
The whole body is fitly joined together and compacted by that which every joint supplies. This means each part has a role
to play and add something special to contribute, such that the body becomes stronger when each part functions in love.
Without boundaries, there will be confusion, stepping on each other, rivalry, offence, wasted energy, and jealousy. But
when every part understands its role and serves faithfully, the whole body is edified.

This study generally teaches us that there is no competition or comparison in the pursuit of the mandate the Lord has given
us. Not every portion will look the same and not every assignment will carry the same visibility. We must stop measuring
usefulness by visibility but each of us must serve in our assigned areas faithfully without competition or jealousy.

Teachings
1. Every Tribe Had Boundaries, Showing That Assignment Must Be Understood and Respected: God’s people were not
meant to live in confusion, disorder, or constant overlap of responsibilities. Each tribe needed to know the portion assigned
to it, the cities within its care, and the boundaries of its stewardship. Assignments had to be understood, embraced, and
respected. Although God calls His people into one corporate purpose, He distributes different responsibilities within that
purpose. In the body of Christ, some are called to teach, some to intercede, some to evangelise in specific communities,
some to organise, some to serve children, some to coordinate welfare, some to support administration, some to provide
counsel, and others to lead. Every believer must understand their portion and serve there faithfully, knowing that
effectiveness comes through clarity of assignment.
Boundaries as seen in our texts are important because they help us focus our energy, maximise our effectiveness, and
avoid unnecessary confusion. A person without boundaries may attempt to do everything and ultimately do nothing well.
A leader without boundaries may interfere in every department and weaken those entrusted with responsibility. A worker
without boundaries may neglect their assigned duty while pursuing what appears more visible or prestigious. The same
principle applies beyond ministry. A student without clear priorities may be distracted by too many activities and neglect
academic excellence. A professional without focus may pursue multiple directions without developing expertise in any. A

 ~ 200 ~

business owner without defined goals may spend time on activities that generate little value while ignoring customers,
products, or market opportunities. Unclear boundaries often result in duplicated efforts, neglected responsibilities, wasted
energy, reduced productivity, and avoidable conflict.

2. Every Part Must Supply Something to the Whole Body: Ephesians 4 vs 16 teaches that the whole body grows by “that
which every joint supplieth.” This means the health of the body of Christ depends on every part functioning because no
part is useless or unnecessary. The whole body is strengthened when each part supplies its own unique measure of grace.
We can only have strong and impactful fellowships when everyone brings the best of what God has given unto them in
terms of grace, gift and goodness into the community of believers. In addition, when Paul says that the whole body grows
by “that which every joint supplieth,” he is using the picture of a human body to explain how Christ intends His Church to
function. In the body, joints connect, support, enable movement, transfer strength, and hold different parts together in
proper alignment. A finger may be small, but without the joints, it cannot bend, grip, write, serve, or function properly. In
the same way, no believer is useless in the body of Christ. Every member may not be as visible as the head, mouth, or
hands, but every joint supplies something necessary for the body’s growth.

This principle of an interconnected body of Christ points to contribution, connection, support, and proper working
together. The Church is not a crowd of independent people but one fold under one Shepherd, one connected body under
one Head, which is Christ. Therefore, God does not want isolated gifts, competing parts, or disconnected believers, but a
living system where every part supplies its measure in love. The tragedy is when any joint refuses to supply, the whole
body feels the weakness Therefore, no part should boast, and no part should feel useless. Every little act of faithful service
becomes part of the strength, movement, and increase of the whole body. This is why every TACEFite must find their duty
post, stay connected to Christ, remain joined to the vision, and faithfully supply their measure for the growth of the great
house.

3. Assignment Requires Focus, Because Not Every Need Is Your Field: There are many needs in the kingdom, but not every
need is your field of assignment. This does not mean we should be selfish, indifferent, or unwilling to help others. Rather,
it means we must serve with wisdom, discernment, and focus. A person who attempts to carry every burden without divine
direction may eventually become weary, distracted, offended, or ineffective. God never intended one person to solve every
problem. Assignments require focus. The tribes of Israel received different portions. Some were located by the sea, some
inland; some received larger territories, while others received smaller ones. If every tribe had abandoned its own
inheritance in pursuit of another tribe's land, confusion, neglect, and disorder would have followed. In the same way,
believers must continually ask: What has God placed in my hand in this season? Where has He called me to serve? What
responsibility am I accountable for before Him?

This principle is equally important in managing the many relationships, requests, and demands that surround us in everyday
life. We cannot become everything to everybody. We are not called to become the assistant Holy Spirit for every person
we meet. Some believers become emotionally exhausted, financially strained, and spiritually depleted because they feel
guilty saying no to any request for help. They give beyond their capacity which leads them to borrow and even to the extent
of not having enough to meet the needs of their immediate family. While we are called to love all people, pray for all
people, and help others within our God-given capacity, not every person who needs help should have unlimited access to
our time, energy, resources, emotions, or attention. For example, a parent must not neglect their family while trying to
solve everyone's problems. Discernment helps us distinguish between compassion and distraction, and between a genuine
burden and an unnecessary weight. There comes a point where spreading yourself too thin becomes destructive to your
own stewardship. God wants us to serve generously, but He also wants us to serve wisely, faithfully, and within the
boundaries of our assignment.

4. Serve with Wisdom and Order: Ephesians 5:15 says, “See then that ye walk circumspectly, not as fools, but as wise.”
Service in God’s house requires wisdom, discernment, and order. A gift may be genuine, but it must be exercised in the
right spirit, at the right time, through the right channels, and under the right authority. Without wisdom, even a good gift
can become a source of offence, confusion, pride, rivalry, distraction, or disorder. God is not only concerned with what we
do, but also with how we do it. Kingdom service must reflect the character of the God we represent, that is, a God of peace,
order, and purpose.

A person may have a teaching gift, but must still submit to leadership and sound doctrine. A person may have prophetic
sensitivity, but must exercise caution, humility, and accountability in sharing what they believe God has revealed for mutual

 ~ 201 ~

testing and acceptance. A person may have leadership ability but must not dominate people or build personal followership.
The Spirit of God does not produce confusion, disorder, or self-exaltation. The work of God must be carried out in love,
humility, wisdom, and submission. This was one of the major challenges in the church at Corinth. The believers were rich
in spiritual gifts, yet many gatherings had become disorderly. People were speaking simultaneously, interrupting one
another, competing for attention, and creating confusion during worship. Some were exercising spiritual gifts without
consideration for the edification of others. Paul did not condemn spiritual gifts; rather, he provided guidance for their
proper use. He taught that “the spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets” (1 Corinthians 14:32). In other words,
spiritual inspiration does not remove personal responsibility or self-control. No one should claim that the Holy Spirit forced
them to act disorderly. Paul therefore, instructed that all things should be done “decently and in order” (1 Corinthians
14:40). Likewise, during the Lord’s Supper, some believers were eating selfishly while others went hungry, turning a sacred
gathering into an occasion for division and disorder (1 Corinthians 11:20–22). Paul corrected them because spiritual
activities, no matter how sincere, must always reflect God's order.

5. Step-by-Step Applications and Practical Implications
• Know your assigned portion: Ask God to show you the specific area where you should serve in this season.
• Respect the portion of others: Do not compete with, despise, or trespass into another person’s assignment.
• Define roles clearly: Local fellowships should have clear responsibilities for prayer, Bible study, follow-up, welfare,
 children, youths, outreach, finance, and administration.
• Supply your measure: Do not remain passive. Identify what you can contribute and serve faithfully.
• Avoid comparison: Do not measure usefulness by visibility, crowd size, title, platform, or public recognition.
• Practise godly boundaries: Love people wisely. Not every need is your field, and not every relationship should have
 unlimited access to your time, emotions, or commitment
• Serve under order: Use your gift in the right spirit, at the right time, under godly structure and accountability.
• Focus on fruitfulness: Concentrate on the field God has assigned to you and labour there with faithfulness, humility,
 and consistency.

Questions for Discussion
 1. Why is it important for believers to understand and respect their assignments?
 2. How can lack of boundaries create confusion, jealousy, rivalry, offence, and wasted energy?
 3. How would you advise a brother who has little time for personal quiet time, his family, or his full-time work
 because he is overwhelmed by numerous ministry responsibilities, frequent ministration schedules, several
 independent online ministry platforms, and multiple counselling commitments?
 4. What does Ephesians 4:16 mean by “every joint supplieth”?
 5. What are practical examples of godly boundaries in service, relationships, commitment or allocation of your time?
 6. Why must a right gift be used in the right spirit, at the right time, under the right order?

Personal Reflection
Do I understand my assigned portion, or am I trying to do everything without clarity? Am I faithful in the field God has given
me, or am I distracted by another person’s assignment? Do I compare my portion with others because theirs looks larger,
more visible, or more celebrated? Am I passive in the body, or am I supplying my measure? Do I respect boundaries in
service and relationships? Do I know when to say yes and when to wait? Am I carrying burdens God has not assigned to
me while neglecting the duty post He has given me? Do I use my gift in the right spirit, at the right time, and under the
right order? Is my service building the body in love or creating confusion?

Prayer Points
 1. Heavenly Father, show me my assigned portion in Your mandate and help me to serve there faithfully without
 distraction.
 2. Lord, deliver me from confusion, comparison, jealousy, rivalry, and personal ambition in service.
 3. Lord, make me a faithful part of the body that supplies its measure in love.
 4. Lord, deliver me from distraction and carrying burdens You have not assigned to me.
 5. Father, help TACEF local fellowships to build clear roles, accountable structures, and fruitful service systems.
 6. Lord, help me to use every gift in the right spirit, at the right time, under the right order.

Week 32: Monday, 5 April 2027 to Sunday, 11 April 2027
Title: Cities of Refuge: Building Communities of Mercy, Healing, and Restoration

Bible Texts: Joshua 20:1-9; Ephesians 4:1-3, 31-32

Bible Texts

Key Extracts from the Bible Texts to Remember and Reflect On
 • Appoint out for you cities of refuge.
 • They shall take him into the city unto them, and give him a place.
 • They shall not deliver the slayer up into his hand.
 • Walk worthy of the vocation wherewith ye are called.
 • With all lowliness and meekness, with longsuffering, forbearing one another in love
 • Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.
 • Let all bitterness, and wrath, and anger, and clamour, and evil speaking, be put away from you.
 • Be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another.

Introduction
This week takes our study into the setting up of the cities of refuge in the land of Israel. After the land had been divided
and boundaries had been established, God instructed Joshua to designate specific cities of refuge where those who had
unintentionally caused the death of another person, as well as those who were vulnerable and at risk of unjust retaliation,
could flee for protection and safety until their case was properly heard and judged according to God's justice and order.
These cities were not created to excuse wrongdoing or encourage lawlessness but were created to prevent reckless
revenge, false accusation, and careless destruction before a matter was properly heard. This act is because God’s justice is
not rash punishment, but righteous, patient and merciful. The cities of refuge also teach us that the Lord’s people must
know how to handle wounded lives, complicated matters, struggling believers, and people who have made regrettable
mistakes. The person who fled to the city had to declare his cause before the elders, and he still had to stand before the
congregation for judgment. This means refuge did not take away accountability. Mercy did not remove truth as grace did
not abolish order. But until the matter was heard, the person was protected from destruction. The city became a place
where justice and mercy worked together.

Ephesians further provides the practical guidelines to how we relate with others who need different forms of refuge by
calling believers to walk in lowliness, meekness, longsuffering, forbearance, kindness, tenderheartedness, and forgiveness.

 ~ 204 ~

It also commands that bitterness, wrath, anger, evil speaking, and malice must be put away. This means the church must
not become a place of anger, uncontrolled accusation, or spiritual cruelty. The fellowship must reflect the forgiveness we
have received in Christ. We must be truthful, but not harsh. We must correct sin, but not crush the repentant and we must
preserve holiness, but not destroy wounded people.

Teachings
1. God Provides Refuge for the Vulnerable, Wounded, and Mistaken: The cities of refuge reveal the heart of God towards
people in danger. The person who fled to the city of refuge was not immediately handed over to destruction but was given
space to be heard. Such person stood at the gate, declared his cause to the elders, and was received into the city until
judgment could be properly made. This shows that God is concerned not only with justice, but also with the process by
which justice is carried out. This means that as believers, we must not condemn
people before they are heard. Matters must not be judged by gossip, anger, assumption, emotion, partial information, or
mob pressure. A believer who has fallen into sin, become wounded, misunderstood, falsely accused, or caught in a
complicated matter must be handled with spiritual maturity, patience, and fairness. The Lord does not delight in reckless
destruction.
It is very important as end-time army that our fellowships do not become places where people hide their struggles until
they collapse, especially because many brethren are struggling silently because they fear shame, rejection, or public
disgrace. Some youths are battling temptations but do not know who to talk to and many carry wounds, confusion, family
pressure, secret guilt, or backsliding tendencies but remain silent because they do not believe the fellowship can handle
their pain with wisdom without turning it into public gossip. This does not mean careless tolerance of sin but that any
wounded soldier can find help before they are destroyed. This also means that leaders must be approachable, confidential,
and mature; and that correction must not come across as cruelty. We must have a heart of a refuge where the wounded
find care, the repentant find restoration, the struggling find counsel, the mistaken find truth and not crushed before they
are heard.

2. Christ Is Our Ultimate Refuge and Eternal High Priest: The cities of refuge point beyond themselves to the saving work
of Christ. They protected a person from immediate destruction, but they could not provide final and eternal redemption.
They gave shelter under the Old Testament order, but Christ gives salvation, forgiveness, peace with God, and eternal
inheritance. Jesus is the true and ultimate refuge for sinners. Every sinner needs refuge because sin exposes man to
judgment. No human being can save himself by personal effort, religious activity, morality, church attendance, or good
intentions. The soul needs a refuge greater than human sympathy. We need a Saviour who can deal with guilt, judgment,
condemnation, fear, and the power of sin. Christ is that refuge. In Him, the guilty can find forgiveness, the condemned can
find justification, the wounded can find healing, and the lost can find salvation.

The cities of refuge also help us understand Christ’s work of atonement as our High Priest. Numbers 35 teaches that the
person who fled to a city of refuge had to remain there until the death of the high priest. Joshua 20 repeats the same
instruction. When the high priest died, the person was released and could return safely to his inheritance. This points
forward to Jesus Christ, our great High Priest. Through His sacrificial death, Jesus secured freedom for everyone who
believes in Him. Through His resurrection, He opened the way to eternal life and our heavenly inheritance. Jesus did not
only shelter us from judgment; He carried our judgment upon Himself. He did not merely delay the punishment for sin; He
fully paid for our sin with His blood. He did not provide temporary protection but eternal redemption. Because Jesus lives
forever as our High Priest, we are safe and secure in Him. He is our refuge, advocate, righteousness, peace, and the One
who gives us access to the Father.

3. Discipline Must Be Redemptive, Not Destructive: The cities of refuge did not deny the seriousness of wrongdoing
because the person who fled still had to declare his cause and stand before the congregation for judgment. However, the
process protected him from reckless destruction. This shows that discipline in the household of God must be redemptive,
not destructive. Redemptive discipline seeks restoration, and is not driven by anger, revenge, embarrassment, gossip, or
the desire to disgrace someone. It is driven by love for God, love for truth, love for holiness, and love for the soul being
corrected. Correction must make sin uncomfortable, but we must not make repentance difficult for the fallen.

This is a very delicate but important balance. If there is no discipline, sin spreads and weakens the fellowship. If discipline
is cruel, wounded people may be destroyed beyond recovery. If correction is hidden when public harm has been done,
others may be weakened and corruption spreads even more. If correction is harsh, the person may be crushed. Therefore,
leaders must depend on the Spirit, the Word, prayer, counsel, and maturity in handling discipline. Every act of correction

 ~ 205 ~

must ask: What truth must be upheld? What harm must be repaired? What danger must be prevented? What repentance
must be encouraged? What restoration process is needed? What confidentiality must be preserved? What accountability
must be established? What support must be provided? In all instances, our goal is preserving holiness and recovery and
not humiliation. Dear revival army, particularly leaders, let us not be careless with wounded soldiers. We must not despise
or mock those who are trying to return to God. We must not gossip in the name of concern, and we must ensure that
discipline in the great house is fair, compassionate, and redemptive.

4. Refuge Does Not Cancel Accountability: Joshua 20:6 says, “And he shall dwell in that city, until he stand before the
congregation for judgment.” This reveals a major kingdom principle. The city of refuge provided protection, but it did not
remove the need for accountability and judgment. Mercy did not cancel responsibility, and refuge was never a licence for
lawlessness. This principle is especially important in the church today, where grace is sometimes misunderstood and
misapplied. The abuse of grace through hyper-grace teachings can create the false impression that repentance, holiness,
and accountability are no longer necessary. Yet biblical grace does not merely protect people from destruction; it also leads
them into truth, transformation, and obedience. A person who has sinned should not be crushed, rejected, or abandoned,
but neither should they be excused without genuine repentance and a willingness to change. A person who has fallen
should be restored with love, but restoration must be accompanied by accountability, discipleship, and evidence of spiritual
recovery. Mercy and holiness must therefore walk together.

There are two dangerous extremes that TACEFites must avoid. The first is harsh condemnation without mercy. This
approach wounds people, promotes fear, discourages honesty, and often causes struggling believers to hide their failures
rather than seek help. The second is careless tolerance without accountability. This approach makes sin comfortable,
weakens conviction, lowers spiritual standards, and gradually corrupts the fellowship. The kingdom way is neither extreme
but upholding the truth with compassion, mercy with order, grace with discipline, forgiveness with fruit-bearing
repentance, and restoration with accountability. God's desire is not merely to forgive people but to transform them into
the likeness of Christ.

In the same vein, Ephesians provides important guidance on how believers should handle matters of correction, discipline,
and restoration. We are commanded to put away bitterness, wrath, anger, clamour, evil speaking, and malice because
these attitudes corrupt the process of restoration. When discipline is administered through bitterness, it becomes
destructive. When accountability is driven by anger, it becomes oppressive. When correction is carried out through gossip,
public embarrassment, or unhealthy exposure, it becomes unsafe and damaging. In the same vein, Ephesians also
commands us to be kind, tender-hearted, and forgiving one another, even as God for Christ's sake has forgiven us. The
standard for dealing with those who have fallen is the mercy that we ourselves have received in Christ. Therefore, we must
build a fellowship culture where people feel safe to seek help, confess struggles, receive counsel, and pursue restoration.
No one should be excused in sin, but neither should anyone be crushed beyond recovery.

5. Step-by-Step Applications and Practical Implications
• Create safe channels for help: Local fellowships and zonal structure must have mature, trusted, prayerful leaders and
 counsellors that struggling members can approach confidentially.
• Hear matters before judging: Do not condemn people by rumour, assumption, past opinion, anger, gossip, partial
 information, or public pressure.
• Run to Christ as refuge: Teach every believer that salvation, forgiveness, and true freedom are found only in Christ, our
 ultimate refuge and eternal High Priest.
• Practise redemptive discipline: Correction must uphold truth, protect the flock, prevent further harm, and help the
 repentant return to the Lord in genuine brokenness.
• Avoid gossip disguised as concern: Do not turn someone’s fall, weakness, wound, or struggle into discussion, mockery,
 or careless sharing.
• Restore through discipleship: Help repentant people rebuild prayer, Word study, fellowship, accountability, restitution
 where needed, and fruit-bearing lifestyle.
• Balance mercy and accountability: Do not crush the repentant, but do not excuse sin. Grace must bring people into
 truth and responsibility.
• Put away bitterness and evil speaking: Correction must not be driven by anger, malice, revenge, or the desire to
 humiliate.
• Build healing communities: Let TACEF fellowships be places of recovery, counsel, forgiveness, confidentiality, healing,
 and renewal.

 ~ 206 ~

• Protect holiness: Make sin uncomfortable for the careless, but make restoration possible for the fallen and the
 repentant.

Questions for Discussion

 2. Why must brethren not be condemned before they are heard?
 3. How can we re-engage a sister who left the fellowship after a personal challenge she shared confidentially with

 5. Why must discipline in the fellowship be redemptive and not destructive?
 6. What are the dangers of harsh condemnation without mercy and careless tolerance without accountability?

Am I the kind of believer wounded people can approach for prayer, counsel, and restoration, or do my words make people
hide their struggles? Do I judge matters by gossip, assumption, anger, or partial information? Do I speak about people’s
failures carelessly? When someone falls, do I desire their humiliation or their restoration? Am I guilty of either harsh
condemnation without mercy or careless tolerance without accountability? Is our fellowship a safe place for struggling
brethren, repentant sinners, backsliders, wounded believers, and young people seeking help?
