Introduction
Our study this week takes a deeper look at the distribution of the tribe of Levi (the Levites) among the remaining eleven
tribes of Israel. After the land had been divided and the various inheritances assigned, the Levites, the special tribe of
priests specially chosen by God to oversee the Tabernacle, worship, priestly service, and the teaching of God's law, came
to Eleazar the priest, Joshua, and the leaders of the tribes, reminding them that the Lord had commanded Moses to give
them cities in which to dwell. In obedience to God's instruction, the children of Israel gave cities to the Levites out of their
own inheritances. Unlike the other eleven tribes, the Levites were not gathered into one large territory separated from the
people. Instead, they were distributed throughout the nation in forty-eight cities spread across the inheritance of the other
tribes. They lived among the other eleven tribes and were not concentrated into one location unlike the other tribes. It
appeared the Lord wanted them to share in the everyday realities of the people that they present before the Lord through
their priestly service.

This unique arrangement teaches a profound kingdom principle that everything that represents God and His worship must
remain close to the people. No tribe was to be left without priestly influence, and no territory was to be spiritually
neglected. The Levites helped preserve covenant instructions, worship, prayer, and spiritual order. Their presence ensured
that the Word of God, spiritual counsel, and worship were not confined to a central location but were accessible wherever
God's people lived. This provides a powerful pattern for the Lord's army today. Revival cannot be sustained from
conventions and major gatherings alone, but it must be rooted in local churches, campus fellowships, families, workplaces,
and communities where people live their daily lives.

Teachings
1. Ministry Must Be Present Among the People and Embedded Within Everyday Life: The Levites were strategically
distributed among the tribes of Israel. They did not receive one large, separate territory like the other tribes. Instead, they
were given cities within the inheritance of the various tribes so that worship, covenant instruction, and spiritual oversight
would be present throughout the land. God did not want any part of Israel to be seperated from priestly influence, spiritual
guidance, or access to His Word. This arrangement reveals an important kingdom principle that kingdom ministry is most
effective when it is close to the people. Every territory needs spiritual coverage. Every community needs access to sound
teaching, godly counsel, and discipleship. If the Word is distant from the people, spiritual weakness will grow. If discipleship
is absent from homes, campuses, and local churches, believers will remain immature. If spiritual guidance is unavailable,
many will struggle silently without help. The Levites among the people teach us that ministry work and revival labour must
not be removed from everyday life.

There is another important lesson here. The Levites did not isolate themselves from the people because of their spiritual
calling and a perceived sense of higher spirituality. They lived among the people they served. Likewise, Jesus, our Great
High Priest, is touched with the feeling of our infirmities because He entered fully into the realities of human life. True
ministry of revival requires closeness, humility, and identification with the people we are sent to. We cannot effectively
serve people whose struggles we do not understand or whose realities we refuse to share. Revival work becomes shallow
when spiritual leaders become distant, inaccessible, or detached from the lives of those they serve. We must remain
humble enough to sit throughout the so-called boring Sunday service to show commitment. We must remain faithful in

 ~ 210 ~

local church even when we feel spiritually mature or highly gifted. The work of revival requires presence, consistency, and
a willingness to stay among the people until God's purposes are established in their lives.

2. Christ: From God Above Us, to God Among Us, to God in Us: One of the most beautiful themes running through the
entire Bible is God's desire to dwell among His people which is also expressed through God’s system of having Levites
distributed among the people and not concentrated in one corner in the land. In the Old Testament, God revealed Himself
primarily as God above His people, the sovereign Lord who ruled from heaven and manifested His presence through
extraordinary encounters. He appeared to Moses in the burning bush, descended upon Mount Sinai in fire and thunder,
and later caused His glory to dwell in the Tabernacle and the Temple. Even though God was with Israel, there remained a
sense of distance. The people approached Him through priests, sacrifices, and sacred structures. His holiness was real, but
access was limited. Throughout the Old Testament, God's redemptive plan was progressively moving towards a greater
reality—the day when He would no longer merely dwell above His people but would come near to them in a new and
personal way.

This promise reached its fulfilment in Jesus Christ. John 1:14 declares, “And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among
us.” In Christ, God became God among us. The eternal Creator stepped into human history, taking on flesh and living among
ordinary men and women. He walked their roads, entered their homes, touched their sicknesses, bore their sorrows, and
died for their sins. This is the wonder of Emmanuel, meaning “God with us.” Through Christ, God was no longer represented
only by a cloud, a pillar of fire, or a sacred building. He became visible, approachable, and accessible. The disciples could
hear His voice, observe His character, and experience His love firsthand. Yet, even this was not the final destination of
God's plan. Before His departure, Jesus made a remarkable promise: “I will not leave you comfortless: I will come to you”
(John 14:18). He spoke of the coming of the Holy Spirit, through whom God's presence would move even closer.

Today, through the ministry of the Holy Spirit, God has become God in us. The New Testament reveals a profound reality:
believers are now the temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:19). God's presence is no longer confined to a building, a
city, or a geographical location. Through salvation, Christ dwells in our hearts by faith, and the Holy Spirit takes up residence
within every believer. This means that God's truth, grace, wisdom, power, and character are intended to be expressed
through His people wherever they are found. Just as the Levites were distributed among the tribes so that every territory
would have access to God's presence and instruction, God's ultimate design has always been nearness to His people. He
moved from dwelling above His people, to dwelling among His people, and now dwells within His people, so that His
presence can fill every territory through transformed lives that faithfully represent Him.

(3) Making Provision for the Levites -Supporting Those Who Labour in the Word and Ministry: One often-overlooked
lesson in Joshua 21 is that while the Levites did not receive a tribal territory like the other tribes, God ensured that they
were not neglected. The same God who assigned them the responsibility of preserving worship, teaching the law, and
maintaining spiritual order also made provision for their welfare. The Levites were given cities to dwell in and pasture lands
for their needs. Their livelihood was tied to the faithfulness of God's people in honouring His instructions concerning
offerings, tithes, and practical support. This reveals an important kingdom principle that whenever God assigns a
responsibility, He also ordains provision for those who carry that responsibility.

This principle continues throughout the Scripture. Jesus taught that “the labourer is worthy of his hire” (Luke 10:7), and
Paul reinforced it by saying, “Even so hath the Lord ordained that they which preach the gospel should live of the gospel”
(1 Corinthians 9:14). In Galatians 6:6, believers are instructed to share all good things with those who teach them in the
Word. First Timothy 5:17–18 further teaches that elders who labour in the Word and doctrine are worthy of honour,
quoting the Scripture, “The labourer is worthy of his reward.” These passages establish that caring for ministers,
missionaries, church workers, and those who devote themselves to kingdom service is an act of biblical stewardship. The
Church must avoid two extremes. The first is neglecting faithful labourers and assuming they should carry every burden
alone because they are “doing God's work.” The second is promoting materialism and turning ministry into a platform for
personal enrichment. Scripture does not support neglect nor extravagance. God's pattern is the provision of needs so that
ministry can flourish and His servants can labour effectively.

The house of TACEF must therefore learn the culture of practical support for ministers. This may involve supporting
missionaries in difficult locations, helping a minister's family, contributing towards ministry needs, caring for elderly
ministers, assisting church workers, or strengthening those who labour faithfully behind the scenes. TACEFites who are
involved in church governance like our Missionary in Church Administration (MICA) must ensure that local ministers are

 ~ 211 ~

well treated with decent wages and other basic necessities of life. We must learn to recognise legitimate needs and respond
with divine leading, wisdom, generosity, and gratitude. We must also distinguish between needs and wants. The kingdom
is not built on the pursuit of comfort, luxury, or excess, but neither should God's servants be abandoned to unnecessary
hardship when the local church has the capacity to help. The same God who distributed the Levites among the tribes also
moved the tribes to make room for them and provide for them.

4. Ministry Must Be Distributed to Preserve Covenant Continuity Across Generations and Territories: One of the reasons
God distributed the Levites among all the tribes rather than concentrating them in a single location was to ensure that
worship, instruction, discipleship, and spiritual oversight would reach every territory and continue across generations. The
Levites were not merely caretakers of the Tabernacle but were custodians of covenant knowledge, teachers of God's law,
preservers of spiritual order, and guides to the people. Their presence among the tribes ensured that no community was
left without access to spiritual instruction and that the knowledge of God would not be confined to a central location. This
arrangement reveals a powerful kingdom principle that God's work is sustained through distributed ministry. Revival
cannot survive on occasional gatherings, conventions, or a few gifted leaders. The truth must be taught, modelled,
practised, and passed on continually from one generation to another and at all local fellowship and family levels.

This is precisely the pattern reinforced in Ephesians 4. Christ gave apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors, and teachers to
the Church, not so that a few people would do all the ministry while everyone else watches, but “for the perfecting of the
saints, for the work of the ministry, for the edifying of the body of Christ.” Ministry gifts therefore exist to equip others. A
teacher must raise people who can teach. A pastor must develop believers who can care for others. An evangelist must
inspire others to win souls. An intercessor must raise more intercessors. A leader must train future leaders. The goal of
ministry is multiplication, not dependence. When ministry becomes centralised around a few gifted individuals, those
leaders become exhausted, members remain immature, and the work becomes vulnerable. If one leader relocates,
graduates, or becomes unavailable, the entire structure may struggle because too few people have been equipped to
continue the work. This is a major burden for TACEF. The vision of revival must not end with those who first received it.
The fire must be intentionally transferred to the next generations.

Introduction
Our study this week brings us to one of the most powerful summary statements in the entire book of Joshua. After years
of warfare, territorial conquest, inheritance allocation, and the establishment of God's order in the land, the Holy Spirit
pauses to give a divine verdict concerning God's dealings with Israel. Joshua 21:45 declares: " Not a single one of all the
good promises the LORD had given to the family of Israel was left unfulfilled; everything he had spoken came true."(NLT
version). These words are a testimony to the unchanging character of God’s faithfulness. The God who made the promise
fulfilled the promise. The God who spoke the word performed the word. The God who began the work completed what
He had declared. Indeed, what makes this testimony remarkable is the long journey behind it. The promise of the land was
first given to Abraham several centuries before Joshua entered Canaan. Abraham died without fully possessing it. Isaac
and Jacob lived as strangers in the land. Israel went into Egyptian bondage for over four hundred years. Moses led them
out but did not enter the Promised Land. An entire generation died in the wilderness because of unbelief. Yet despite
delays, failures, oppositions, and human weaknesses, God's promise remained alive. The covenant survived every obstacle
because its success depended on God's faithfulness rather than human perfection.

This lesson is particularly important for us today as God’s end-time revival army in the great house of TACEF. We live in a
generation that desires immediate results. Many become discouraged when prayers appear unanswered, revival seems
delayed, ministries grow slowly, or personal expectations remain unfulfilled. Yet, Joshua 21 teaches us that God's
faithfulness is not measured by speed but by certainty. His promises may take time, but they do not fail. Delay is not denial
when God remains committed to His covenant. One of the beautiful truths in this chapter is that God did not merely give
Israel the land but He also gave them rest round about and delivered all their enemies into their hands. God's faithfulness
included inheritance, victory, protection, and peace. In the same way, God's plans for His people extend beyond survival.
He desires to bring us into kingdom usefulness, covenant rest, and the full expression of His purposes in our lives.

 ~ 214 ~

Therefore, Week 34 calls us to strengthen our confidence in God's faithfulness, learn to rest in Him while continuing to
labour diligently, and trust that every promise He has spoken concerning our lives, families, local churches, ministries, and
the TACEF revival mandate will find full expression in His appointed time.

1. God Fulfils What He Speaks Because His Character Cannot Fail: The central testimony of Joshua 21 is not Israel's strength
but God's faithfulness. The chapter does not celebrate military excellence or human achievement. Instead, it celebrates
the reliability of God's covenant. Israel possessed the land because God fulfilled what He had spoken. Throughout Scripture,
God's faithfulness is presented as one of His defining attributes. Numbers 23:19 declares, "God is not a man, that he should
lie; neither the son of man, that he should repent." Hebrews 10:23 tells us to hold fast our profession because "he is faithful
that promised." Titus 1:2 speaks of "God, that cannot lie." These passages remind us that God's promises are secure
because His character is secure. Many believers wrongly place more confidence in circumstances than in God's Word. For
these types of people, when circumstances appear favourable, faith rises but when circumstances become difficult, faith
weakens. Yet biblical faith is rooted in God's character rather than visible evidence.

This truth is especially important in seasons of uncertainty like economic challenges, delayed opportunities, delayed
manifestations of divine promises in family, ministry frustrations, and societal pressures. Yet God's covenant remains intact
even when circumstances appear contrary. What God has spoken remains true regardless of how circumstances may
appear. Dear TACEFites, build your confidence on God's character. His Word remains trustworthy and His promises remain
secure. The same God who fulfilled His covenant to Abraham, Moses, Joshua, and Israel remains faithful today.

2. Delay Is Not Denial When God Is Preparing the Promise: One of the greatest attacks against faith is the assumption that
delay means failure. Yet Scripture repeatedly demonstrates that God often works through long seasons of preparation
before bringing promises to fulfilment.
The promise of the land took centuries to unfold. Joseph's dreams required years of suffering before fulfilment. David
waited many years between anointing and kingship. Even the coming of Christ involved generations of prophetic
expectation before fulfilment. God's delays are never meaningless. Often, He uses waiting seasons to prepare both the
inheritance and the person who will receive it because character must be formed, faith must be strengthened, pride must
be broken, dependence upon God must deepen and preparation often takes longer than manifestation.
The danger during waiting seasons is unbelief. Many believers conclude that because God has not acted according to their
timetable, He has forgotten them. Yet God's silence is not abandonment. His delay is not denial. His timing is often different
from ours because His wisdom exceeds ours.
This principle applies strongly to revival. Every genuine move of God in history passed through seasons of prayer,
preparation, labour, and waiting. Revival is rarely instantaneous. It is cultivated through prolonged season of consecration,
discipleship, and persistent faithfulness.

This teaching also comes as a strong consolation to every TACEFites who are trusting God concerning marriage, fruit of the
womb, admission, career growth, family restoration, ministry fruitfulness, business expansion, financial breakthrough,
spiritual growth, and kingdom assignments. Joshua 21 reminds us that God's promises remain alive even when fulfilment
appears delayed. Therefore, let us hold fast the profession of our faith without wavering. Let us keep trusting God's timing.
Let us continue praying, serving, obeying and believing. The God who promised remains faithful.

3. The Lord Gives Rest Round About: Joshua 21:44 records that the Lord gave Israel "rest round about." This statement
reveals a dimension of God's blessing that many believers overlook. God did not merely bring His people into inheritance,
but He also brought them into rest. However, the “rest” described here points to a deeper New Testament reality. Hebrews
4 teaches that there remains a rest for the people of God. This rest is not merely physical. It is spiritual. Many people spend
their lives pursuing peace through external achievements. They assume they will rest after securing a promotion,
completing a degree, getting married, buying a house, growing a business, or solving a major problem. Yet life continually
presents new challenges. External circumstances can never provide lasting peace. True rest comes from confidence in God.
Isaiah 26:3 declares: "Thou wilt keep him in perfect peace, whose mind is stayed on thee." The key to rest is where the mind
remains fixed. A mind fixed on problems becomes anxious, but a mind fixed on God becomes peaceful.
This explains why Jesus could sleep during a storm while others panicked. It explains why Paul and Silas worshipped in
prison. It explains why Abraham continued believing despite impossible circumstances. Their confidence rested in God's
faithfulness. Every revival army must learn this lesson. We cannot effectively labour for God while living under constant
fear, anxiety, comparison, pressure, or discouragement. Kingdom work requires both diligence and rest. We must work
hard while trusting deeply. We must labour faithfully while resting in God's sovereignty. Dear TACEFites, enter into God's

 ~ 215 ~

rest. Let your confidence be rooted in His faithfulness rather than your circumstances. Trust Him enough to labour without
fear and wait without anxiety.

4. God Watches Over His Word to Perform It: The climax of Joshua 21 is the declaration that not one good thing failed of
all that God had spoken. This truth appears repeatedly throughout Scripture. Jeremiah 1:12 says: "I will hasten my word to
perform it." Isaiah 55:11 declares that God's Word will not return unto Him void. First Samuel 3:19 records that God allowed
none of Samuel's words to fall to the ground. God's commitment to His Word is one of the strongest foundations for faith.
Human promises will fail and same for government, institution, friends and even our own commitments occasionally fail.
Yet God's Word remains dependable because His character is unchanging.

Psalm 138:2 declares that God has magnified His Word above all His name. This highlights His commitment to the integrity
of what He has spoken. He is jealous for the fulfilment of His Word. This truth should transform how we pray. Throughout
Scripture, great men and women of faith approached God through His promises. Moses reminded God of His covenant.
Daniel prayed according to Jeremiah's prophecy. Nehemiah prayed based on God's promises. They held God by His Word
because they understood His commitment to fulfil what He had spoken. In this regard, each of us must therefore become
students of Scripture. We must know God's promises concerning salvation, holiness, wisdom, guidance, fruitfulness,
protection, provision, revival, and eternity. Faith grows when we know what God has actually said. Dear TACEFites, learn
to pray God's Word. Learn to stand upon His promises, learn to trust His covenant for what God has spoken remains
stronger than what circumstances suggest.

Ephesians 3:20 concluded the intensity of God’s ability by reminding us that God is able to do "exceeding abundantly above
all that we ask or think." One of the remarkable aspects of God's faithfulness is that He often does more than we originally
expected. Israel expected land but God gave them land, victory, and rest. Dear TACEFites, do not reduce God to the size of
your circumstances. The God who fulfils promises is also the God who exceeds expectations.

5. Step-by-Step Applications and Practical Implications
• Trust God beyond delay: Do not conclude that God has forgotten His promise because fulfilment appears slow. Hold
 on to His Word in seasons of waiting, knowing that delay is not denial when God is still working.
• Hold God by His Word: Learn to pray with the promises of Scripture. Remind yourself and declare before God that none
 of His good words will fail, because He watches over His Word to perform it.
• Enter into God's rest: Do not allow anxiety, fear, comparison, pressure, or uncertainty to rule your heart. Keep your
 mind stayed on God and receive the peace that comes from trusting His faithfulness.
• Trust God for deliverance from enemies: Do not fear visible or invisible opposition. The same Lord who delivered Israel's
 enemies into their hands is able to deliver you from every force resisting His purpose.
• Rest without becoming careless: God’s rest is not an invitation to spiritual laziness. When God settles you, opens doors,
 gives peace, or answers prayers, steward the blessing with gratitude, discipline, and renewed consecration.
• Believe God for more than expected: Ephesians 3:20 reminds us that God is able to do exceeding abundantly above all
 we ask or think. Do not limit God to your present imagination, calculation, or experience.
• Encourage weary believers: Strengthen TACEFites who are discouraged by delay in marriage, admission, fruit of the
 womb, career growth, business result, family restoration, or ministry impact. Remind them that God's Word cannot
 fail.
• Turn fulfilled promises into thanksgiving: When God answers, do not become proud, careless, or forgetful. Let every
 fulfilled promise lead to worship, testimony, humility, and deeper commitment to the Lord.

SECTION 8: Unity, Misunderstanding, and Corporate Responsibility: How the Army Protects Unity While Preserving Truth

The journey of God’s end-time army now moves into the delicate season of unity, communication, corporate responsibility,
and preservation after battle. After many victories had been won and the land had begun to be possessed, the eastern
tribes returned to their inheritance beyond Jordan. They had fought faithfully with their brethren, but they now had to
carry the same covenant burden back to their homes, families, lands, and communities. This teaches us that the fire of
revival must not remain only on the battlefield, in conventions, retreats, camps, fellowships, or collective gatherings. A
true soldier does not only burn when surrounded by other soldiers. The burden must travel with every TACEFite into the
home, marriage, workplace, campus, local church, village, city, and new assignment.

 ~ 219 ~

God’s army may be separated by location, role, season, age, marriage, graduation, relocation, work, or ministry placement,
but the covenant identity must remain one. Distance must not kill commitment. Blessing must not produce withdrawal
and our victory or liftings in life must not become an excuse for comfort. The eastern tribes returned with much wealth,
but Joshua reminded them to share, steward, and walk faithfully before the Lord. This teaches that blessing carries
responsibility. When God gives victory, resources, platforms, families, jobs, opportunities, education, relocation, and
influence, they must be used with generosity, accountability, love, and covenant purpose.

This eighth section therefore calls TACEFites to protect unity without compromising truth. We must avoid gossip, suspicion,
factionalism, and hasty judgement. We must not judge before we listen. We must not allow misunderstanding to wound
the Body. We must communicate burdens, decisions, plans, and intentions clearly so that brethren are not confused or
discouraged. At the same time, unity must not become carelessness. After victory, the army must keep the fire burning,
cleave to the Lord, remain separated from ungodly influence, and continue to walk as children of light. The Lord’s army
must be united, truthful, watchful, holy, and deeply responsible.

Week 36: The Eastern Tribes Returning Home - Carrying the Burden Beyond the Battlefield: The eastern tribes teach us
that some soldiers may return to different locations, but the burden must travel with them. Though, they were going back
across Jordan, they were still part of God’s covenant people. Distance did not change identity. TACEFites who graduate,
relocate, marry, change roles, enter NYSC, begin new jobs, move abroad, or return to local churches must carry the revival
burden with them. We must not leave the fire at the camp. The burden must continue at home, in family life, work, church,
school, and workplace.

Week 37: The Altar of Witness - Resolving Conflict God’s Way: The altar built by the eastern tribes teaches that good
intentions can be misunderstood when communication is poorly done. The rest of Israel assumed rebellion and nearly
went to war, but careful enquiry and truthful explanation preserved unity. This teaches that believers must not judge
before they listen. In friendship, marriage, fellowship, workplace culture, leadership, and local church administration,
communication protects unity, truth, and covenant trust. TACEFites must avoid suspicion, gossip, factionalism, and hasty
judgement. Unity is not automatic; it must be intentionally preserved through patience, love, and truth.

Week 38: Keeping the Fire After the Battle Is Won: Joshua’s warning to Israel teaches that victory must not produce
carelessness, spiritual pride, or relaxed consecration. After many battles had been won, Israel still had to obey the Word,
cleave to the Lord, and remain separate from ungodly influence. The Christian walk continues after initial conquest.
TACEFites must understand that holiness is not a short-term demand but a continuous walk in light, wisdom, obedience,
and separation from darkness. We must guard our friendships, appetites, relationships, ambitions, social media habits,
academic pressure, workplace culture, and secret life.

Week 39: One Shall Chase a Thousand - The Power Behind One Consecrated Life: Joshua’s reminder that one shall chase
a thousand teaches that numerical smallness is not weakness when God is with His people. One consecrated life can affect
many in a church, class, hostel, office, family, campus, or even a city. Ephesians reminds us that the exceeding greatness
of God’s power works toward believers, and that Christ is exalted above every power. TACEFites must not despise small
numbers or hidden locations. One TACEFite backed by God’s power can pioneer a new work, shift a spiritual atmosphere,
confront opposition, influence many lives, and stand victoriously in Christ.

Introduction
This week’s study brings us to a major transition in the journey of Israel. The Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half tribe of
Manasseh had received their inheritance on the other side of Jordan, but they did not remain there while their brethren
from the remaining nine and a half tribes fought alone. They crossed over with the rest of the remaining tribes of Israel
and stood with them through the battles of possessing the remaining Promised Land. They left the comfort of their own
inheritance to support the larger covenant assignment. Now that the Lord had given rest to their brethren and all the lands
have now been conquered, Joshua called them, commended their obedience, blessed them, and released them to return
to the land of their possessions.

This release was not ordinary, automatic, or based only on desire. Joshua did not release them simply because they wanted
to return home. Before he said, “Now return ye, and get you unto your tents,” he first gave testimony about their readiness.
He said, “Ye have kept all that Moses the servant of the LORD commanded you.” He also said, “Ye have not left your brethren
these many days.” He further said, “Ye have kept the charge of the commandment of the LORD your God.” These three
statements show that there were foundational pillars before their covenant release into their next level. They had a

 ~ 221 ~

personal walk of obedience, sustained fellowship and submission to the body, and a life of consecrated discipleship. Only
after these testimonies came the release, the blessing, and the return to their own lands.

This teaches us that there are divine conditions for new levels of divine release, settlement, relocation, marriage, ministry
advancement, leadership transition, and next-level responsibility. The next level that God has promised us is not entered
by desire but entered through readiness, obedience, faithfulness, service, and proven discipleship. This means that the
Lord may delay the release of some brethren into their Promised Land and their specific “tents” because the foundational
requirements have not yet been fulfilled. This delay is not punishment but part of divine preparation. God knows that a
person who has not learnt obedience, accountability, fellowship, service, and consecration in the present season may not
be able to carry the weight of the next season when they are released to the Promised Land whether in the form of career
expansion, relocation to a new country, settlement in marriage, release into divine calling or enlargement into new
business.

Ephesians deepens this lesson through the example of Tychicus, whom Paul called “a beloved brother and faithful minister
in the Lord.” Though, Paul and the Ephesian believers were separated by distance, love, fellowship, communication,
comfort, grace, and peace continued to bind them together. The Church remains one body across locations. Grace and
peace sustain separated labourers. Faithfulness is not only tested when everyone is gathered together; it is also tested
when brethren are apart, when duties change, when visibility reduces, when supervision is absent, and when personal life
becomes busy. Therefore, this week calls TACEFites to unto readiness for divine release. Before we pray, “Lord, release
me,” we must also pray, “Lord, prepare me.” Before we ask for the next tent, we must ask for the faithfulness, submission,
and consecration that will preserve us there.

Teachings
1. Divine Release into the Next Tent Requires Foundational Readiness: The release of the eastern tribes into their lands
was not ordinary. Joshua did not simply say, “You may go.” He first examined and affirmed the evidence of their readiness.
He said they had kept what Moses commanded, obeyed Joshua’s voice, stayed with their brethren, and kept the charge of
the commandment of the Lord. This means that their release into the next tent rested on a tested foundation. This is a
very important principle in the journey of God’s people. There are conditions for every next level of greatness, settlement,
enlargement, and progress that we desire or seek. The desire to move forward is not enough. The fact that a person wants
marriage, promotion at work, business enlargement, or incremental responsibility does not mean the person is ready for
it. God prepares the vessel before He releases the vessel. In our text of study, we see three testimonies of readiness for
the next level of divine settlement. First, Joshua said, “Ye have kept all that Moses the servant of the LORD commanded
you.” This speaks to a personal walk of obedience. Before the eastern tribes were released into their inheritance, they had
shown that they could obey instruction. Many people want the next level, but they have not yet built the foundation of
obedience required to sustain it.

The second testimony was, “Ye have not left your brethren these many days unto this day.” This speaks to sustained
fellowship, submission to the body, and faithfulness to shared burden. The eastern tribes did not abandon their brethren
because their own inheritance had already been given. They stood with the rest of Israel until the common assignment
was fulfilled. This teaches that God watches how we treat the work of others before He releases us into our own tents.
Some people want to move on, but they have not been faithful where God planted them. Some want to build their own
businesses, but they have not learnt accountability and service while working with others. Some want to relocate, marry,
graduate, or enter new assignments, but they have many personal gaps that must be intentionally fixed. The third
testimony was, “Ye have kept the charge of the commandment of the LORD your God.” This speaks to a life of discipleship
and consecration. It is not only about obeying one instruction but about carrying the charge of the Lord as a way of life.
Dear TACEFites, the next tent you desire for your life is not automatic. Divine settlement has a process. The Lord who
blesses also prepares; the Lord who releases also examines; the Lord who sends also forms. Let us therefore be faithful in
the present season. Let us be faithful in that which belongs to another, as Jesus taught in Luke 16:12, “And if ye have not
been faithful in that which is another man’s, who shall give you that which is your own?” This means that faithfulness in
another person’s assignment is often a test before God commits our own portion into our hands. Let us learn to treat the
things of others with the same care, diligence, and honour we desire for our own. If you want God to build your own home,
learn to treat another person’s home well as if it is yours. If you want to build your own business enterprise, learn to work
for others with honesty, excellence, and commitment as though the work were yours.

 ~ 222 ~

2. Some Soldiers Return to Different Locations, but the Burden Must Travel with Them: The eastern tribes had fought
faithfully with their brethren. They had left their own inheritance on the other side of Jordan and joined the rest of Israel
in the battles of possession. Joshua testified concerning them: “Ye have not left your brethren these many days unto this
day.” This was a powerful testimony of commitment, sacrifice, and shared burden. They did not say, “Our own land has
already been given to us, so let others fight their own battles.” They understood that the assignment of God’s people was
bigger than their own comfort. This shows that God’s soldiers can serve together for a season and then be released into
different locations, roles, and responsibilities. Some may graduate, marry out of the ministry, go for NYSC, relocate to
different nations, change jobs, return to village churches, enter new leadership roles and some may step away from visible
central activities because of family, work, or ministry demands. But the burden of the Lord must not be left behind.

This is a major lesson for TACEFites. Many people burn for God only when they are in a strong fellowship environment.
They pray when there is a retreat. They serve when there is a convention. They are fervent only when friends are around.
But when they leave that environment, the fire begins to reduce. This should not be so. A true revival soldier carries the
burden beyond the battlefield. The burden for souls and passion for revival must travel with us. A TACEFite going for NYSC
must carry the burden into the place of primary assignment. A student who graduates must carry the burden into the
workplace. A sister who marries must carry the fire into her home and new family. A family who relocates abroad must
carry the burden into that new country. A professional moving into a new role must carry Christ into the office. A business
owner must carry the fear of God everywhere they find themselves.
Dear TACEFites, wherever you go, go as a soldier of Christ. Wherever life places you, carry the burden of the Lord.

3. Distance Must Not Kill Covenant Commitment or Weaken Spiritual Identity: The eastern tribes were returning across
Jordan, but they were still part of God’s covenant people. Their geography changed, but their identity did not change. Their
tents were on the other side of Jordan, but their God was still the God of Israel. Their location was different, but their
covenant remained the same. Joshua therefore charged them carefully: “Take diligent heed to do the commandment and
the law.” In other words, do not allow distance from the main body to weaken your obedience to God. Distance can test
identity. When people are far from familiar spiritual structures, their true convictions are revealed. A young believer who
was strong on campus may face a different test during NYSC when there is no active fellowship nearby. A brother who was
faithful in a local assembly may begin to struggle when he relocates to another country where church life is different and
work pressure is high. A sister who was accountable as a single may face new pressures in marriage, family demands, and
in-laws. A worker who was disciplined when surrounded by brethren may begin to compromise in a workplace where
corruption, ungodly talk, and immorality are normal.

The Lord’s revival army must understand that spiritual identity is not location dependent. We are not Christians only in our
local fellowship. We are not holy only in church. We are not prayerful only during retreats, fellowships, or family altars. We
are not committed only when leaders call us. We belong to Christ everywhere. At work or at home, in school or during
NYSC, as single people or in marriage, in Nigeria or in another country, as TACEFites in local churches, as TACEFites in a
College of Theology, or as full-time ministers, our identity must remain the same.

Dear TACEF Missionaries on the Altar (MOTA) and Missionaries in Church Administration (MICA), do not become strangers
to the vision of revival because you have taken on ministerial or administrative roles in the church. Every lifting you receive
must deepen the vision, strengthen your connection to the brethren, and draw many souls to the Lord. It must not detach
you from fellowship weekly meetings, online fellowships, physical gatherings, and the shared covenant responsibility of
the great house. The higher the Lord lifts us, the more faithful, humble, connected, and fruitful we must become.

4. Blessing Must Lead to Responsibility, Stewardship, and Continued Obedience: Joshua blessed the eastern tribes and
sent them away. He also reminded them that they were returning with much riches, very much cattle, silver, gold, brass,
iron, and very much raiment. They were not returning empty-handed. Victory had produced resources. Their obedience
had been fruitful. But Joshua did not allow blessing to become self-centred enjoyment. He said, “Divide the spoil … with
your brethren.” This means blessing must be carried with responsibility. When God blesses a believer, that blessing must
not lead to self-centeredness, pride, withdrawal, or forgetfulness. It must lead to stewardship, generosity, and
responsibility. The eastern tribes had fought with their brethren and had received wealth, but they also had to share rightly
and steward the blessing wisely.

Many believers lose spiritual sharpness when blessing comes. A person who prayed earnestly for a job may become too
busy for God after employment comes. A brother who sought God for business growth may become spiritually cold when

 ~ 223 ~

the business enlarges. A sister who prayed for marriage may gradually withdraw from service after children start coming.
A family that asked God for relocation may become disconnected from fellowship after arriving in another country. A
student who prayed for admission may forget God once school life begins. This is why blessing must be handled carefully.
Joshua’s final charge also shows that the next tent is not a place of reduced consecration. He told them to love the Lord,
walk in all His ways, keep His commandments, cleave unto Him, and serve Him with all their hearts and all their soul. This
means that our release into the next level must deepen obedience, not reduce it. The battlefield may change, but the
demand of God remains. Dear TACEFites, when the Lord blesses you, carry the blessing responsibly. Share with others,
strengthen the weak, support the work, encourage the brethren, honour God with your resources, steward opportunities
wisely, and never allow comfort to make you withdraw from service.

5. Step-by-Step Applications and Practical Implications
 • Ask God to prepare you before release: Do not only pray for the next level; pray for the discipline, character, and
 consecration needed to sustain it. For example, if you are seeking God for marriage partner, do not just pray to
 find the right person, also pray to be the right person.
 • Stay faithful to the body: Do not abandon brethren, local fellowship, or assigned responsibilities because your own
 opportunity has opened.
 • Carry the burden beyond meetings: Do not leave the fire of revival at conventions, retreats, camps, or fellowship
 gatherings. Take it back into daily life.
 • Prepare for transitions spiritually: Before graduation, NYSC, marriage, relocation, job change, business expansion,
 or leadership change, pray for grace to remain faithful.
 • Stay connected to the body: Distance must not become isolation. Keep fellowship, accountability, communication,
 prayer partnership, and love with brethren.
 • Steward blessing responsibly: Use jobs, marriage, business growth, academic success, relocation, resources, and

Key Extracts from the Bible Texts to Remember and Reflect On
 • They built there an altar by Jordan, a great altar to see to.
 • The whole congregation of the children of Israel gathered themselves together at Shiloh, to go up to war against

 • What trespass is this that ye have committed?

 • Speak every man truth with his neighbour.

Introduction
As we continue to learn more about what defines an exceeding great army, our study this week brings us to one of the
most practical and delicate moments in the journey of Israel. The two and a half tribes that are also called the eastern
tribes (the children of Reuben and the children of Gad and the half tribe of Manasseh) had faithfully served with the other
nine and a half tribes (also called the western tribes) in the battles of possession and had been released by Joshua to return
to their own lands. As they came to the borders of the Jordan, they built a great altar. This immediately alarmed the rest
of Israel because it appeared they were setting up an alternative place of worship, something God had forbidden, as it
could lead to idolatry and divide His people. Their intention was not rebellion but to create a place where they can serve
God and preserve their covenant identity for future generations and ensure that their children would never be told, “Ye
have no part in the LORD” since they were on the other side of Jordan. Unfortunately, the rest of Israel misunderstood this
act of sincerity and assumed that the eastern tribes had rebelled against God.

This misunderstanding almost became a civil war among brethren. The whole congregation gathered at Shiloh to go up to
war against the eastern tribe who are of course smaller in size. This is worrisome because these were not strangers
attacking strangers but covenant brethren almost fighting. These were the same eastern tribes who had laboured with
them, fought with them, and stayed with them until they secured all their inheritance. Yet one misunderstood action
almost erased the memory of their past faithfulness. This teaches us that conflict can arise even among the most sincere
people, godly people, covenant people, married people, business partners, friends, leaders, ministers, and brethren in the
same revival vision. Good intentions can be misread when communication is unclear.

Ephesians gives us the New Testament foundation for resolving such conflicts. Paul calls believers to walk with meekness,
longsuffering, and forbearance in love, endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. He also reminds
us that there is one body, one Spirit, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, and one God and Father of all. This means that
disagreements must be handled through the consciousness that we belong to one another. We must speak truth, but truth
must be spoken as members of one body. We must defend holiness, but holiness must not become an excuse for
impatience, suspicion, anger, public accusation, or careless destruction of relationships. Therefore, this week calls
TACEFites to learn how to resolve conflicts God’s way. We must learn to ask questions before making conclusions, listen
before reacting, verify facts before sharing stories, and communicate clearly before assuming motives.

Teachings
1. Good Intentions Can Be Misunderstood When Communication Is Unclear: The eastern tribes built an altar by Jordan,
and it was “a great altar to see to.” To the western tribes, the altar looked like rebellion. They thought it was another altar
for sacrifice, a violation of covenant order, and a direct threat to the oneness of Israel to have only one national altar. Their
concern was serious because they remembered the sin of Israel at Baal-peor and Achan. They knew that one person’s sin
could bring trouble upon the whole congregation. In that sense, their concern for holiness was not wrong. What was wrong
was that they nearly went to war before fully understanding the motive behind the action. This teaches that good
intentions can be misunderstood when communication is not properly done.

 ~ 227 ~

The eastern tribes built the altar as a witness to remind their children that they also belong to God just as the other
Israelites on the western side, but they did not first communicate clearly enough to the rest of Israel. Their action carried
a good intention, but the meaning was not known to others. This happens often in daily life. A husband may keep quiet
because he is tired, but his wife may interpret it as rejection. A wife may delay responding to a message because she is
overwhelmed, but her husband may think she is being disrespectful. A business partner may make a decision quickly to
save an opportunity, but the other partner may feel excluded or betrayed. A fellowship President may change a programme
arrangement because the guest minister did not arrive on time, but other executives may think there is hidden bias or
personal agenda.

Communication protects unity and covenant relationships. In marriage, couples must not assume that love alone will
explain everything. They must explain decisions, feelings, expectations, finances, boundaries, pressures, and concerns. In
business partnerships, partners must communicate clearly about money, responsibilities, ownership, deadlines, risks, and
decisions. In friendships, people must learn to say, “This hurts me,” “I did not understand what you meant,” or “Please
explain what happened,” instead of withdrawing silently or spreading offence. In fellowship, leaders must explain plans,
burdens, and instructions clearly so that others are not confused or feel slighted. This also applies in ministry and doctrinal
matters. A minister may make a statement in a long sermon, but a short clip may circulate online without the full context.
In the age of short clips on our social media pages, screenshots, forwarded voice notes, and social media reactions,
believers must be careful. Not everything seen in a clip represents the full message. We must not build judgement on
fragments.

2. Do Not Judge Before You Listen: The western tribe of Israel that constituted the nine and a half tribes nearly went to
war because of an assumption that they have not taken time to clarify. They heard that the eastern tribes had built an
altar, and they gathered at Shiloh to go up against them in battle. Yet, before fighting, they sent Phinehas and ten princes
to speak with them. This step was wise and godly. Though, their emotions were strong and their concern was serious, they
still created room for enquiry and consultation and this decision saved Israel from destroying its own innocent brethren.
This is a major lesson in conflict resolution. We must not judge before we listen. While the western tribes were right to
care about the risk of the eastern tribes raising a strange altar before the Lord as a form of idolatry, any show of zeal
without careful enquiry can destroy relationships.

This principle is needed in marriage. Before a husband concludes that his wife is careless, he should ask what is happening
around her. Before a wife concludes that her husband is insensitive, she should ask what pressure he is facing. Couples
must not punish one another for unspoken assumptions. They must learn to pause, listen, and speak with honour. A useful
practice is to ask, “What did you mean by that?” “Can you help me understand?” “Is there something I am missing?” “This
is how I felt; is that what you intended?” These simple questions can prevent many unnecessary battles. This principle is
also needed among business partners and friends. Before accusing a partner of dishonesty, verify the records. Before
accusing a friend of betrayal, ask for the full story. Before reacting to a delayed payment, missed call, changed plan, or
failed commitment, seek clarity. Sometimes people are careless, but sometimes they are under pressure. Sometimes there
is a wrongdoing, but sometimes there is misunderstanding. Listening does not mean ignoring truth; it means refusing to
judge without knowledge.

Dear TACEFites, patience to seek clarity is not weakness and giving benefit of doubt is not compromise. Listening before
judging is wisdom. The Lord’s army must not destroy its own brethren through haste.

3. Truthful Communication Protects Unity: When the eastern tribes were confronted, they answered clearly. They did not
respond with insult, anger, or counter-accusation. They explained their motive that the altar was not built for burnt offering
or sacrifice but was meant to be a witness between them and the other tribes so that future generations would know that
they had a part in the Lord. Their explanation changed the atmosphere. When Phinehas and the princes heard their words,
“it pleased them.” The crisis was resolved because truth was spoken clearly. This shows that truthful communication
protects unity. Ephesians 4:25 says, “Wherefore putting away lying, speak every man truth with his neighbour: for we are
members one of another.” Lies, half-truths, silence, secrecy, emotional manipulation, exaggeration, and defensive speech
weaken trust. When people do not speak truth, assumptions will grow. When people hide motives, suspicion grows.

Apostle Peter also admonishes us to be ready always to give an answer to every man that asks the reason of the hope that
is in us, with meekness and fear (1 Peter 3 vs 15). This means that believers must not be dismissive when others seek
understanding. We must be careful with statements such as, “Can’t you see?” “Do I have to explain everything?” “Can’t

 ~ 228 ~

you understand why I did this?” or “Can’t you just trust my judgment?” While these words may seem reasonable to the
speaker, they often increase confusion, discourage honest questions, and leave the listener feeling hurt or dismissed. Many
conflicts are like numbers 6 and 9. One person is seeing from one side, and another person is seeing from the other side.
Both are describing what they see, but because they are standing in different positions, they interpret the same matter
differently. This is why calm explanation is important. What looks obvious to one person may not be obvious to another.

In marriage, truthful communication means couples must speak honestly, but with honour. A husband should not hide
financial pressure until it becomes a crisis. A wife should not silently build resentment and then explode later. Couples
should talk about expectations, money, intimacy, family interference, spiritual life, parenting, emotional needs, and
workload. They should not weaponise silence. They should not use past mistakes to crush one another. Truth spoken early,
gently, and prayerfully can save a home from years of bitterness. In business partnership, truthful communication means
records must be clear, agreements must be written, roles must be defined, and money must be accounted for. Many
Christian partnerships fail not because the people are bad, but because many things are not discussed and legally
documented. One person assumes ownership, another assumes employment. One person assumes equal profit, another
assumes commission. One person is bearing hidden costs; another is expecting immediate returns. Brethren must not
spiritualise poor documentation. Agreement, reporting, accountability, and clarity are important in business.

4. One Lord, One Faith, and One Body Must Govern How We Manage Conflicts: Ephesians reminds us that there is one
body, one Spirit, one hope, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, and one God and Father of all. This means that conflict among
believers must be handled with the consciousness of shared identity. We are not enemies. We are members of one body.
When one part wounds another, the whole body suffers. When ministers fight publicly, the next generation becomes
confused. When believers insult one another online, unbelievers mock the faith. When couples fight carelessly, children
are affected. When business partners fight without honour, trust is destroyed. When fellowship members divide into
camps, revival mandate is weakened. We must also reiterate that unity does not mean pretending that error, sin, abuse,
dishonesty, or rebellion does not matter. The western tribes were right to care about holiness. But the way we handle
conflicts must reflect Christ. We must not use truth as a weapon of pride and we must not correct with bitterness. We
must not expose because we enjoy shame and we must not fight publicly when private enquiry is still possible.

As believers, when conflict arises, believers should follow a godly process. First, pause and pray before reacting. Anger
often feels urgent, but wisdom slows down. Second, seek the full facts. Ask what happened, who was involved, what was
said, what was meant, and whether there is missing context you need to remind yourself as a way to calm down. Third, go
to the person directly where possible. Do not first report to everyone except the person involved. Fourth, listen with
patience and with benefit of doubt, especially where there has been a history of faithfulness. Remember that the eastern
tribes had laboured with their brethren; their past faithfulness should have encouraged careful enquiry. Fifth, speak truth
clearly and respectfully. Sixth, involve mature witnesses or leaders if the issue remains unresolved. Seventh, agree on
correction, boundaries, or next steps where needed. Eighth, protect the unity of the body by refusing gossip, mockery, and
revenge.

Managing anger is also part of conflict resolution. When anger rises, do not speak immediately if your words will wound.
Take time to pray. Write down the issue before speaking. Ask yourself, “What exactly hurts me?” “What facts do I have?”
“What am I assuming?” “What outcome do I want?” “Will my words heal or scatter?” Avoid shouting, insults, threats,
sarcasm, public embarrassment, and bringing up old matters that are not related. In marriage, do not argue to win; speak
to understand and rebuild. In business, do not turn disagreement into character assassination. In fellowship, do not convert
offence into camps. In ministry, do not make the Body of Christ a theatre of personal battles. The Lord’s army must be
mature enough to preserve unity, resolve conflicts, correct errors, and keep the bond of peace.

Step-by-Step Applications and Practical Implications
• Pause before reacting: Do not respond in anger, offence, or pressure. Pray first and ask God for wisdom.
• Separate facts from assumptions: Write down what you know, what you heard, what you saw, and what you are
 assuming.
• Seek full context: Before reacting to a short clip, screenshot, rumour, or forwarded message, seek the full message, full
 conversation, and reliable witnesses.
• Ask clarifying questions: Use questions such as, “Please, what did you mean?” “Can you explain what happened?” “Is
 there something I am missing?” “This is how I understood it; is that correct?”

 ~ 229 ~

• Give benefit of doubt where appropriate: Especially in marriage, friendship, partnership, and ministry relationships
 where there has been a history of faithfulness.
• Speak truth with love: Do not lie, hide, exaggerate, insult, mock, or manipulate. Speak clearly, humbly, and respectfully.
• Avoid social media battles: Do not turn ministry disagreement, doctrinal concern, or personal offence into public
 entertainment that confuses younger believers.
• Manage anger wisely: Slow down, pray, breathe, write the issue down, avoid insults, and choose the right time and
 tone for discussion.
• Document business and ministry agreements: Put roles, finances, expectations, ownership, reporting, and
 responsibilities in writing with proper legal framework.
• Protect the Body: Refuse gossip, suspicion, revenge, and careless speech that weakens unity.

Questions for Discussion
 1. Why did the altar built by the eastern tribes create a major misunderstanding among the rest of Israel?
 2. What can we learn from the fact that Israel nearly went to war because of an assumption?
 3. Why is it important to listen before judging, especially in marriage, friendship, fellowship, and business
 partnership?
 4. I heard from a seemingly reliable source that our fellowship leader is involved in an extramarital affair and was
 allegedly caught in the act. How should I handle the matter as an ordinary member, and how should it be handled
 if I am an executive in the fellowship?
 5. A couple has become increasingly concerned about a young disciple who has been living with them. They have
 observed that the monthly internet data they purchase is consistently exhausted within the first week of the
 month. They are also concerned about his personal hygiene, particularly persistent body odour, and have noticed
 that he frequently falls asleep in the living room. They value their relationship with him and are worried that raising
 these issues may damage it. However, they are becoming increasingly uncomfortable and would appreciate
 guidance on how to address these concerns with love, wisdom, and honesty.
 6. Why is it dangerous to judge a minister or believer only by a short clip, screenshot, or social media post?

Personal Reflection
Do I judge people before listening to them? Do I react quickly to rumours or one-sided stories? Have I wounded anyone
through hasty judgement, anger, gossip, or careless words? In my marriage, friendships, business relationships, fellowship,
or ministry relationships, do I communicate clearly or expect people to understand my intentions without explanations?
Do I give benefit of doubt, especially to people who have shown faithfulness before? When I disagree with someone, do I
seek peace and truth, or do I seek to win? How do I handle anger? Do my words heal, clarify, and restore, or do they scatter
and wound? Am I helping to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace?

Prayer Points

fruit of the Spirit is in all goodness and righteousness and truth; 10 Proving what is acceptable unto the Lord. 11 And have

things which are done of them in secret. 13 But all things that are reproved are made manifest by the light: for whatsoever
doth make manifest is light. 14 Wherefore he saith, Awake thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead, and Christ shall give
thee light. 15 See then that ye walk circumspectly, not as fools, but as wise, 16 Redeeming the time, because the days are
evil. 17 Wherefore be ye not unwise, but understanding what the will of the Lord is.

Key Extracts from the Bible Texts to Remember and Reflect On
 • The LORD had given rest unto Israel from all their enemies round about.
 • The LORD your God is he that hath fought for you.
 • Be ye therefore very courageous to keep and to do all that is written.
 • Turn not aside therefrom to the right hand or to the left.
 • Come not among these nations.
 • Cleave unto the LORD your God.
 • Now are ye light in the Lord.
 • Walk as children of light.

Introduction
Our weekly study brings us to a very sensitive point in the journey of Israel. The Lord had given them rest from their
enemies round about. Battles had been fought, victories had been won, territories had been divided, and the people had
seen the hand of God in undeniable ways. Yet Joshua, in his old age, called the leaders and people together with a strong
warning. He reminded them that the victories they enjoyed did not come by their own strength, wisdom, or greatness.
“The LORD your God is he that hath fought for you.” This reminder was necessary because success can easily enter into the
head of a people who forget the God who gave it.

This is a major warning because victory, promotion or enlargement can become dangerous when it produces spiritual
pride, relaxed consecration, or a false sense of arrival. A person who has prayed for years for a job can become too busy
for God after employment comes. A family that waited on God for a miracle baby can become distracted by the blessing
and gradually lose their sense of service to the same Lord who gave the baby. A believer who relocates abroad can begin
to feel too enlightened or too established to remain connected to the work of the Lord. A minister who receives lifting in
the church can become distant from the vision that nurtured him. A professional who receives promotion can begin to
treat spiritual duties as secondary. This is why the fire must be guarded after the battle is won.

 ~ 232 ~

Joshua also warned Israel about their relationship with other remaining nations. They must not mention the names of their
gods, serve them, or bow to them. This means that after victory, the greatest danger may no longer be open warfare but
quiet mixture. The gods of the land can come among God’s people through friendships, relationships, partnerships,
entertainment, ambition, fashion, language, social media, and cultural pressure. What Israel was commanded to avoid
physically, the believer must avoid spiritually and morally. We must not allow the values of the world to enter our hearts
and destroy our covenant walk with God. Ephesians expounds these warnings even further. We were sometimes darkness,
but now we are light in the Lord; therefore, we must walk as children of light. We must have no fellowship with the
unfruitful works of darkness. TACEFites must therefore learn to remain separated without pride, holy without arrogance,
loving without compromise, and successful without losing the fear of God.

Teachings
1. Victory Must Not Produce Carelessness: Joshua began by reminding Israel that it was the Lord who fought for them.
This was a very serious and weighty statement. It was a spiritual safeguard against pride because a person may begin to
think, “My hard work did it. My intelligence did it. My discipline did it. My network did it. My prayer life did it. My sacrifice
did it.” While diligence, prayer, and discipline are important, the testimony of the redeemed must remain clear: “The LORD
your God is he that hath fought for you.” Success becomes dangerous when it enters the head. This can happen after
promotion, relocation, business breakthroughs, ministry visibility, academic success, marriage, childbirth, healing, financial
lifting, or recognition. The same person who once prayed fervently can gradually diminish in consecration and service unto
the Lord. The same person who once loved fellowship can begin to withdraw. The same person who once sought counsel
can become proud. The same person who once trembled at God’s Word can begin to live by personal convenience.

As God’s end-time revival army, we must understand how a miracle baby must not replace the God who gave the child. A
new job must not swallow the time of prayer. A promotion must not make a believer look down on others or begin to feel
too big for the subgroup, ministry, or service unit where God has placed him. No lifting should make anyone feel far above
the members of his local fellowship or too elevated to remain accountable. A relocation abroad must not become a journey
into spiritual coldness. A growing business must not become an idol. Ministry recognition must not become a throne of
self-importance and detachment from other brethren. As we always say in the great house of TACEF that every lifting that
we receive of the Lord must push us deeper into gratitude, dependence, holiness, and service.

Dear TACEFites, do not allow success to enter your head. Do not become bigger than the altar that raised you. Do not
become too busy for the God who helped you. Do not become too important for fellowship, discipleship, prayer, and
accountability. The Lord who fought for you must still be the Lord you cleave to after the victory.

2. The Word Must Still Govern the Life after Visible Success: Joshua said, “Be ye therefore very courageous to keep and to
do all that is written in the book of the law of Moses.” This instruction came after many victories had already been won.
This means the Word of God is not only needed before and during the battle, but it is even more needed after the battle.
The Word must guide us in waiting seasons, fighting seasons, and resting seasons. This is where many believers miss it.
When they are trusting God for something, they appear very submissive to the Word. They ask for counsel, pray, fast,
attend fellowship, avoid sin and seek God’s will. But after the answer comes, they begin to relax. They now make decisions
by status, exposure, emotions, cultural pressure, or convenience. This should not be so.

The Word that governed us in the valley must still govern us on the mountain. Joshua said they must not turn aside to the
right hand or to the left. This means obedience must be consistent, balanced, and total. The Word of God must remain the
final authority, even when our status changes. Ephesians says we must prove what is acceptable unto the Lord. This means
every choice must be tested by God’s will, not by whether it is popular, profitable, exciting, fashionable, or socially
acceptable. The question is not “Can I do it?” but “Is it acceptable unto the Lord?” The question is not, “Will it work?” but
“Does it please God?” The question is not, “Will people approve?” but “Is it light or darkness?” Dear TACEFites, keep living
by the Word after the victory and liftings. Let the Scripture govern your promotion, marriage, relocation, parenting,
business, ministry, friendships, and spheres of life. The believer who stops obeying after success has allowed success to
become a doorway to decline.

3. Separation Preserves Inheritance from the gods of the Land: Joshua warned Israel, “Make sure you do not associate
with the other people still remaining in the land. Do not even mention the names of their gods, much less swear by them or
serve them or worship them.” (NLT version). This was a clear boundary. Israel had received inheritance, but that inheritance
could be corrupted if they allowed the gods of the land to come among them. Victory gave them access to the land, but

 ~ 233 ~

separation was needed to preserve the inheritance. This remains a strong lesson for every believer today. The gods of the
land may not always appear as carved images but they can appear as values, appetites, relationships, ambitions, ideologies,
habits, entertainment, and lifestyles that compete with God. They can enter through ungodly friendships, careless media
consumption on Netflix or TikTok, corrupt business partnerships, immoral relationships, prideful social circles, feminine-
focused groups that oppose Christian marriage, dishonest networks, or cultural practices that weaken the fear of God.
What we allow among us can eventually rule over us.

A genuine revival army must therefore be careful about friendship. Our closest friend must not be someone who makes us
love sin more, mock holiness, or treat the things of God lightly. Our best friend cannot be someone who pulls our hearts
away from God. The closest friend of a believer should be someone who helps us love God more, obey God better, pray
more, think more purely, and stand more firmly. We can have unbelievers around us, be in class with them, work with
them, and treat them with kindness, but our deepest covenant friendships must strengthen our walk with God, not weaken
it. This also applies to relationships and partnerships. A sister should not maintain a close male relationship with someone
who keeps drawing her into immoral conversations, sharing ungodly videos, making suggestive comments, or weakening
her purity. A brother should not continue in a private emotional attachment that makes him hide, lie, compromise, or drift
from prayer. Separation is not hatred but a path of covenant preservation.

Ephesians says, “Have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness.” This does not mean we should be proud, harsh,
rude, or isolated from the people we are called to reach. It means we must not share in darkness. We must not become
comfortable with what grieves God. We must not laugh at their ungodly comedy, spend time watching contents that
diminish the essence of Christ or partner with what corrupts our obedience. Dear revival army in the great house of TACEF,
set clear boundaries against the gods of the land. Guard your friendships, conversations, social media, entertainment,
business partnerships, emotional attachments, and secret habits.

4. Cleaving to the Lord Is the Secret of Preservation: Joshua did not only say, “Avoid the nations.” He also said, “But cleave
unto the LORD your God, as ye have done unto this day.” The answer to compromise is not only avoidance but an intentional
attachment to God. A believer who only avoids evil without cleaving to the Lord will soon become dry and vulnerable. True
preservation comes when the heart remains joined to God in love, worship, obedience, and daily fellowship.

“To cleave” means to hold fast, cling, remain joined, and refuse separation. This is the secret of keeping the fire after the
battle is won. After promotion, cleave to the Lord. After relocation, cleave to the Lord. After marriage, cleave to the Lord.
After childbirth, cleave to the Lord. Lord. After business growth, cleave to the Lord. Ephesians says, “See then that ye walk
circumspectly, not as fools, but as wise.” This means we must not drift and not assume that yesterday’s fire will
automatically carry today’s obedience. We must redeem the time because the days are evil.

Dear TACEFites, cleave to the Lord after every victory. Do not only remember God when you need a miracle. Do not only
seek Him when battles of life are hard. Do not only attend fellowship when you are looking for help. Love Him in rest as
much as in war time. Serve the Lord in abundance as much as in need. Follow Him in the new country, new home, new
role, new office, new home, new business, and new season.

5. Step-by-Step Applications and Practical Implications
· Return every victory to God: After promotion, marriage, childbirth, relocation, healing, financial breakthrough,
 academic success, or ministry exploits, deliberately give glory to God and remain humble.
· Do not let success reduce consecration: Guard against spiritual pride, prayerlessness, fellowship withdrawal, reduced
 accountability, and careless living after God has helped you.
· Keep obeying the Word after success: Let Scripture continue to govern your marriage, parenting, job, business,
 ministry, relationships and other decisions.
· Test every choice by God’s approval: Do not ask whether something is profitable, popular, or exciting. Ask whether it
 is acceptable unto the Lord.
· Set boundaries against the gods of the land: Refuse influences, practices, relationships, and environments that weaken
 your covenant walk with God.
· Choose friends who strengthen your love for God: Your closest friends should help you serve God more, pray, grow,
 and remain pure.
· Avoid ungodly emotional attachments: Do not maintain any relationships that introduce immoral conversations,
 ungodly videos, secrecy, compromise, or spiritual decline.

· Reject corrupt partnerships: Do not join business, ministry, academic, or social partnerships that require dishonesty,
 compromise, vanity, or silence about truth.
· Guard your phone and media life: Do not allow darkness to enter your heart through what you watch, share, laugh at,
 follow, or repeatedly consume.
· Cleave to the Lord daily: Build a steady life of prayer, Word, fellowship, accountability, and service.

Week 39: Monday, 24 May 2027 to Sunday, 30 May 2027
Title: One Shall Chase a Thousand: The Power Behind One Consecrated Life

Bible Texts: Joshua 23:9-10; Ephesians 1:19-23; Ephesians 6:10

Bible Texts
Joshua 23:9-10: 9 For the LORD hath driven out from before you great nations and strong: but as for you, no man hath been
able to stand before you unto this day. 10 One man of you shall chase a thousand: for the LORD your God, he it is that
fighteth for you, as he hath promised you.

Ephesians 1:19-23: 19 And what is the exceeding greatness of his power to us-ward who believe, according to the working
of his mighty power, 20 Which he wrought in Christ, when he raised him from the dead, and set him at his own right hand
in the heavenly places, 21 Far above all principality, and power, and might, and dominion, and every name that is named,
not only in this world, but also in that which is to come: 22 And hath put all things under his feet, and gave him to be the
