Key Extracts from the Bible Texts to Remember and Reflect On
 • The LORD hath driven out from before you great nations and strong.
 • No man hath been able to stand before you unto this day.
 • One man of you shall chase a thousand.
 • The LORD your God, he it is that fighteth for you.
 • The exceeding greatness of his power to us-ward who believe.
 • According to the working of his mighty power
 • Finally, my brethren, be strong in the Lord.

Introduction
This week brings us to one of the most powerful statements in Joshua’s final charge to Israel: “One man of you shall chase
a thousand.” Israel had become a covenant community in the Promised Land. Territories had been conquered, lands had
been divided, and the people were beginning to grow and multiply in their inheritance. Yet Joshua spoke in a way that
showed how God still sees each person through the lens of divine impact and what one consecrated life can accomplish
for Him. He was not merely addressing the people as a crowd; he was reminding each person that their strength was never
in their number, size, status, experience, or natural ability. Their strength was in the Lord who fought for them. Great
nations and strong enemies had been driven out, not because Israel was naturally superior, but because God was with
them. Therefore, even one covenant man standing with God could accomplish what natural strength could not explain.

This is a major encouragement to every TACEFite. Numerical smallness is not weakness when God is present. One believer
in a family can become a spiritual doorway for salvation. One student in a class can shift the atmosphere of that class. One
NYSC corps member in a village can become a witness for Christ. One Spirit-filled worker in an office can carry the light of
God into a dark environment. One TACEFite in a local church, campus, or city can become the seed of revival. We must not
despise the day of small things, because God can do much with one consecrated life. This truth is seen in the history of
TACEF. Many fellowships in churches and campuses were not started by large groups. Many were pioneered by one
burdened teenager, one young person in his or her twenties, one student, one youth, one young worker, or one young
minister who carried the fire of God into a difficult place. Many had no support, no instrument, no transport fare, no stable
finance, and no immediate acceptance. Indeed, one consecrated life can catalyse a move of God and one prayerful life can
open the door for many to encounter Christ.

However, the principle of “one” is not only about one person standing alone. It also speaks to oneness as a spiritual
principle. In marriage, God makes husband and wife one flesh. That oneness requires openness, transparency, trust, shared
planning, shared burdens, shared stewardship, and no hidden life. In fellowship, the disciples were in one accord, and the
Spirit moved among them. A fellowship may have many people, but if there is no oneness of heart, its strength is weakened.
Therefore, this week calls us to recognise the power of one consecrated life and the power of a people made one before
God.

 ~ 237 ~

Teachings
1. Numerical Smallness Is Not Weakness When God Is with One Consecrated Life: Joshua said, “One man of you shall
chase a thousand.” This statement shows that the covenant strength of God’s people cannot be measured by physical
number. One person with God is not ordinary. One believer carrying the presence, burden of revival and power of God can
stand and survive in any place and become an instrument of divine change. The question is not only, “How many are we?”
The deeper question is, “Is God with us?”. Many believers become discouraged when they are alone. A TACEFite may
relocate to a city where there is no familiar fellowship structure. A student may find himself or herself as the only serious
believer in a class. A NYSC corps member may be posted to a place where prayer, holiness, and discipleship are not valued.
A worker may be in an office where immorality is normal. A young minister may be sent to a local church where he seems
alone with no one to support. In such moments, we must be reminded that one person with God can become an army.
This is why no believer should say, “I am the only one, so nothing can happen.” God does not need a crowd before He
begins a move. He can begin with one. He can begin with one praying mother, one sincere student, one faithful worker,
one burdened corps member, one consecrated MOTA minister, one courageous sister, one honest businessman, one
consecrated teacher, one youth who refuses compromise, or one TACEFite who carries the fire of revival into a new
environment.

In the history of TACEF, we have heard of how a young person would arrive in a church or campus and discovered that
there was no active TACEF mandate or organised fellowship platform. Yet instead of relaxing and being quiet, that one
person began to pray. He or she began to speak to two or three people, shared the burden, invited brethren, visited homes,
followed up young converts, and kept showing up even when attendance was low. Breaking new ground is not easy. Some
pioneers had to face loneliness, rejection, lack of encouragement, academic pressure, financial limitation, transport
difficulties, spiritual attacks, and the pain of being misunderstood. Some had examinations, early career pressure, or family
expectations, yet they carried the burden with tears, prayers, discipline, sacrifice, and consistency. Many of the fellowships
that later became established did not start with a crowd but with one person who believed that God could use a
consecrated life.

The danger of our time these days is that many people wait for others to join before they start something for God. They
wait for a committee before they evangelise. They wait for official recognition before they serve. But Joshua’s word teaches
us that one person backed by God is not powerless. God can use one consecrated life to begin a move of revival through
intercession. Dear TACEFites, do not despise your smallness or perceived loneliness. Do not despise your current location.
If you are the only one standing for Christ in that home, office, class, hostel, department, local church, village, campus, or
city, stand well. One consecrated life with God can become the beginning of a thousand testimonies.

2. One Shall Chase a Thousand - One Soul-Winner Can Lead Many Sinners to Christ: The phrase “one shall chase a
thousand” can also help us understand the power of personal evangelism. It is possible for one believer to become a
channel through which many sinners are brought to Christ. The word “chase” reminds us that soul-winning requires pursuit
or running after something. Souls do not always come to us; sometimes we must go after them with prayer, love, wisdom,
and the gospel. Philip is a clear example in the book of Acts. He went down to the city of Samaria and preached Christ unto
them. One man entered a city, and the city heard the gospel. Joy came to the entire city of Samaria because one man was
available. Nehemiah also began with a burden when he heard about the broken walls of Jerusalem. He wept, prayed,
fasted, and eventually became the vessel through whom rebuilding began. Esther stood at a dangerous point in history,
and God used her position to preserve many lives. These examples show that one person, rightly positioned before God,
can catalyse a move that touches many.

This is very important for TACEFites. Every believer is called to be a soul-winner. Every TACEFite must carry a burden for
souls. One member in a local church can begin to pray for salvation of souls in the church. One student can reach
classmates. One professional can witness wisely in the workplace. One family can open their home for prayer and follow-
up. One NYSC corps member can begin a fellowship in a place where there was none. Many TACEF fellowships and revival
burdens grew because one person carried personal evangelism seriously. One young brother invited classmates repeatedly
until a Bible study began. One young sister followed up younger girls patiently until they became stable in faith. One person
in a local church kept visiting brethren after Sunday service until a weekly meeting became possible. One person on campus
carried handbills, spoke to classmates, prayed with course mates, and helped weak believers find their feet. These were
not always public exploits, but they were powerful seeds of revival. In essence, “One shall chase a thousand” means God
can multiply the effect of one obedient witness. One tract given prayerfully can open a conversation unto salvation.

 ~ 238 ~

Dear TACEFites, become personal soul-winners. Do not wait until a general outreach is announced before you speak to
 someone about Christ. One believer can chase a thousand sinners with the love and truth of Christ and lead many into the
 kingdom.

 3. Divine Backing Multiplies Human Efforts: Joshua gave the reason why one man could chase a thousand: “For the LORD
 your God, he it is that fighteth for you, as he hath promised you.” The secret was not the greatness of the man; it was the
 greatness of the God behind the man. What is small in human hands becomes mighty when God breathes upon it and
 provides the divine backing. What looks weak naturally becomes strong when the power of God is present. Ephesians
 explains this through the phrase, “the exceeding greatness of his power to us-ward who believe.” This power is not ordinary.
 It is the mighty power that raised Christ from the dead and seated Him far above all principality, power, might, dominion,
 and every name that is named. This is why Ephesians 6:10 says, “Be strong in the Lord, and in the power of his might.” Our
 strength must be in the Lord, not in our gifts, titles, education, experience, personality, exposure, popularity, family
 background, money, beauty, intelligence, or spiritual history. A gifted person who is not strong in the Lord will fall. A
 minister who is not strong in the Lord will diminish in value and a professional who is not strong in the Lord will
 compromise.

 In this regard, whatever we achieve in life must produce deeper dependence, not pride or independence. When God uses
 one person to bless many lives, that person must become more humble. When God uses a TACEFite to start a fellowship,
 lead souls to Christ, catalyse a revival move in a local church, or minister powerfully in an open air crusade, such a person
 must not begin to think that everything depends on him or her. The Lord is the One fighting. The Lord is the One opening
 doors. The Lord is the One touching hearts. The Lord is the One giving fruits. Dearly beloved in the great house, let every
 open door make you more dependent on the Lord and let every testimony humble you. Let every lifting, visibility and
 promotion return you to the altar. One person can do much for God, but only when that person remains under the power,
 authority, and government of Christ.

 4. The Power of One Also Teaches Oneness in Marriage and Covenant Labour: The principle of “one” is not only about
 one person standing alone. It also speaks to the power of oneness. In marriage, God makes husband and wife “one flesh”.
 This oneness is not only physical; it is spiritual, emotional, financial, practical, and covenantal. A husband and a wife must
 learn to live with openness, transparency, trust, shared planning, and shared stewardship. Where there are secrecy,
 suspicion, hidden spending, hidden emotional attachments, and divided vision, the strength of oneness is destroyed. The
 Scripture says concerning the first marriage that they were both naked and were not ashamed. This speaks to openness
 without shame, transparency without fear, and trust without hidden life. Husband and wife should learn to pray together,
 plan together, save together, build together, invest together, decide together and serve God together. There should be no
 secret financial life that damages trust. There should be no hidden emotional connection with strangers that weakens the
 covenant. There should be no private attachment that competes with the marriage. One flesh means two lives willingly
 joined under God in love, truth, honour, and responsibility.

 This is also important for fellowship. In Acts of Apostle when the Holy Ghost came, the disciples were in “one accord”. A
 fellowship may have many members, but if there is no oneness, its strength is reduced. Oneness is not the same as mere
 attendance. People may sit in the same meeting and still carry different hearts, private agendas, jealousy, bitterness,
 competition, suspicion, and disunity. True oneness means one burden, one love, one submission to Christ, one pursuit of
 revival, and one desire to see souls saved.

 A local fellowship, subgroup/ministry, or family altar must therefore protect oneness. We must avoid gossip, unhealthy
 competition, factions, careless words, and suspicion. We must learn to communicate clearly, forgive quickly, and honour
 one another. When the people are one in God, their impact is multiplied. Being in “one accord “can turn a small fellowship
 into a powerful witness and a channel of revival for a generation.

 5. Step-by-Step Applications and Practical Implications
· Do not despise small beginnings: One TACEFite in a city, campus, class, workplace, hostel, family, or local church can
 become the beginning of a move of God.
· Stand well when you are alone: Do not compromise because no one is watching or because no other serious believer is
 around you.
·

· Break new ground with courage: Begin with prayer, seek godly counsel, share the burden, invite one or two people, follow
 up consistently, and keep labouring even when attendance is small.
· Do not wait for perfect conditions: Many fellowships began with one young person who had no large team, no resources,
 and no encouragement, but continued faithfully.
· Become a personal soul-winner: Pray for sinners, speak to people about Christ, invite them to fellowship, follow them up,
 and disciple them patiently.

SECTION 9: How God’s Army Preserves Love, Remembers Grace, Chooses the Lord, and Turns Confession into Faithful
Obedience
The journey of God’s end-time army now moves into the final covenant appeals of Joshua. After battles had been fought,
territories had been divided, rest had been given, and testimonies had been established, Joshua began to press the people
into deeper covenant responsibility. He knew that the greatest danger after blessing is not always an external enemy; it is
often inward drift. A people can possess land and lose love. They can enjoy promises and forget covenant. They can
celebrate God’s faithfulness and still begin to tolerate strange gods, wrong attachments, and careless compromise.
Therefore, Joshua’s final words call Israel to guard their hearts, remember the Lord’s faithfulness, choose Him deliberately,
and serve Him sincerely.

God’s army must not only win battles but must also preserve covenant love after victory. The Lord who brings His people
into inheritance also calls them to take heed unto themselves. Love for God must be guarded because spiritual decline
often begins quietly in the heart before it appears openly in lifestyle. A person may still attend programmes, carry a title,
serve in a unit, sing, teach, preach, or appear active, while affection for God is already weakening inwardly. This is why
wrong associations, corrupted entertainment, ungodly relationships, careless ambitions, social media appetite, secret sin,
prayerlessness, and worldly desires must not be tolerated. What is tolerated can later dominate. What is allowed to remain
can become a snare, a trap, a scourge, and a thorn.

This ninth section therefore calls TACEFites to examine the heart behind the activity. We must not measure spirituality by
attendance, service, title, visibility, or outward involvement. We must keep asking, “Is my heart still burning for God?” We
must choose the Lord personally and daily, not merely live on the decisions of fathers, mothers, leaders, or past
generations. We must put away modern idols such as social media addiction, get rich quick, ungodly relationships,
popularity, comfort, pride, academic ambition, and self-rule.

Week 41: Take Good Heed Unto Yourselves: Loving God Sincerely in the Days of Blessing: Joshua warned Israel to take
good heed unto themselves and love the Lord their God. This teaches that love for God must be guarded, especially in the
days of blessing, rest, lifting, and possession. Spiritual drift begins in the heart before it appears in behaviour. A person
may still look active outwardly while affection for God is declining inwardly. Wrong associations, careless relationships,
worldly entertainment, ungodly ambitions, prayerlessness, and social media appetite can slowly reduce spiritual sensitivity.
TACEFites must therefore guard their affections and watch the inner life carefully. We must not only ask whether we are
still attending, serving, or visible; we must ask whether our hearts are still burning for God.

Week 42: Not One Thing Hath Failed: Covenant Faithfulness and the Danger of Forgetfulness: Joshua reminded Israel
that not one thing had failed of all the good things which the Lord had spoken. God had kept His covenant fully, but Joshua
warned that covenant blessing carried covenant responsibility. A people who forget where God brought them from will
soon tolerate compromise and spiritual drift. Memory strengthens covenant loyalty and Ephesians also calls us to
remember our former state and present grace: we were once far off, but have been made nigh by the blood of Christ.
TACEFites must remember past deliverances, answered prayers, revival roots, and the mercy of God, so that testimony
produces humility, gratitude, holiness, and faithful obedience rather than pride, entitlement, and forgetfulness.

Week 43: Choose You This Day: Covenant Loyalty in a Compromising Generation: Joshua rehearsed God’s dealings with
Israel and then called them to choose whom they would serve. This teaches that every generation must make its own
covenant choice. We cannot live only on the decisions, sacrifices, and convictions of past generations. Each TACEFite must
personally choose Christ. Covenant loyalty requires deliberate rejection of idols, including hidden sins, cultural pressure,
ungodly relationships, popularity, academic ambition, and self-rule. Serving God requires daily choices that align with truth,
holiness, self-denial, obedience, and the will of God. Families must also choose the Lord through regular household altars,
godly order, intentional discipleship, and clear separation from spiritual mixture.

Week 44: We Will Serve the Lord: Turning Confession into Covenant Commitment
Israel declared, “We will serve the LORD,” but Joshua reminded them that service must be serious, sincere, and sustained.
Public confession must become private obedience and daily faithfulness. Ephesians teaches that believers must serve not
with eye-service, as menpleasers, but as servants of Christ, doing the will of God from the heart. TACEFites must therefore
reject careless service. Punctuality, preparation, humility, accountability, excellence, follow-up, and consistency must mark
the lifestyle of the revival army. Covenant service is more than emotional vows, public declarations, titles, or visible activity
but something that is lived, not merely spoken. We must serve the Lord sincerely in both visible and hidden places, and
our commitment must outlive emotion.

Introduction
Our study this week is a very emotional one which brings us to one of the most solemn warnings in Joshua’s final charge
to Israel. After victories, possession, rest, and the visible fulfilment of God’s promises, Joshua did not only congratulate the
people. He warned them. He said, “Take good heed therefore unto yourselves, that ye love the LORD your God.” This shows
that the days of blessing can also become dangerous days if the heart is not carefully guarded. The same people who saw
the hand of God, entered the land, and enjoyed divine faithfulness could still go back if they allowed their love for God to
grow cold. Joshua did not say, “Take heed” casually. He said, “Take good heed”, which in other versions is captured as “Be
very careful” in ESV and “Now, vigilantly guard your souls” in Message version. We can therefore understand that this
warning means to pay careful attention and to watch yourself closely. It means they must not assume that because they
once loved God deeply, they can no longer drift.

The warning is very serious because Joshua also said that if Israel went back and cleaved to the nations around them, those
nations would become snares, traps, scourges, and thorns until they perished from the good land God had given them.
This teaches that God’s mercy must never be taken for granted. God is good, patient, loving, and faithful, but He is also
holy, righteous, and fearful in judgement. The same God who gave the land could allow His people to perish from it if they
rejected His covenant and disconnected from Him. It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God. Therefore,
this week calls every revival army to examine the heart, not only outward activity. We must ask, “Is my heart still burning
for God?” We must watch what we love, what we tolerate, what we watch, who we keep as friends, where we go, what
we laugh at, what we call harmless, and what is slowly shaping our appetite. A simple ungodly TikTok video can weaken
consecration, a so-called reunion party can dig a pit of perversion, a professional get-together can become a doorway into
worldliness, and an uncontrolled use of social media habit can quietly corrupt the heart.

 ~ 244 ~

Teachings
1. Love for God Must Be Guarded Because Backsliding Begins in the Heart: Joshua said, “Take good heed therefore unto
yourselves, that ye love the LORD your God.” The first thing he asked Israel to guard was not their land, wealth, houses,
farms, positions, or victories. He asked them to guard their love for God. This is because spiritual drift begins in the heart
before it appears in one’s lifestyle. A person does not usually fall in one day. Something first begins to shift in the affection,
desire, appetite, and attention of the heart. Backsliding begins when a believer starts yielding to small temptations. At first,
the conscience may still be sensitive. The person knows that what is being watched, discussed, imagined, pursued, or
tolerated is not right. But instead of fleeing, the person lingers. Instead of cutting it off, the person explains it away. Instead
of confessing quickly, the person hides it. This is how resistance begins to weaken. What once looked dangerous begins to
look manageable. What once brought conviction begins to feel normal. After yielding repeatedly, self-justification begins.
The believer starts creating reasons for compromise. “Everybody does it.” “It is not that serious.” “At least I still attend
fellowship.” “I am not as bad as others.” “God understands.” “This is just entertainment.” “This is just networking.” “This
is just friendship.” These excuses are dangerous because they protect sin from being judged. The moment a person begins
to defend what the Holy Spirit is convicting him or her about; backsliding is already gaining ground.

If the matter is not immediately dealt with, detachment from the Lord follows. Prayer becomes difficult. The Word of God
becomes dry. Fellowship becomes boring, counsel becomes irritating, and correction feels like attack. The person begins
to avoid people who can discern the decline. The heart becomes more comfortable with darkness and less comfortable
with God’s presence. This is why Joshua said, “Take good heed.” The heart must be watched before drift becomes
destruction. A further danger is the searing of the conscience. When a person keeps resisting conviction, the inner alarm
becomes weaker. What used to bring tears no longer troubles the heart. What used to be confessed is now defended.
What used to be avoided is now enjoyed. The Holy Spirit is grieved and gradually silenced in that area of the person’s life.
This is one of the most frightening stages of backsliding when a person can still appear active, but inwardly, the fear of God
is fading.

2. “Take Good Heed” Means Living Carefully in a Crooked World: Joshua did not merely say, “Be careful.” He said, “Take
good heed therefore unto yourselves.” This is a strong call to spiritual watchfulness. It is similar to Paul’s instruction to
Timothy: “Take heed unto thyself, and unto the doctrine.” To “take good heed” means to live with godly caution. It means
knowing that not everything that looks harmless is harmless. Some things are not sinful in their first appearance, but they
carry an atmosphere, appetite, or influence that can weaken the soul. A film may look like ordinary entertainment, but it
may plant images, desires, language, and attitudes that fight consecration. A Netflix video may appear casual, but one
ungodly storyline can weaken purity and reduce spiritual sensitivity. A believer must be careful about what enters through
the eyes and ears, because the heart feeds on what it receives.

“To take good heed”means being careful about where we go and what we associate with in an increasingly polluted society.
While we are called to be friendly and not isolate ourselves, we must understand the boundaries of what we permit
wherever we find ourselves. A so-called reunion can look innocent, but it may reconnect a believer with old lifestyles, old
conversations, old attractions, and old desires that God once delivered him or her from. A professional get-together can
begin as networking event but become a bait into worldliness, drunkenness, dishonesty, ungodly bonding, or careless
relationships. Not every invitation should be honoured and not every environment is safe for a consecrated life.

“To take good heed” also speaks to the need to watch our social media appetite. A person may not physically go to ungodly
places, but through the phone, the heart can travel far into darkness. Reels, films, jokes, music, trends, arguments, and
images can slowly shape desire. The person may still attend fellowship, but the mind is being discipled by the world. This
is why every TACEFite must ask: “What is this content doing to my love for God? Is it making me pure or careless? Is it
making me prayerful or cold? Is it making me love Christ or love the world?”

3. Wrong Attachments Can Become Snares, Traps, Scourges, and Thorns: Joshua’s warning becomes even clearer when
we consider the four things he said the remaining nations would become if Israel cleaved to them: “snares,” “traps,”
“scourges in your sides,” and “thorns in your eyes.” These words show that wrong attachments do not remain harmless. A
snare catches a person quietly before he realises he is being held. In contemporary life, a snare may begin as a harmless
chat, an innocent-looking friendship, a social media habit, an afterparty with old friends, a professional circle, or
entertainment that slowly awakens wrong desires. A trap is a stronger form of captivity. It is when the person now finds it
difficult to leave what he once thought he could control. The friendship has become emotional dependence, the online

 ~ 245 ~

content has become a habit, the secret compromise has become a pattern, and the worldly circle has become a place
where the person now feels more comfortable than in the presence of God.

A scourge in the side speaks of something that repeatedly wounds, troubles, weakens, and reduces strength. This is what
happens when wrong relationships, ungodly appetites, bitterness, pride, careless entertainment, or continued
disobedience begin to wound the conscience and drain spiritual strength. The person may still be active outwardly, but
inwardly there is guilt, instability, loss of peace, prayerlessness, and repeated defeat. A thorn in the eyes speaks of anything
that blinds spiritual vision. When the gods of the land enter the heart, the person may no longer see sin as sin. Spiritual
discernment becomes blurred. What was once clearly wrong now appears negotiable. What once grieved the heart now
feels normal. This is why Joshua’s warning is so serious. The world of sin first attracts, then entangles, then wounds, and
finally blinds.

Yet the Lord does not leave His people helpless. Paul teaches clearly, “There hath no temptation taken you but such as is
common to man: but God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able; but will with the
temptation also make a way to escape, that ye may be able to bear it” (1 Corinthians 10:13). This means that before a
snare becomes a trap, God will often provide a way of escape through His Word, the warning of the Holy Spirit, godly
counsel, a disturbed conscience, an inner check, or the courage to cut off what is dangerous. The problem is not that God
gives no escape but the problem is that many people ignore the escape because they still want the compromise. We must
therefore take good heed, remain in Christ, and respond quickly when God shows us the exit.

4. God’s Mercy Must Not Be Taken for Granted: Joshua’s warning in verse 13 is one of the most fearful parts of this
passage. It says that the same God who gave Israel the land warned that they could perish from that good land if they
turned away from Him. This shows that covenant blessing carries covenant responsibility. Grace should make us fear God
more, not less. He said, “Know for a certainty that the LORD your God will no more drive out any of these nations from
before you …until ye perish from off this good land which the LORD your God hath given you.” This means that if Israel
chose to go back and cleave to what God warned them against, they would face the consequence of that choice. God had
fought for them, but He would not continue to fight for their compromise. God had shown mercy, but His mercy was not
permission to live anyhow. God is good, but we must not take Him for granted. God is loving, but He is also holy. God is
merciful, but He is also righteous. God forgives, but He does not support us to continue to live carelessly in sin after we
have known the truth.
This is why the fear of the Lord is necessary. The fear of the Lord is not torment or scary, but a deep awareness that God
must not be mocked or treated lightly. It makes a believer tremble at the Word of God. It makes us confess quickly, repent
sincerely, avoid dangerous doors, and honour the Lord in secret. Hebrews says, “It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands
of the living God.” At the same time, this warning is also mercy. God warned Israel before destruction came. The warning
itself was an act of love. When God warns us through His Word, through the Holy Spirit or through repeated inner
conviction, He is giving us opportunity to return. The wise believer does not despise warning but responds quickly before
a snare becomes bondage and before a thorn becomes blindness. As a member of God’s exceeding great army, make it a
lifestyle to always fear the Lord and do not take His goodness for granted.

Step-by-Step Applications and Practical Implications
· Watch your heart before you watch your activity: Do not measure your spirituality by attendance, title, service, or
 visibility. Ask whether your heart is still burning for God.
· Deal with temptation early: Do not linger around what you know is weakening your conscience. Flee quickly, confess
 quickly, and seek help where necessary.
· Reject self-justification: Stop defending what the Holy Spirit is convicting you about. Excuses weaken repentance.
· Restore spiritual sensitivity: If prayer is becoming difficult, the Word of God is becoming dry, fellowship is becoming
 irritating, or correction feels like attack, take it seriously.
· Guard your eyes and ears: Be careful with films, videos, music, jokes, reels, and online contents that slowly corrupt
 desire and diminish consecration.
· Discern gatherings carefully: Not every reunion, professional get-together, casual hangout, friendly sleep-over
 invitation, social event, or friendly invitation is safe for your soul.
· Watch your friendships and attachments: Do not cleave to people, relationships, partnerships, or circles that reduce
 your love for God.
· Fear the Lord: Do not take God’s goodness for granted. His mercy is real, but His judgement is also real.

· Respond quickly to warning: When God warns you through His Word, the Holy Spirit, counsel, correction, or inner
 conviction, do not delay.
· Stay rooted and grounded in love: Let your love for Christ be sincere, deep, daily, and practical.

Title: Not One Thing Hath Failed: Understanding Covenant Faithfulness

Bible Texts: Joshua 23:14-16; Ephesians 2:11-13

Bible Texts
Joshua 23:14-16: 14 And, behold, this day I am going the way of all the earth: and ye know in all your hearts and in all your
souls, that not one thing hath failed of all the good things which the LORD your God spake concerning you; all are come to

upon you, which the LORD your God promised you; so shall the LORD bring upon you all evil things, until he have destroyed
you from off this good land which the LORD your God hath given you. 16 When ye have transgressed the covenant of the
LORD your God, which he commanded you, and have gone and served other gods, and bowed yourselves to them; then
shall the anger of the LORD be kindled against you, and ye shall perish quickly from off the good land which he hath given
unto you.
Ephesians 2:11-13: 11 Wherefore remember, that ye being in time past Gentiles in the flesh, who are called Uncircumcision
by that which is called the Circumcision in the flesh made by hands; 12 That at that time ye were without Christ, being aliens

Key Extracts from the Bible Texts to Remember and Reflect On
 • Not one thing hath failed of all the good things which the LORD your God spake concerning you.
 • All are come to pass unto you.
 • Not one thing hath failed thereof.
 • Wherefore remember.
 • Strangers from the covenants of promise.
 • Having no hope, and without God in the world.

 • Ye who sometimes were far off are made nigh by the blood of Christ.

Introduction
Our 52-week annual study into the making of a great and exceeding army takes us to this crucial point in Joshua’s final
charge, when he brought Israel face to face with two solemn truths. First, God had been completely faithful. Not one thing
had failed of all the good things the Lord had spoken concerning them. Every promise, every victory, every step into
inheritance, and every divine intervention testified that God is a covenant-keeping God. Israel could look at their journey
and say, “The Lord has kept His word.” Secondly, Joshua warned them that the same covenant that brought blessing also
carried responsibility. If they transgressed the covenant of the Lord, served other gods, and bowed themselves to them,
the anger of the Lord would be kindled against them. This means covenant is not a casual relationship without
responsibility. Covenant brings privilege, access, protection, and blessing, but covenant also carries terms, accountability,
and consequences when we fail. God is faithful to His promises, but His people must not respond with forgetfulness,
entitlement, rebellion, or careless living.

A covenant relationship with God means that we do not belong to ourselves. We are brought near by grace, redeemed by
blood, and called into a holy relationship with the Lord. In the Old Testament, Israel’s covenant with God shaped their
worship, choices, relationships, family life, justice, and obedience. In the New Testament, believers are made nigh by the
blood of Christ. We are not strangers from the covenants of promise anymore. We now live under the lordship of Christ,
and His blood calls us into love, holiness, and faithful service. Grace does not make covenant lighter; grace makes our
covenant relationship deeper. This is why Paul told the Ephesians to remember. “Wherefore remember,” he said. They
were once without Christ, aliens, strangers from the covenants of promise, having no hope, and without God in the world.
But now, in Christ Jesus, those who were once far off are made nigh by the blood of Christ. Remembering where God
brought us from keeps grace alive. Forgetfulness produces careless choices and strange attachments. A revival army that
forgets mercy may soon begin to despise covenant responsibility.

 ~ 249 ~

Therefore, this week calls each and everyone of us to walk with covenant awareness. We must not do wickedly against the
covenant of the Lord. We must not treat grace as permission to live carelessly. We must remember our journeys, past
deliverances, answered prayers, revival roots, and the mercy of God that brought us near.

Teachings
1. Covenant Relationship with God Must Shape How We Live: Joshua said, “When ye have transgressed the covenant of
the LORD your God.” This statement shows that Israel’s relationship with God was not ordinary. They were not merely a
people who received help from God but were a people in covenant with God. The Lord had chosen them, delivered them,
guided them, preserved them, fought for them, and brought them into an inheritance. In response, they were to love Him,
obey Him, worship Him alone, and walk according to His commandments. A covenant is a binding relationship with solemn
commitment. It carries promises, responsibilities, privileges, and boundaries. In ordinary life, people understand this
principle. Marriage covenant demands faithfulness, honour, responsibility, openness, and exclusive commitment.
Employment contracts carry duties, expectations, and accountability. National citizenship carries rights and
responsibilities. In a deeper and holier way, covenant with God means that the believer belongs to the Lord and must live
with the consciousness of divine ownership.
This is why covenant awareness must moderate what we do. A covenant person cannot live anyhow. A believer cannot
say, “It is my body, my money, my time, my career, my relationship, my phone, my ambition, my marriage, my business,
my children and my life.” No. We are bought with a price. Covenant reminds us that Christ has a claim over our bodies,
thoughts, appetites, relationships, decisions, and future. We must ask, “Does this honour the covenant? Does this please
the Lord? Does this reflect the blood that brought me near?”. “To do wickedly against covenant” according to Daniel 11:32a
as we learned in one of our past programmes last year is to act as if the covenant does not matter. Israel would do wickedly
against covenant if they turned to other gods, mixed with ungodly nations in disobedience, and bowed to what God had
forbidden. Today, a believer can do wickedly against covenant by returning to old sins, joining ungodly partnerships, living
dishonestly, defiling the body, despising fellowship, speaking carelessly, refusing correction, treating his or her spouse in a
negative way, or choosing relationships that pull the heart away from Christ.

2. Covenant Privilege Carries Covenant Responsibility and Accountability: Joshua reminded Israel that not one thing had
failed of all the good things the Lord had spoken. Then, he warned them that if they sin against the covenant, judgement
would also come. This is a serious balance as we learned in our study last week. God’s covenant faithfulness is full and
reliable. He keeps His promises. He fulfills His Word. He does not forget His people, yet covenant blessing does not remove
covenant responsibility. Israel enjoyed covenant privilege. They were delivered from bondage, carried through the
wilderness, given victory over enemies, brought into the land, and given inheritance, but they were not free to live anyhow.
Their privilege required loyalty. Their inheritance required holiness. Their covenant relationship required faithful response.
The same Lord who promised good things also warned against evil things if they despised the covenant. This is very
important for believers today because grace does not remove accountability and mercy does not make sin safe. The blood
of Christ brings us near without any work that we did, but nearness must produce reverence, gratitude, obedience, and
love.

We also see that covenant comes with terms. In the Old Testament, Israel was repeatedly called to love the Lord, obey His
commandments, reject idols, preserve holiness, and teach the next generation. In the New Testament, the believer is called
to abide in Christ, walk in the Spirit, put off the old man, put on the new man, flee sin, love the brethren, serve sincerely,
and follow peace and holiness. We are not saved by works, but the grace that saves us teaches us to deny ungodliness and
worldly lusts. This means that every blessing must be handled with responsibility. If God gives a job, it must not become
an excuse for prayerlessness. If He gives relocation, it must not become a journey into spiritual coldness. If He gives
marriage, it must not become a reason to withdraw from service and holiness. Covenant privilege must produce deeper
obedience, not detachment from God.

3. Forgetfulness Opens the Door to Decline: Paul told the Ephesians, “Wherefore remember.” Joshua also called Israel to
remember that not one thing had failed. These reminders are spiritually powerful. Memory is not just mental recollection
but a covenant discipline. When God’s people remember rightly, they remain humble, grateful, loyal, and obedient. When
they forget, they drift into pride, entitlement, strange attachments, and compromise. Decline begins when covenant is
forgotten. A person who forgets mercy may begin to take grace for granted. A person who forgets answered prayers may
become arrogant after the answer comes. A family that forgets how God helped them may stop building the altar that
sustained them. A minister who forgets the secret place may begin to depend on title, platform, or public recognition. The
Ephesians were told to remember that they were once without Christ, strangers from the covenants of promise, having no

 ~ 250 ~

hope, and without God in the world. This is a deep reminder. Every believer must remember the tragedy of life without
Christ and the mercy of being brought near by His blood. When we remember, worship becomes sincere and holy living
becomes precious.

Dear TACEFites, we must remember our journeys. Remember when God opened doors that seemed impossible. Remember
when He saved souls, restored families, healed broken hearts, provided in difficult seasons, gave admission when you did
not meet the cut-off mark, gave jobs when you did not have the desired qualifications, protected your risky journeys,
supplied needs, gave children, preserved marriages, revived fellowships, and raised helpers. Remember the prayers, tears,
teachings, corrections, and burdens that preserved the vision. A people that remembers well will not become arrogant
because memory protects testimony from becoming pride. In the same vein, forgetfulness can also affect marriage and
family life. A couple may forget the vows they made before God. They may forget how they prayed before the wedding.
They may forget the mercy that brought them together, the counsel they received, and the covenant they entered. When
marital covenant is forgotten, careless friendships, secrecy, emotional distance, hidden spending, harsh words, and
unfaithfulness can enter. Remembering covenant helps a husband and wife return to love, honour, openness, prayer,
forgiveness, and responsibility.

4. Marital Covenant Requires Faithfulness, Boundaries, and the Fear of God: The principle of covenant must also be
understood in marriage. Marriage is not merely emotional attraction, ceremony, family approval, or social status. It is
covenant before God. Malachi speaks strongly about dealing treacherously against the wife of one’s youth and says, “Yet
is she thy companion, and the wife of thy covenant.” This means that marital unfaithfulness is not only an offence against
a spouse but the peak of wickedness against the covenant. A believer must therefore treat marital covenant with great
seriousness. A married person must guard affection, conversations, emotional attachments, phone privacy, social media
behaviour, finances, travel, friendships, and personal boundaries. Covenant faithfulness is not only avoiding the final act
of sexual immorality but refusing the small doors that lead there. There must always be covenant boundaries in all our
dealings. A married man should not cultivate private emotional closeness with another woman in a way that competes
with his wife. A married woman should not keep a secret emotional connection with another man in a way that opens
emotional intimacy. A spouse should not hide chats, delete conversations to avoid accountability, share personal marital
frustrations with someone who may become an emotional replacement, or maintain a friendship that feeds secrecy. These
things may look small, but they can become pathways to betrayal. In the same way, there are certain words, tones, and
expressions a married man or woman must not use carelessly with another person. Words such as “dearest,” “darling,”
“my love,” and other affectionate expressions that carry emotional or romantic meanings should be avoided.

Marital fidelity also requires openness. Husband and wife should learn to talk truthfully, plan together, pray together,
manage finances responsibly, and build trust. Secret spending, hidden debts, secret accounts used for selfish living,
undisclosed commitments, and financial dishonesty can wound covenant trust. A home cannot be strong where there is
secrecy, suspicion, and a divided life. “One flesh” as we learned in our Week 39 study requires shared life, shared
stewardship, and shared direction. Faithfulness also requires guarding speech and comparison. A spouse must not
constantly compare his or her partner with someone outside the marriage. A husband must not speak to another woman
with tenderness, attention, and emotional energy he refuses to give his wife. A wife must not honour another man’s
counsel more than her husband’s place in the home. Marriage must be protected from careless admiration, emotional
wandering, and ungodly counsel.

5. Step-by-Step Applications and Practical Implications
 · Live with covenant awareness: Remind yourself daily that you belong to God and must not live as though your life
 is your own.
 · Let covenant moderate your choices: Before making decisions, ask whether the choice honours Christ and the
 covenant relationship you have with God.
 · Do not do wickedly against the covenant: Reject secret sin, dishonesty, ungodly relationships, careless speech,
 spiritual laziness, and rebellion.
 · Handle privilege responsibly: Do not allow employment, relocation, promotion, marriage, children, business
 growth, ministry enlargement, or comfort to diminish your consecration
 · Reject spiritual entitlement: Do not assume God owes you blessings because of past service, titles, sacrifice, or
 visibility.
 · Let testimony produce humility: Every open door, answered prayers, and fulfilled promise should lead to gratitude,
 holiness, and deeper consecration.

 ~ 251 ~

· Respect marital covenant: Guard your heart, conversations, friendships, phone habits, and emotional
 attachments.
 · Build openness in marriage: Pray together, plan together, discuss finances truthfully, forgive quickly, and avoid
 secret decisions that damage trust.
 · Set clear boundaries: Do not maintain relationships, chats, or emotional closeness that you cannot present openly
 before God and your spouse.
 · Serve God with reverence: Covenant blessing is glorious, but covenant accountability is serious.

Introduction
Our study this week takes us to a point in Joshua’s final address when he gathered Israel at Shechem and brought them
before God. He reminded them of the story of God’s faithfulness from Abraham to the conquest of the Promised land. He
explored how Abraham had been taken out from an idolatrous background, that Israel had been delivered from Egypt, that
the Red Sea had opened before them, that their enemies had been defeated, and that they now lived in lands and cities

 ~ 254 ~

they did not build. Joshua wanted the people to see that their whole journey was mercy in its full manifestation. Their
history was not the story of human greatness but a story of divine deliverance and divine faithfulness.

After rehearsing God’s works, Joshua placed a decision before them: “Choose you this day whom ye will serve.” This is one
of the strongest statements on human choice and covenant responsibility in the Scripture. God had loved them, delivered
them, helped them, warned them, and brought them into inheritance; yet He did not force them to serve Him like
machines. He called them to choose. This reveals a deep truth about the way God deals with man. God created man with
a will. From the Garden of Eden, we see the benevolence of God in giving man room to obey Him willingly. God gave Adam
instruction, placed a boundary before him, warned him, and allowed him to choose obedience or disobedience. Choice is
therefore central to covenant loyalty. Every generation must make its own choice. We cannot live only on the decisions of
our fathers, mothers, leaders, or past generations. We must personally choose the Lord.

The book of Ephesians helps us understand what this choice looks like in the New Testament. Paul says we must no longer
walk as other Gentiles walk. We must put off the old man, be renewed in the spirit of our mind, and put on the new man
created in righteousness and true holiness. Serving God is not anyhow emotion. It is not merely saying, “I love God.” It is
daily sanctified decision-making. It is the will of man being yielded to the will of God. It is saying like Jesus, “Nevertheless
not my will, but thine, be done.” The believer’s will must be surrendered, corrected, renewed, disciplined, and aligned with
the will of God. This week therefore calls TACEFites to make deliberate covenant choices in a compromising generation.
We must reject spiritual mixture. We must put away modern idols such as social media pollution, ungodly relationships,
secret sin, pride, get rick quick money, popularity, self-rule, and careless living. We must also understand that serving God
begins at home. Joshua did not only say, “I will serve the Lord.” He said, “As for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.”
The home is the principal church. God deals deeply with households. Families must become altars of prayer, discipleship,
holiness, and revival.

Teachings
1. God Allows Man to Choose, but Every Choice Carries Covenant Consequence: Joshua said, “Choose you this day whom
ye will serve.” This shows that God does not remove human will. He calls, teaches, warns, helps, and reveals His works, but
He still brings man to the point of decision. From the Garden of Eden, man was created with the capacity to choose. God
placed Adam in a beautiful garden, gave him provision, work, fellowship, and clear instructions. The tree of the knowledge
of good and evil stood as a boundary. Adam could obey God or disobey Him. This was not because God was weak. It was
because God wanted man to love, trust, and obey Him willingly. He made man in His image, not as an animal driven only
by instinct or as a machine controlled without moral responsibility. Human will is part of our dignity, but it also makes us
accountable. The fact that we can choose does not mean every choice is safe. Choice is real, but consequence is also real.
Adam chose wrongly and brought sin and death into human experience. Israel could choose the Lord or choose strange
gods, but each path had consequences.

This is why choice must be guided by covenant. God gives man the ability to choose, but He does not leave man without
truth. He gives commandments, warning, counsel, correction, Scripture, the Holy Spirit, and godly examples. Joshua did
not ask Israel to choose in ignorance. He first rehearsed God’s faithfulness. He showed them what God had done. He
reminded them of deliverance, protection, provision, and inheritance. Their choice was to be made in the light of knowing
who God is and mean to them. The same applies to us. When a believer chooses sin, it is not because God has given no
light. The Word has spoken, the Spirit has warned, the conscience has witnessed, counsel may have come, and examples
may have been seen. God does not force us, but He faithfully places light before us.

Every generation must choose. Every person must choose. Every home must choose. God’s faithfulness does not cancel
our responsibilities. His mercy does not remove decision. His grace empowers us to choose rightly, but it does not choose
for us against our will. Therefore, the question before every TACEFite is clear: whom will you serve?
2. The Believer’s Will Must Be Surrendered, Renewed, and Aligned with God’s Will: The deepest choice a believer must
make is the surrender of the will to God. The human will naturally wants its own way. It wants comfort, control, recognition,
pleasure, success, and personal fulfilment. But the disciple of Christ must learn to bring the will under the government of
God. Jesus showed us the pattern in Gethsemane when He prayed, “Nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done.” This is
the highest form of surrendered obedience. God has a will for His people. There is the perfect will of God, where a person
walks in full alignment with God’s desire, timing, method, and purpose. There are also situations where people press for
what God does not truly desire for their highest spiritual good. Israel once demanded a king like other nations, and God
allowed it, but it came with bad consequences. In our daily lives, a person may insist on a marital choice of a spouse, specific

 ~ 255 ~

job, relocation, business set-up, or ministry opportunity that looks attractive, even when the leading of God is not aligned.
This is permissive allowance and should never be mistaken for perfect approval.

This is why believers must not merely ask, “Can I do this?” We must ask, “Is this the will of God?” We must not only ask,
“Is this opportunity open?” We must ask, “Is God leading me into it?” We must not only ask, “Do I like this person?” We
must ask, “Is this relationship agreeing with the plans and purpose of God for my life?” We must not only ask, “Will this
job pay more?” We must ask, “Does the acceptance of this offer give me peace and will this work preserve my walk with
God, my family altar, my integrity, and my assignment?” The will of God must become the believer’s governing question.
In Ephesians, Paul speaks of understanding what the will of the Lord is. In Romans, he speaks on proving what is that good,
acceptable, and perfect will of God. This shows that the will of God is discerned by a surrendered life and a renewed mind.

Dearly beloved, we must not live by impulse, pressure, emotion, comparison, fear, or appetite. We must bring our will to
the altar and say, “Lord, not my will, but Thine be done.” The safest life is not the life that gets everything it wants but the
life that wants what God wants.

3. Covenant Loyalty Requires Putting Away Idols and Rejecting Spiritual Mixture: Joshua did not only say, “Choose.” He
also said, “Put away the gods.” A true choice for God requires a true rejection of all other alternatives. Israel could not
serve the Lord sincerely while keeping the gods of Egypt or the gods of the Amorites. Covenant loyalty demands separation.
To choose God is to refuse the rival powers, desires, and attachments that compete with Him. An idol is anything that takes
the place of God in the heart. It may not be a carved image. It may be money, popularity, beauty, academic ambition,
career success, comfort, pleasure, reputation, a relationship, a phone, social media, personal control, or even ministry
visibility. Whatever rules the heart, shapes decisions, consumes affection, controls time, and competes with obedience can
become an idol. TACEFites must identify modern idols that are waging war against us within. Social media addiction can
become an idol when it controls attention more than prayer and the Word of God. Ungodly relationships can become idols
when a person would rather displease God than lose that relationship. Money can become an idol when gain becomes
more important than righteousness. Popularity can become an idol when a person wants applause more than holiness.
Academic ambition can become an idol when success is pursued at the expense of God. Comfort can become an idol when
convenience kills sacrifice.

We also see from our text of study that spiritual mixture is dangerous because it allows a person to keep religious activity
while refusing full surrender. A person may combine speaking in tongues with careless living, church attendance with
compromise, service with an unchanged character, prayer meetings with bitterness, worship with pride, ministry with self-
promotion, and public zeal with private disobedience. This mixture weakens the soul because the person feels active, but
the heart is divided. Joshua’s command was decisive: put away the gods. Do not manage them. Do not decorate them. Do
not explain them. Do not hide them. Put them away. Covenant demands decisive separation. If a relationship is pulling you
from God, put it away. If a habit is weakening your conscience, put it away. If entertainment is corrupting your appetite,
put it away. If secret sin is draining your fire, confess and forsake it. Beloved brethren, we must choose Christ without
mixture. The Lord is worthy of a whole heart. The army that will serve Him in a compromising generation must make clean
choices, firm choices, holy choices, and daily choices.

4. Serving God Begins at Home -The Home Is the Principal Church: Joshua declared, “As for me and my house, we will
serve the LORD.” This statement shows that covenant loyalty must not stop with personal confession. It must enter the
home. The home is the principal church because it is the first place where life, character, discipline, love, instruction, and
spiritual culture are formed. Before a person serves publicly, the home is already shaping the heart.

God has always dealt deeply with homes. He said concerning Abraham, “For I know him, that he will command his children
and his household after him.” This means God trusted Abraham not only as an individual but as a household leader.
Abraham would not keep covenant as a private matter but would teach his children and household to keep the way of the
Lord. This is a strong burden for Christian parents, guardians, husbands, wives, and leaders of homes. God wants homes
that serve Him together.

The New Testament also gives beautiful pictures of homes used by God. Aquila and Priscilla took Apollos unto them and
expounded unto him the way of God more perfectly. Their home became a place of discipleship. Philip’s home produced
four daughters who prophesied, showing that the atmosphere of a home can nurture spiritual gifts. The household of
Onesiphorus is remembered with honour because of service and refreshment to God’s servant. These examples show that

 ~ 256 ~

homes can become centres of teaching, hospitality, prophetic life, encouragement, service, and revival. “As for me and my
house” also means collective choice. While each person must personally choose the Lord, the home must create an
atmosphere where choosing God is taught, modelled, encouraged, and protected. Families should set aside family fasting
days, family prayer days, annual family retreats, family thanksgiving days, testimony reviews, or family covenant planning
sessions. These practices are not for religious display, but they help the home remember God, hear God, serve God, and
walk together.

5. Step-by-Step Applications and Practical Implications
 · Accept responsibility for your choices: Do not blame environment, friends, family background, pressure, or culture
 for decisions you must make before God.
 · Choose Christ personally: Do not live only on the faith of parents, leaders, or past generations. Make your own
 covenant decision.
 · Submit your will daily: Pray sincerely, “Lord, not my will, but Thine be done,” especially when your desire conflicts
 with God’s Word.
 · Discern God’s will carefully: Do not mistake an open door for divine approval. Test relationships, jobs, relocations,
 business opportunities, and ministry platforms by divine leading, the Word, prayer, peace, counsel, and spiritual
 fruit.
 · Reject idols deliberately: Identify anything that competes with God in your heart and put it away quickly.
 · Practise daily cross-bearing: Choose obedience when the flesh wants comfort, pleasure, pride, revenge, or
 shortcut.
 · Build a household altar: Let prayer, the Word, worship, and spiritual conversation have a regular place in your
 home.
 · Create family spiritual rhythms: Consider family fasting days, prayer days, annual family retreats, and family
 discipleship conversations.
 · Disciple children intentionally: Teach them the Word, model godliness, guide their friendships, shape their media
 habits, and help them know the Lord personally.
 · Protect the atmosphere of the home: Watch what enters through screens, conversations, visitors, celebrations,
 and daily practices.
 · Make your home useful to God: Let your home become a place of counsel, hospitality, encouragement, teaching,
 prayer, peace, and revival.

Title: We Will Serve the Lord: Turning Confession into Public Faith and Covenant Commitment

Bible Texts: Joshua 24:16-28; Ephesians 6:6-8

Key Extracts from the Bible Texts to Remember and Reflect On
 • God forbid that we should forsake the LORD.
 • Therefore will we also serve the LORD.
 • He is a jealous God.
 • Put away the strange gods which are among you.
 • The LORD our God will we serve, and his voice will we obey.

Introduction
This week brings us to the people’s response to Joshua’s call: “Choose you this day whom ye will serve.” Their answer was
quick, strong, and enthusiastic: “God forbid that we should forsake the LORD, to serve other gods.” They remembered how
God brought them and their fathers out of Egypt, preserved them on the way, drove out their enemies, and gave them the
land. Their confession sounded right, grateful, and spiritual. They declared, “Therefore will we also serve the LORD; for he
is our God.” Yet Joshua did not allow their confession to remain shallow. He challenged the depth of their response. He
said, “Ye cannot serve the LORD: for he is an holy God; he is a jealous God.” Joshua was not discouraging them from serving
God. He was confronting casual Christianity. He was warning them that covenant service is not cheap enthusiasm,
emotional excitement, public identity, or religious language. To serve the Lord requires sincerity, truth, holiness,
obedience, and total allegiance. God is not only a blessing-giving God; He is a holy and jealous God who must not be mixed
with idols.

This is a serious warning for TACEFites in this generation. It is easy to sing worship songs, post Bible verses, attend
fellowships, answer Christian names, identify with a revival movement, and say, “We will serve the Lord,” when things are
convenient. But true discipleship is tested when obedience becomes costly, when the workplace is corrupt, when campus

 ~ 259 ~

culture mocks holiness, when friends are drifting, and when social pressure demands compromise. The Lord is raising a
generation that must not downplay faith in order to blend into a crooked world. The letter of Paul to the Ephesians also
brings the same burden into daily service. Paul says we must not serve with eyeservice as menpleasers, but as servants of
Christ, doing the will of God from the heart. This means true service is not performance that people see or pretense that
we masquerade. It is not religious activity for recognition. Covenant service must be sincere, daily, accountable, and faithful
in both visible and hidden places.

Joshua then set up a stone of witness. This shows that spiritual decisions need remembrance and continuity. TACEFites
therefore need modern stones of witness like personal devotion, journaling of God’s faithfulness, accountability circles,
and covenant reminders that help us remain true to the Lord after emotional moments have passed.

Teachings
1. Guarding Against Casual Christianity: The people answered Joshua with strong words: “God forbid that we should
forsake the LORD.” Their confession was sincere in sound, but Joshua pressed deeper. He said, “Ye cannot serve the LORD:
for he is an holy God; he is a jealous God.” This was a shocking response. Joshua was not rejecting their desire to serve God
but he was destroying casual optimism that was not well thought through. He wanted them to understand that serving
God is a covenant matter, not a light emotional vow. The Lord is holy, and those who serve Him must not treat His name,
His Word, His altar, or His covenant casually. This is very important to understand in context because we live in an age of
casual Christianity, where many people claim to be born again while their choices openly contradict the holiness of God. It
is an age where some believers sing worldly songs freely, enjoy corrupt entertainment in the name of fun, and feed their
hearts with comedy, jokes, music, films, and social media content that gradually weakens reverence for God. It is an age
where some speak loudly in tongue, and still defend going to night clubs, ungodly parties, and careless living as if holiness
no longer matters.

Casual Christianity is also seen when those who carry spiritual titles live contrary to the truth they profess. It is painful
when a school principal who is also a pastor is the one coordinating a school-wide examination malpractice, or when a
believer in the workplace manipulates records and still claims that God understands since he pays his tithes. It is troubling
when so-called spirit-filled workers in pre-marriage courtship are living together when they are not married and they do
not see anything wrong in it. The messages on our altars today no longer condemn sins or point us to eternity and thus
have created this era of casual Christianity where we have a faith that declares loyalty, but avoids sacrifice; sings loudly,
but does not surrender deeply; enjoys God’s blessings, but resists His holiness; and wants divine help without the cost of
living like Jesus. It wants prayers answered, but does not want idols removed. It wants Christian identity without cross-
bearing.

2. Public Faith Must Be Bold and Without Shame: The people did not whisper their decision. They publicly declared, “We
will serve the LORD.” Joshua also told them, “Ye are witnesses against yourselves that ye have chosen you the LORD, to
serve him.” This shows that faith has a public dimension. There are times when a believer must openly declare allegiance
to Christ, not for pride or religious display, but as a witness to truth, covenant, and holy identity. In our contemporary
times, many believers are being pressured into silence. Some downplay their faith so they can blend into workplace culture.
Some hide their convictions on campus to avoid mockery. Some avoid speaking for Christ in professional circles because
they fear being labelled. Some keep quiet when truth is being attacked because they do not want to lose acceptance. Some
appear spiritual in church but become invisible as Christians in the office, classroom, marketplace, neighbourhood, or
online space. This should not be so.

We must understand that we are living witnesses, ambassadors of Christ, apostles in the workplace, on campuses, in
communities, in families, in professional spaces, and in public life. The Lord has not called us to blend into darkness but to
shine as light. Bold public faith must also be matched with a holy life. It is not enough to say, “I am a Christian,” if our
lifestyle denies Christ. A believer who declares Christ but lies at work, cheats in business, joins corrupt practices, keeps
ungodly relationships, comes to work late, or lives secretly in sin weakens the testimony of the gospel. Public profession
without genuine holiness is dangerous. Our lives must speak as clearly as our words. We must raise a generation of bold
faith champions. These are believers who can stand for Christ without shame. They will not be silent when truth is needed.
They will not laugh at sin in order to belong. They will not join careless conversations to look modern. They will not hide
their convictions because of promotion, friendship, relationship, academic posture, or professional ambition. They will be
wise, humble, gracious, and firm. Beloved, let people around you know that you belong to Christ, not only because you say
it, but because your life carries the evidence of His lordship.

 ~ 260 ~

3. True Service Is Sincere, Not Eye-Service: Paul says in Ephesians 6:6, “Not with eyeservice, as menpleasers; but as the
servants of Christ, doing the will of God from the heart.” This speaks directly to the quality of service God expects. True
service is not only what we do when people are watching. It is not public activity or emotional vow, but it is doing the will
of God from the heart. Joshua pressed Israel beyond words to take them from speaking as casual men pleasers to a people
that have weighty understanding of their public confession. The people said, “We will serve the LORD,” but Joshua required
seriousness. He told them to put away strange gods and incline their hearts unto the Lord. This means that service must
be inward before it is outward.

Eye-service is a major danger in kingdom work. It is serving well only when leaders are present. It is arriving early only
when a senior person is watching. It is preparing well only when one will be publicly acknowledged. It is becoming active
only when there is visibility. It is working with excellence only when there is praise. It is spiritual performance without
sincere devotion. Paul says the believer must not serve this way. We serve as servants of Christ because we please God
and not men. We must reject careless service. The Lord’s work deserves punctuality, preparation, humility, accountability,
excellence, and consistency. A prayer leader should pray before leading prayer. A singer should live a life that supports the
song. A treasurer should keep proper records. A worker should not treat God’s assignment as a side issue.

In the same vein, service must also outlive emotion. Many people make vows in charged spiritual moments, but after some
days, the fire reduces. They promise to pray, evangelise, attend fellowship, support the work, live holy, or serve more
faithfully, but the commitment fades when emotion fades. True covenant service is sustained after the music stops, after
the convention ends, after the retreat is over, after the leader has left, after the applause is gone, and after the excitement
reduces. This is why daily faithfulness matters. Beloved, we live to please God and not men, so we must serve because His
work deserves our best.

4. Spiritual Accountability Preserve Covenant Commitment: After Israel declared their choice, Joshua did something very
important. He made a covenant with the people, set them a statute and an ordinance, wrote the words in the book of the
law of God, and set up a great stone under an oak by the sanctuary of the Lord. He said the stone would be a witness, lest
they deny their God or forget their public declaration to serve the Lord. This teaches that spiritual decisions must be
preserved by reminders, accountability, and continuity.

People can forget what they promised in moments of deep conviction. A person can weep at the altar and later return to
old habits. A family can make a commitment to restore prayer and later become busy again. A stone of witness, as
referenced in our study through the story of Joshua, is anything that helps us remember, review, and remain accountable
to covenant decisions we have made with God. Today, we may not set up physical stones under oak trees, but we need
intentional practices that perform the same function. Personal journaling and time-based accountable tracker can help a
believer record God’s dealings, instructions, and commitments. Having a discipler and accountable partner can gently hold
us accountable and family altars can preserve household devotion.

We must understand that accountability is not control but a covenant protection. A believer who has no one who can ask
questions may drift unnoticed. A worker who never reports may become careless. A leader who is not accountable may
become careless. A family that never reviews its spiritual health may become cold. A young believer without discipleship
may be carried away by worldliness. A professional without godly accountability may gradually normalise compromise in
the workplace. We need witnesses that remind us of what we told God. These are not legalistic burdens but are structures
that help conviction become action.

We must also create benchmarks for our walk with the Lord. A person can review media habits weekly to see if they are
drifting into ungodly pollution of the heart. A couple can review their family altar and finances. A worker can ask, “Am I
still serving sincerely, or have I become casual?” Beloved, commitments to God must be remembered, protected, and lived.

5. Step-by-Step Applications and Practical Implications
 · Reject casual Christianity: Do not reduce faith to songs, emotional vows, quotable quotes posting on social media
 or religious language without heart-felt commitments and genuine obedience.
 · Count the cost of discipleship: Serving God requires holiness, surrender, separation, humility, obedience, and total
 allegiance.
 · Put away strange gods: Remove every habit, relationship, ambition, secret sin, and attachment that competes
 with God.

 ~ 261 ~

· Profess Christ boldly: Do not hide your faith in the workplace, campus, professional gatherings, or online spaces.
 · Let your life support your confession: Public faith must be matched with genuine holiness, integrity, and purity.
 · Stand for truth wisely: Be bold without being rude, firm without being proud, and gracious without compromising.
 · Reject eye-service: Serve as unto the Lord, not to impress leaders, gain titles, or receive applause.
 · Serve with excellence: Prepare well, arrive on time, keep records, follow up people, communicate clearly, and treat
 God’s work with honour.
 · Let commitment outlive emotion: Do not abandon vows after the atmosphere changes. Keep obeying after the
 meeting, retreat, or convention ends.
 · Build stones of witness: Use journaling, accountability, mentorship, family altars, spiritual reviews, and
 documented commitments to preserve your decisions.
 · Stay accountable: Allow godly people to ask you questions that help preserve your walk with God.

Ephraim, on the north side of the hill of Gaash. 31 And Israel served the LORD all the days of Joshua, and all the days of the
elders that overlived Joshua, and which had known all the works of the LORD, that he had done for Israel.

Key Extracts from the Bible Texts to Remember and Reflect On
 • Joshua the son of Nun, the servant of the LORD, died.
 • Israel served the LORD all the days of Joshua.
 • And all the days of the elders that over lived Joshua.
 • There arose another generation after them.
 • Which knew not the LORD.
